title_r: Close and Conceptual Replications of Waytz, Dungan, &amp; Young (2013) Studies 2b and 4
abstract_r: Waytz, Dungan, and Young (2013) conducted four studies to test the hypothesis that valuing fairness over loyalty is more strongly associated with willingness to blow the whistle on transgressors than valuing loyalty over fairness. We conducted a close replication of Study 2b, and a conceptual replication of Study 4, using at least 2.5 times the sample sizes of the original studies. Although we replicated Study 2b, we failed to replicate Study 4. We summarize these findings, and speculate as to why we failed to replicate Study 4.

title_r: Revisiting Easterly and Levine (1997): Replication and extension
abstract_r: We replicate and extend the findings from Easterly and Levine (1997) arguing that ethnolinguistic fractionalization is negatively associated with several development indicators. We re-estimate the authors’ original regressions and control for several determinants of development which are correlated with ethnolinguistic fractionalization: a country’s level of partitioning (proportion of the population who belong to ethnic groups split by borders), its colonial history (whether it was formerly a colony) and regional effects (whether it is located in Africa or Latin America). In contrast with Easterly and Levine (1997), we find no evidence that ethnolinguistic fractionalization is associated with any of the development indicators. Rather, for each development indicator where, in comparison with Easterly and Levine (1997), ethnolinguistic fractionalization loses its statistical significance, we find that one of our control variables is statistically significant and takes the expected sign given the correlation between ethnolinguistic fractionalization and the control variable. Our results therefore raise the possibility that the original estimates from Easterly and Levine (1997) suffer from omitted variable bias in that they misattribute the effect of partitioning, colonial history and regional effects to the level of ethnolinguistic fractionalization.

title_r: Productivity premia for many modes of internationalization - A replication study of Békes / Muraközy, Economics Letters (2016)
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate estimation results from Gábor Békés and Balázs Muraközy, Measuring productivity premia with many modes of internationalization, published in Economics Letters (2016). In this paper the authors use comparable firm-level data for seven European countries based on the EFIGE dataset to estimate the productivity premia of firms with various modes of internationalization by several empirical methods to demonstrate how results differ due to the method applied. While the EFIGE data are available free of charge from the web one core variable used by Békés and Muroközy is not, because total factor productivity (tfp) as computed by the authors is based on data from a commercial data base and, therefore, is available for users with a license to this database only. The freely available EFIGE data, however, come with another tfp-variable that can be used instead. In this replication study I use the EFIGE data with this publicly available tfp-variable to replicate (parts of) the estimations of Békés and Muraközy (2016) to see whether their results hold with the widely used public use version of the EFIGE data, too. It turns out that the big picture that emerges from using both productivity measures tends to be very similar. The use of the public use version of the EFIGE data for empirical investigations that deal with productivity, therefore, seems to be feasible.

title_r: Federal minimum wage hikes do reduce teenage employment. A replication study of Bazen & Marimoutou (Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 2002)
abstract_r: In 2002 we published a paper in which we used state space time series methods to analyse the teenage employment-federal minimum wage relationship in the US (Bazen and Marimoutou, 2002). The study used quarterly data for the 46 year period running from 1954 to 1999. We detected a small, negative but statistically significant effect of the federal minimum wage on teenage employment, at a time when some studies were casting doubt on the existence of such an effect. In this note we re-estimate the original model with a further 16 years of data (up to 2015). We find that the model satisfactorily tracks the path of the teenage employment-population ratio over this 60 year period, and yields a consistently negative and statistically significant effect of minimum wages on teenage employment. The conclusion reached is the same as in the original paper, and the elasticity estimates very similar: federal minimum wage hikes lead to a reduction in teenage employment with a short run elasticity of around -0.13. The estimated long run elasticity of between -0.37 and -0.47 is less stable, but is nevertheless negative and statistically significant.

title_r: Re-examining the effect of inoculation messages on anti-vaccine conspiracy attitudes: A conceptual replication of Banas et al (2023)
abstract_r: This is the first study to attempt replication of Banas et al (2023) on inoculation messages. The original experiment demonstrated that inoculation messages could stimulate resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories. However, a gap was identified in this study where exposing participants with inoculation scripts did not stimulate motivational threat, the key component that drives the attitude to defend specific beliefs. In this replication study, we also included conspiracy mentality as the moderator variable that might influence the strength of the association between inoculation scripts and anti-vaccine conspiracy theories. Findings from this study shows that logic-based and fact-based inoculation scripts were perceived differently by participants. Logic-based scripts were perceived as the script that exposed more evidence (fact) compared to fact-based and baseline scripts. Contrary to the original findings, the study failed to replicate the effect of inoculation treatments on anti-vaccine conspiracy attitudes. Instead, prior attitudes on anti-vaccine conspiracy theories, involvement and conspiracy mentality were shown as the significant predictors.

title_r: „Delivering Feedback: Supervisors´ Source Credibility and Communication Competence“ – a replication study (Westerman et al., 2018)
abstract_r: According to Sedlmeier and Renkewitz (2018, S. 615) the replication crisis’ key study is the so-called Reproducibility Project: Psychology (OSC, 2015). It shows that only 36% of the examined studies can be replicated successfully, in other words: with a significant effect like in the original study. For this reason, we are interested in finding out if Westerman et al. (2018) results can be replicated. Prior studies (Ilgen, Fisher, & Taylor, 1979) (Sussman & Sproull, 1999) discovered that feedback is essential to increase employee’s performance. Knowing this, the study researches the influence of valence, synchronicity and channel of feedback on the perception of the supervisor, competence and credibility. Being admired, seen as competent and respected by one’s staff results in the supervisor being seen as more effective (Yukl & Falbe, 1991) and increases their work satisfaction.

abstract_r: This study is a replication and extension of Ulrich (1991). We ask, to what extent is the restorative effect of nature on affective stress moderated by personality? Additionally, only a subset of the measures collected will be analyzed; our project is focused on measures of personality and psychological restoration (as captured by self-report scales of affective stress), and therefore excludes physiological data collected). title_r: Conceptual replication of Hyman & Sheatsley (1950) Study 2
abstract_r: The overarching aim of this research is to test if induced reciprocity can promote peoples acceptance of a climate change mitigation law, targeting reduced plastics. I will test this using the reciprocity paradigm as developed and tested by Hyman & Sheatsley (1950). In the original study, American participants answered two questions: 1) if “communist countries should allow American reporters in and allow them to report the news back to American papers” and 2) if “America should allow communist reporters into the United States and allow them to report back to their papers”. Participants reported more support for allowing communist reporters when that question was asked after the question about allowing American reporters. This finding was replicated by Klein et a., (2014), with a slight modification/specification of country (North Korea). The rationale is that “When confronted with a decision about allowing or denying the same behavior to an ingroup and outgroup, people may feel an obligation to reciprocity, or consistency in their evaluation of the behaviors“ (Klein et al., 2014). Hence, Hyman & Sheatsley’s experimental setup In this research I will test if the reciprocity effect can be replicated for acceptance of 1) a carbon tax, 2) raised fuel prices, and 3) a meat tax. I will randomize the order so that half of the participants will state their attitudes to the tax in China first, and the other half will state their attitudes to the tax in USA. 1) I expect that US-Americans will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a tax of higher fuel prices in China than in their home country. 2) I hypothesize that US-Americans will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a tax or raised fuel prices in their home country when this rating is done after rating the tax of raised prices in China compare to when the rating is done before rating the tax or raised prices in China. Hypotheses 1) I expect that US-Americans will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a carbon plastic, a meat tax or raised prices on fuel in China than in their home country. 2) I hypothesize that US-Americans will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a tax or raised prices in their home country when this rating is done after the rating in China compare to when the rating is done before the rating in China. Study type/design Participants located in USA will be recruited via Amazons Mechanical Turk (MTurk) and randomized to answer the question about acceptance of a tax or prices in 1) their home country and 2) in China. Hence, I will randomize the order so that half of the participants will state their acceptance for the tax in China first, and the other half will state their attitudes to the tax in their home country first. Moreover, participants will be randomized to answer on of the issues, either 1) a carbon tax, 2) a meat tax, or 3) raised prices on fuel.

title_r: What makes us lie: An online conceptual replication of Zhong, Bohns, and Gino (2010)
abstract_r: A previous study showed that darkness could increase fraud by creating a sense of “illusory anonymity” that lets individuals expect that they would be difficult to be perceived by others (Zhong et al., 2010). However, according to the conceptual metaphor theory (CMT), the alternative possibility that the results were caused by the White-Black metaphor could not be denied. In our earlier studies (Liu & Yamada, 2020a, 2020b), we did not find that the color metaphor factors (either the color of the screen background or the color of the team that participants belong to) could affect fraud. Additionally, we obtained a zero effect of colors by using two one-sided tests (TOST) in both the two studies. Before we conclude that the White-Black metaphor cannot influence fraud, we would like to confirm that fraud in the online task we used can be influenced by the room brightness employed by Zhong et al. In the present study, we try to let participants change the room brightness themselves (turning lights on/off in the night) by instructions and check fraud under different brightness conditions. It is foreseeable that some participants will not follow the instructions. However, if we can obtain an effect size to some degree (i.e. not a zero effect), we would conclude that the White-Black metaphor could not influence fraud, but the illusory anonymity account can be accepted.

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r: In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through three studies--one direct replication, one extension, and a meta-analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. title_r: A registered replication of study 2 in Furukawa et al. (2016 | JJSP)
abstract_r: Background: Imagine we are going to distribute limited resources to three persons (self, a friend (A), and a friend (B)). When we feel guilt to the friend (A), we provide more resources (e.g., time, money) to this person (De Hooge, Nelissen, Breugelmans, & Zeelenberg, 2011; Furukawa, Nakashima, & Morinaga, 2016; Rebega, Benga, & Miclea, 2014). The question is where the additional resources come from (i.e., self or a friend (B)). De Hooge et al. (2011) showed that people took these resources from a friend (B), not themselves. In contrast, Rebega et al. (2014) and Furukawa et al. (2016) reported that when people felt guilt, they reduced their own resources and increased the resources to the friend (A). Furukawa et al. (2016) also showed that for lower relational mobility individuals, feelings of guilt increased the resources to the friend (A) and decreased the resources to themselves. But for higher relational mobility individuals, the feelings of guilt did not influence money distribution. Aim: I will examine the replicability of study 2 in Furukawa et al. (2016) written above.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Site. A pre-registered replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we will conduct an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk.

title_r: Replicating and extending Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Exp. 2)
abstract_r: Introduction: Framing refers to how information is presented and structured in communication (Goffman, 1974)—what aspects are emphasized, how issues are categorized, and what language choices are made. Linguistic framing can significantly shape perception, emotion, and behavior, particularly in public discourse. Even minor changes in wording can influence people's interpretations and decisions, especially when those changes involve metaphorical language (Brugman et al., 2019; Flusberg et al., 2024). A seminal study by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011) demonstrated that metaphorical frames can guide reasoning about social issues. In their experiments, participants were presented with a description of a crime problem framed either as a "beast preying on the city" or a "virus infecting the city." The type of metaphor affected participants' policy preferences: the "beast" metaphor led to more punitive, enforcement-focused solutions, while the "virus" metaphor elicited support for reform-oriented interventions. Notably, participants were often unaware of the metaphor’s influence on their thinking. However, as Flusberg et al. (2024) point out, the effects of metaphorical framing should not be assumed to generalize across cultures, historical periods, or languages. Moreover, in light of the ongoing replication crisis in psychology, it is essential to test the robustness of such findings (Camerer et al., 2018). Several replication attempts have yielded mixed results. For instance, Christmann and Göhring (2016) observed similar effects in a German-speaking sample, although some methodological differences were present. In contrast, Steen et al. (2013), who included additional controls, found no significant metaphor effects—raising questions about the specific conditions under which metaphorical framing is effective. Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015) later responded with further analyses, clarifying aspects of the original findings and addressing key criticisms. The present study aims to contribute to this body of research by replicating and extending the original Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Exp. 2) work. It investigates not only whether metaphorical framing reliably influences reasoning about crime, but also whether this effect generalizes across different populations or is moderated by some individual or contextual variables. By addressing inconsistencies in prior replication efforts, this study seeks to offer a more comprehensive understanding of how metaphor shapes human reasoning about complex societal issues. Methods Ethics statement The study will adhere to the ethical standards for research with human participants and has received approval from the Ethics Committee at the University of Granada with the approval number: 3788/CEIH/2023. Informed consent will be obtained from all participants before they take part in the study, and all participant data will be anonymous. Participants For this experiment, we used G*Power version 3.1.9.7 to estimate the sample size required for a 2 X 2 chi-squared test with 1 degree of freedom, alpha of .05, and power of 90%. We selected a power of 90% rather than 80%, as recommended by Lakens (2022), to reduce the risk of Type II errors in replication studies. The first two free-response format questions in this study were designed to closely follow Experiment 2 of Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011), who reported an effect size of .209 (Cohen’s w). However, since we also included a binary forced-choice question (see “Materials and procedure” section), we preferred to use the more conservative effect size (Cohen’s w = .14) reported by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015). This effect size corresponds to the pooled data from their first experiment and Experiment 4 of Steen et al.’s (2014), in which participants (N = 876) were presented with a five options forced-choice question. We chose not to use the effect size from the binary forced-choice question in Thibodeau and Boroditsky’s (2015) second experiment, as it included the term “patrols” as a response option and it has already been demonstrated that the role of a police officer is ambiguous (Thibodeau & Boroditsky, 2011). As a result, we established the minimum usable sample size in 537 participants. As our experiment is online and we expect to have 25% attrition rate after applying exclusion criteria (see below), we will recruit 672 participants. Additional participants may be recruited until reaching the minimum sample size of N = 672. Participants will be recruited through two platforms: Prolific (https://www.prolific.com) and the SONA platform of the Mind, Brain and Behavior Research Center of the University of Granada (https://ugr-cimcyc.sona-systems.com). Both platforms ensure the anonymity of the participants. Inclusion criteria for participation are as follows: • Participants must be 18 years old or older. • Participants must be native Spanish speakers and living in Spain, to reduce the risk of language proficiency and culture becoming a confounding factor (for a review, see Flusberg et al., 2024). Exclusion Criteria Additionally, we will exclude: • Participants who participate in the study more than once. • Participants who complete the survey in an amount of time deemed too long (more than 10 minutes) or short (less than 1 minute), as this may indicate a lack of engagement with the task. • Participants who do not respond correctly to a verification question included at the end of the survey. • Participants who do not complete all required questions, provide responses that are unintelligible, impossible to code in one of the two categories (“enforce” or “reform”, see below) or irrelevant. Materials and procedure The questionnaire will be programmed and run on the LimeSurvey platform of the University of Granada. The procedure will closely replicate that of Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011, Experiment 2). Participants will be redirected from Prolific or SONA to the LimeSurvey questionnaire. After providing informed consent, participants will be randomly assigned to either the "crime-as-beast" or "crime-as-virus" condition (see below). They will then be instructed to read a short news report followed by short questions on its content. The short news report will be preceded by the following warning: “Lee el texto con atención porque cuando pases a la siguiente pantalla, ya no podrás volver a él.” [Read the text carefully because once you move to the next screen, you will not be able to go back to it.]. The short news report will be a text describing the crime problem in the fictional city of Carballa. This text and the three questions presented afterwards have been directly translated into Spanish from the materials used in the original study by Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011). The original English text was translated into Spanish using a multi-step process to ensure accuracy and cultural appropriateness. Firstly, two bilingual speakers (MO and JPGS) of English and Spanish independently translated the text into Spanish. A third bilingual speaker of English and native Spanish speaker (JS) reviewed both translations and created a single revised version. The final Spanish translation was then reviewed and approved by an expert in English philology (JVM). Finally, an English native speaker who is also a Spanish-English bilingual and was unaware of the topic of this study when translating the texts (AA), carried out a backward translation. All the authors of this study agreed that the original and the backward translated text were conceptually similar. This rigorous translation process aims at minimizing any potential confounding effects due to translation. All materials produced during this translation process can be found in the data repository. The finalized text describing the crime problem in the fictional city of Carballa that participants will read is: “El crimen es un/a {bestia/virus} que asola la ciudad de Carballa. Hasta hace cinco años, Carballa estaba en buen estado, sin vulnerabilidades evidentes. Desafortunadamente, en los últimos cinco años, las defensas de la ciudad se han debilitado y la ciudad ha sucumbido al crimen. Actualmente hay más de 55.000 incidentes delictivos al año – con un aumento de más de 10.000 por año. Hay una preocupación de que, si la ciudad no recupera su fortaleza pronto, puedan comenzar a desarrollarse problemas aún más graves.” [Crime is a {beast/virus} ravaging the city of Carballa. Five years ago Carballa was in good shape, with no obvious vulnerabilities. Unfortunately, in the past five years the city’s defense systems have weakened, and the city has succumbed to crime. Today, there are more than 55,000 criminal incidents a year – up more than 10,000 per year. There is a worry that if the city does not regain its strength soon, even more serious problems may start to develop.] After reading the text, participants will press a button to continue, and they will be unable to go back to the previous screen. Each question will be presented in a new screen and the text describing crime in Carballa will be absent for the three first questions, but present for the fourth question: - Question 1: “En tu opinión, ¿qué debería hacer Carballa para reducir el crimen?” [In your opinion what does Carballa need to do to reduce crime?] - Question 2: “¿Cuál es el papel que debe cumplir un agente de policía en Carballa?” [What is the role of a police officer in Carballa?] - Question 3: "Si tuvieras que elegir entre las dos siguientes opciones, ¿qué debería hacer Carballa para reducir el crimen? o Usar medidas punitivas (Es decir, centrarse en las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad y/o proponiendo modificaciones del sistema de justicia penal, como por ejemplo 'imponer penas más severas' o 'construir más cárceles'.) or o Usar medidas preventivas (Es decir, investigar las causas subyacentes y/o proponiendo reformas sociales, como por ejemplo 'arreglar la economía', 'mejorar la educación' o 'proporcionar atención

title_r: Affect labelling with words and emojis: a replication and extension of Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021)
abstract_r: A body of previous literature mostly gives the message that affect labelling downregulates negative emotions, and many of the proposed mechanisms are in line with distancing-related processes. For instance, the distraction account suggests affect labelling reduces negative emotions because the task itself diverts people’s attention away from the aversive stimuli (images/videos in most cases); the symbolic conversion account indicates that it is the conversion between information modalities (from images to language mostly) that helps create psychological distancing from the original stimuli and reduces its emotional impact. Nevertheless, in the series of studies conducted by Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021), affect labelling has been found to consistently increase positive emotion intensity but showed no effect on negative emotions. Similarly, Xi and Vinson (2022 & 2023, in preparation) found that affect labelling enhanced positive emotional responses to positively-valenced sentences (thus, a situation in which symbolic conversion did not take place) but the effect on negative emotions appeared unstable. In addition, Xi and Vinson (2023, in preparation) included a condition in which participants were asked to use emojis, rather than words for affect labelling. Effects of emoji labelling (putting feelings into emojis) did not differ from the traditional affect labelling task (emotion word labelling/putting feelings into words) in terms of their effects on emotion intensity. These findings together challenge the symbolic conversion account: in these studies affect labelling influenced emotional responses whether there was symbolic conversion or not, and this opposite direction of effect (increased emotions for positive stimuli) does not align with the distancing process as indicated by distraction or symbolic conversion accounts. In order to gain a better understanding of the effects and mechanisms of affect labelling, and to fully test the symbolic conversion account, we need to test whether effects of affect labelling can be observed in circumstances where conversion does not take place, and linguistic labels are not used: affect labelling for image stimuli, using emotional emojis instead of words. To do this, our first step is to replicate Vlasenko, Rogers and Waugh (2021) (Experiment 1) with timing modifications as in Xi & Vinson (2023, in prep) and additionally testing whether the same pattern persists when we compare the effects of emotion word labelling and emoji labelling on emotional responses to affective images (Experiment 2), before we firmly reject the symbolic conversion account. We also take into consideration the individual difference factor of trait worry in both Experiments to better understand how labelling affects emotion-related processes.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000, Study 2) Using Temperature Anchoring and a Season-Related LDT (2)
abstract_r: This study conceptually replicates Study 2 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. According to SAM, anchoring occurs through the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge, driven by hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In the original study, participants first completed a standard comparative anchoring task (judging whether the average price of a new car was higher or lower than U.S. $11,000 or $22,000), followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). After the LDT, they estimated the average price of a new car in an absolute judgment task. The results supported SAM, demonstrating a significant interaction between anchor condition and word type in the LDT. In the present study, we conducted a conceptual replication of this design, using an anchoring task involving temperature estimates and an LDT employing season-related words (summer- and winter-related words). Data collection was completed on June 10, 2025 (Japan Standard Time). As of this preregistration, the data have not yet been accessed or analyzed. This preregistration specifies the planned analysis procedures. The majority of the experimental procedures and hypotheses follow Mussweiler and Strack (2000) and our previous study (https://osf.io/hcbxu, https://osf.io/wgm94, https://osf.io/57cty).

title_r: Gabriel_JournAppPsych_2011_egX9 - Hickman - Direct Replication - 4z88
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Gabriel et al (2011) is: The impact of task accomplishment satisfaction on changes in daily affect is larger for direct care nursing tasks than for indirect care nursing tasks. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “[W]e expected that task accomplishment satisfaction (or lack thereof) for these tasks would have stronger effects on changes in affect than would task accomplishment satisfaction for indirect care tasks.” The claim was tested using hierarchical linear modeling with post-shift negative affect as the dependent variable, indirect care task satisfaction and direct care task satisfaction as level 1 predictors, with pre-shift negative affect included as Level 1 covariates. At Level 2, the model included ratings of nurse-physician relationship quality, psychological resilience, and the two-way interactions between these two predictors and the two task satisfaction measures. title_r: Dataset for: Wiswede, D., & Ruesseler, J. (2021). Intermodal priming of cognitive conflict? A failed replication of Mager et al. (2009). Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.
abstract_r: Codebook for: Wiswede, D., & Ruesseler, J. (2021). Intermodal priming of cognitive conflict? A failed replication of Mager et al. (2009). Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. The present study was conducted to verify a promising experimental setup from another research group which demonstrated an inversed Stroop-effect (much faster responses for incongruent relative to congruent Stroop trials) following a mismatching tone. In the matching condition, which was an almost exact replication of the original study, participants were required to indicate whether word colour and word meaning were matching, whereas in the response conflict condition, instruction was the same as in a classical Stroop task and required the participants to respond to the word colour. As in the original study, each trial was preceded by a sine tone which was deviant in pitch in 20% of the trials. Results: The main result was that the Stroop effect was not inversed after deviant tones, neither under the matching task instruction nor under the response conflict task instruction. The Stroop effect was unaffected by the previous “conceptual mismatch”. Conclusion: The current study failed to replicate the astonishing concept of “conflict priming” reported in previous work and does not open the doors for a new window on sequences of conflicts. Nevertheless, the failed replication is valuable for future research, since it demonstrated that “Conflict Priming” as a facilitation of processing of conflict trials following deviant tones, does not exist.

title_r: Profit motives, environmental motives, and perceived corporate greenwashing revisited: A replication and extension of de Vries et al. (2015)
abstract_r: As the climate change crisis has become more evident, a growing number of businesses and organizations have gotten involved in sustainability efforts. But not all corporate sustainability efforts are applauded: sometimes the public accuses companies of greenwashing, i.e., overstating the extent to which the company is environmentally friendly. There is little research on the factors that influence perceived greenwashing amongst the public. Here, we report a replication and extension of one of the few studies of this topic, Experiment 2 in de Vries et al. (2015, https://doi.org/10.1002/csr.1327). The original study found that people perceived more greenwashing when an oil company communicated an environmental motive for a sustainability investment (carbon capture and storage), as opposed to a profit motive, d = 0.98 [0.37, 1.59]. The present pre-registered replication (n = 516) did not find support for this effect, with very little difference in perceived greenwashing depending on communicated motive, d = -0.09 [-0.38, 0.21]. As extensions, we included a condition where a mixed motive (both environment and profits) was communicated, tested the effect using a different type of company than the original, included a measure of general attitudes to the company in addition to perceived greenwashing, and included measures of individual differences in attitudes towards corporate social responsibility and belief in climate change. The most noteworthy exploratory finding was that attitudes were more positive when an environmental or a mixed motive was communicated rather than a profit motive.

title_r: The effect of order-label training on generalization, a replication study of Ramscar et al., (2010)
abstract_r: In this preregistration we describe a detailed plan to replicate Ramscar et al. (2010) paper about the effect of the order of presentation of feature-label pair association on symbolic learning. We attempt an exact replication of the original study except (1) that the participants are recruited and tested online and (2) a further task is added at the end of the experiment. We will also looking at the data from the original two test tasks separately, as well as combined, in order to further elucidate the nature of these tasks. The experiment is a word learning experiment in which participants learn associations between pictures of novel objects and written labels (e.g. wug). Critically, there are two learning-conditions – in the feature-label condition pictures are presented before labels, in the feature-label condition labels are presented before pictures. In both conditions there are three labels which are associated with six classes of fribbles, with each subcategory of fribbles having a set of discriminating features (Figure 1, circled features). However, critically, 1.1. 2.1 and 3.1 (high-frequency items) are encountered three times as often as subcategories 1.2 2.2 and 3.2 (low frequency items) (there is also a fourth “easy” control category of blue fribbles). Due to the way that body shape is shared across subcategories, it can be seen that for low frequency items, body shape is a high salience feature which has been strong associated with an alternative label to the correct label. According to discriminative learning theory, participants in the feature-label condition should be better able to ignore shape and learn the discriminating features which determine which labels should be used. Following Ramscar et al., (2010) after exposure to the language, we include 2AFC tests testing generalization where participants had to choose which of four novel fribbles went with a label/ which of four labels went with a novel fribble. We also follow this with a new contingency judgment task that links the theoretical predictions about the resulting learning weights from error-driven learning, to the participants’ ratings behaviour of the feature-label association plausibility. The participants’ judgment is predicted to roughly reflect the learning weights of the model when learning is completed. We expect that this pre-registration will establish (1) a robust paradigm that can be used as starting point for future studies online, (2) a sensitive task capturing estimates of learning weights across participants, providing a direct comparison to the predictions based on the RW model (Rescorla, Wagner, and others (1972)). We base our predictions on Ramscar et al., (2010), although our predicted effect sizes are based on data from an unpublished study that replicates Ramscar et al., (2010) effects* , and – for the additional contingency task – from our own pilot data. Our primary research question is as follows: Does Feature-Label-Ordering affect discrimination learning? In particular, when participants are confronted with novel exemplars, is there an advantage in terms of generalization of predictive cues for feature-label over label-feature in the low frequency condition? ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ * The reason we use this data rather than from the published study is that we have it available in a format where it is possible to run the necessary logistic mixed effect models to obtain our predicted effects

title_r: No Evidence that Experiencing Physical Warmth Promotes Interpersonal Warmth: Two Failures to Replicate Williams and Bargh (2008)
abstract_r: Williams and Bargh (2008) reported that holding a hot cup of coffee caused participants to judge a person’s personality as warmer, and that holding a therapeutic heat pad caused participants to choose rewards for other people rather than for themselves. These experiments featured large effects (r = .28 and .31), small sample sizes (41 and 53 participants), and barely statistically significant results. We attempted to replicate both experiments in field settings with more than triple the sample sizes (128 and 177) and double-blind procedures, but found near-zero effects (r = –.03 and .02). In both cases, Bayesian analyses suggest there is substantially more evidence for the null hypothesis of no effect than for the original physical warmth priming hypothesis.

title_r: Fork of The effect of order-label training on generalization, a replication study of Ramscar et al., (2010)
abstract_r: We describe a second attempt to replicate Ramscar et al. (2010) paper about the effect of the order of presentation of feature-label pair association on symbolic learning. We already have conducted one experiment however our key hypothesis concerning a potential difference between learning conditions wasn’t there. We found evidence for the null for an overall benefit of LF over HF (i.e. for the main effect) as well as evidence for the null for same difference for low frequency items only (where our prediction is strongest). Evidence for an interaction between frequency and learning conditions was also ambiguous. One challenge for conducting experiments online is that the resolution and size of the display are unknown, prohibiting control of the size of stimuli presented to participants. We acknowledge that this issue might be one potential explanation for these pattern of results. In addition to this, we have realised that the stimuli presented were not of the same dimension as in the original Ramscar et al., 2010 paper – Stimuli in this experiment were smaller. We hypothesize that these factors in combination with the brief presentation (around 175ms) might have impacted our participants ability to visually detect the fribble’s inner features and therefore making it impossible to isolate the predictive from irrelevant features which is a prerequite of seeing the predicted effects. All the details of this second replication attempt will be exactly as pre-registered in the main project except for three changes: (1) Fixed stimuli size, (2) Stopping rule and (3) Data collection procedures

title_r: Conceptual replication of Hyman & Sheatsley (1950)
abstract_r: The overarching aim of this research is to test if induced reciprocity can promote peoples acceptance of a climate change mitigation law, targeting reduced plastics. I will test this using the reciprocity paradigm as developed and tested by Hyman & Sheatsley (1950). In the original study, American participants answered two questions: 1) if “communist countries should allow American reporters in and allow them to report the news back to American papers” and 2) if “America should allow communist reporters into the United States and allow them to report back to their papers”. Participants reported more support for allowing communist reporters when that question was asked after the question about allowing American reporters. This finding was replicated by Klein et a., (2014), with a slight modification/specification of country (North Korea). The rationale is that “When confronted with a decision about allowing or denying the same behavior to an ingroup and outgroup, people may feel an obligation to reciprocity, or consistency in their evaluation of the behaviors“ (Klein et al., 2014). Hence, Hyman & Sheatsley’s experimental setup In this research I will test if the reciprocity effect can be replicated for acceptance of a tax on plastics in 1.1) USA, 1.2) India, and 1.3) UK versus 2.1) China. I will randomize the order so that half of the participants will state their attitudes to the tax in China first, and the other half will state their attitudes to the tax in USA, India, or UK first. 1) I expect that US-Americans, Indians, or Britons, will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a plastic tax in China than in their home country. 2) I hypothesize that US-Americans, Indians, or Britons will express stronger positive attitudes towards adding a plastic tax in their home country when this rating is done after rating the tax in China compare to when the rating is done before rating the tax in China.

title_r: Effect of Losses and Gains on Working Memory Performance: A replication and extension of Massar et al 2020 Front Hum Neurosci (effort-based decision making and performance)
abstract_r: Human decision-making is often driven by a motivation to avoid losses than to pursue gains, a phenomenon called loss aversion. Based on our previously published study (Massar et al., 2020, Exp3), loss incentives motivated participants more than gains in working memory performance at the highest level of N-back we tested, the 4-Back. We aim to replicate and extend the study with a larger sample size to verify whether results still hold. Specifically, we discovered that loss incentives motivated performance more than the gains incentive on the 4-back task, and we wish to verify this finding with a larger sample size. This finding had surprised us, considering that there have been no consistent results on this matter in the literature (e.g. Carsten et al 2019; Belayachi et a. 2015). Even in our previously published study, there was no consistent finding because losses did not motivate performance in the motivated vigilance task (Massar et al 2020, Exp1&2), as losses did in the N-back task, so we aim to test whether our previous findings on the working memory task are valid. Furthermore, as an innovative addition, we intend on incorporating pupillometry as a measure of physiological effort into our N-back study design so that we can test whether pupil diameter changes during loss versus gain conditions.

title_r: Acquiring false information from narrative fictions: A conceptual replication and extension of Appel & Richter (2007)
abstract_r: Within the planned study, narrative fictions are understood as written stories that primarily deal with non-real events, objects and persons, whereby this limited reference to reality is both intended by the author and recognized by the recipients (e.g., Gertken & Köppe, 2009). Although people often encounter narrative fictions in everyday life, relatively little empirical research has been conducted on their psychological effects and the underlying mechanisms. Existing studies show that factually incorrect information embedded in narrative fictions can cause substantial changes in readers' beliefs despite the known limited reference to reality (e.g., Rapp et al., 2014). In one of the few studies on the topic that includes more than one measurement point, Appel and Richter (2007) demonstrated that such changes in belief can even increase over time – a phenomenon that corresponds to an absolute sleeper effect. Here, 81 participants recruited through a university (mostly students) read either a fictional story that contained both true and false claims about real-world issues, or a control story. There were great short-term persuasion effects from the false information; these effects were even greater in a group with a 2-week measurement delay. Belief certainty (i.e., how sure the readers were of their beliefs) was reduced immediately after reading, but returned to the baseline level after 2 weeks. The pattern of findings was interpreted in such a way that beliefs acquired through reading fictional narratives are integrated into world knowledge. The aim of the planned experiment is a conceptual replication and extension of this study. The experiment is planned to be identical to the original study except for two major differences: first, the participants will not be recruited at a university only in order that the generalizability of findings extends to a broader population; secondly, different reading stimuli (based on an excerpt from Homer's Odyssey) will be used than in Appel and Richter (2007). This will help clarify whether the findings occur independently of this specific textual material.

title_r: A Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000) Study 1
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication of Study 1 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. SAM explains anchoring as the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge through hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In their study, participants completed a standard anchoring task (estimating Germany’s mean annual temperature, with anchors set at either 5 or 20 degrees) followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). The results supported SAM, showing faster responses to winter words in the LDT under the low-anchor condition. Our study is a conceptual replication of their study, conducted online to assess the reproducibility of the effect.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: The effect of prompts on the sharing of news headlines in social media: a pre-registered replication study of Capraro and Celadin (2023).
abstract_r: Misinformation, such as fake news and conspiracy theories, is contaminated among information on the internet. Specifically, research has found that 40% of information in the medical domain from the internet has been found to be misinformation (Waszak et al., 2018). Today, various studies are being conducted to help prevent the spread of such misinformation. For example, increasing the sharing of accurate information by having people assess the accuracy of another article before a sharing task (Pennycook et al., 2020) or giving simple online literacy tips can reduce the sharing of misinformation (Epstein et al., 2021). Such methods of manipulating sharing on SNSs have been demonstrated. However, while misinformation can be reduced, it is challenging to encourage the sharing of correct information. Capraro and Celadin (2023) found that adding a short sentence (prompt) to the 'share' option presented in the sharing task increased the sharing of correct information and reduced the sharing of misinformation. However, the participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, resulting in a biased sample. Therefore, to confirm the generalizability of Capraro and Celadin’s (2023) findings, the present study will conduct a replication study using a different sample to examine the viability of a method that promotes sharing of correct information and reduces the sharing of misinformation.

title_r: Effect of Post-Learning Wakeful Rest breaks and Social Media Use on Retention: A Replication and Extension of Martini et al., 2020
abstract_r: How people engage with their environments after learning something can change how well the newly learned information “sticks” in long term memory. The goal of this proposed study is to replicate past findings that found that social media use after learning harms learning compared to a wakeful rest period. In these wakeful rest periods, participants close their eyes and lay their head down, a process that lowers the amount of stimuli the brain needs to process, potentially freeing up cognitive resources to dedicate to consolidating newly learned material. While researchers have found social media harms learning compared to wakeful rest, this line of research did not use an active control condition (e.g. spatial tasks) that can help tease out whether an effect of social media vs. wakeful rest is due to social media being harmful, or wakeful rest being beneficial. Additionally, these previous studies are statistically underpowered, not preregistered, and conducted with older social media (circa 2015) before short form videos became popular. The purpose of this study is to replicate and expand upon this research. Specifically, this study will ask participants to memorize English-Icelandic word pairs. Additionally, we will look at important individual differences such as stress, emotion, and neurodivergent tendencies (ADHD and Autism like tendencies, non-official diagnoses) and how they might interact with how students are impacted by social media use or wakeful rest after learning. Retention within this study will be assessed through free-recall and recognition tasks.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Weissman et al. (2020, Experiment 2)
abstract_r: The congruency sequence effect (CSE) refers to a smaller congruency effect after incongruent trials than after congruent trials. Robust CSEs often appear in the prime-probe task, wherein an initial prime (usually a distractor) precedes a subsequent probe (usually a target). Recent findings indicate a CSE appears in mean probe reaction time (RT) and mean probe error rate (ER), however, even when participants respond to both the initial prime and the subsequent probe, such that there are no distractors (Grant & Weissman, 2019; Weissman, 2019; Weissman et al., 2017). Furthermore, a CSE appears in this “modified prime-probe task” even when subjects respond to the prime and probe in each trial using fingers on different hands (Weissman, Grant, and Jones, 2020). These findings indicate that “response-general” control processes (i.e., control processes that can modulate multiple responses) give rise to the CSE. However, several questions remain unanswered about the nature of response-general control processes.

title_r: Does priming analytic thinking reduce conspiracy beliefs? High-powered preregistered replications of Study 2 and Study 4 from Swami et al. (2014)
abstract_r: Analytic thinking is reliably associated with lower belief in conspiracy theories. However, evidence for whether increasing analytic thinking can reduce belief in conspiracies is sparse. As an exception to this, Swami et al. (2014) showed that priming analytical thinking through a verbal fluency task (i.e., scrambled sentence task) or a processing fluency manipulation (i.e., difficult-to-read fonts) reduces belief in conspiracy theories. While these studies are the most cited experimental research on reducing belief in conspiracy theories, they are yet to be replicated. To probe the robustness of these effects, we propose two preregistered, highly powered (i.e., 95%) direct replications of two of the original studies (i.e., Studies 2 and 4). As such, the proposed studies have the potential to contribute to the robustness of experimental research on belief in conspiracies, as well as to inform urgently needed insights on ways to reduce it.

title_r: Ambivalence of Neutral Ratings: A conceptual Replication of Anvari et al. (2023) Regarding Affective Norms for German Sentiment Terms Using Different Response Formats
abstract_r: Our study is based on the work of Anvari, Bachmann, Sanchez-Burks, and Schneider (2023). They examine the Affective Norms for English Words (ANEW) (Bradley, M. M., & Lang, P. J., 1999; 2010) database and, in particular, the question of whether words that are classified as 'neutral' on a bipolar valence scale can actually in some cases be ambivalent. The ANEW provides normative ratings for English words on bipolar scales of valence (emotional positivity vs. negativity) and arousal (degree of activation or deactivation) and is often used in psychological studies to select stimuli that elicit specific affective responses. Valence measures how positive or negative a word feels, while arousal measures how stimulating or calming it is. "Neutral" words tend to fall in the middle of a bipolar valence scale, which theoretically indicates a lack of positive or negative emotional activation. The ambivalent nature of words can be reflected in a neutral response on a valence scale when the answer represents a compromise between positive and negative emotional states. However, the distinction between true neutrality and ambivalence is crucial in emotion research. True neutrality implies the absence of emotional responses, while ambivalence involves the simultaneous experience of both positive and negative reactions. This distinction is important for studies that aim to use "neutral" stimuli as a baseline for non-emotional responses, as ambivalent words may introduce confounding emotional elements. Anvari et al. (2023) employed three methods to assess ambivalence: subjective ambivalence ratings, objective ambivalence calculated using a specific formula, and the minimum statistic (MIN stat), which represents the lower of two ratings given on two unipolar scales for the positivity and negativity of a stimulus. A higher MIN stat score indicates a greater intensity of ambivalence, as this method objectively captures ambivalence by emphasizing the lesser of the positive and negative ratings, thereby reducing the risk of one emotional response overshadowing the other. This approach differs from the conventional 9-point valence scale, which typically assesses emotional polarity on a bipolar rather than a unipolar scale. Additionally, Anvari et al. (2023) employed the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale to assess valence and arousal. The SAM scale is a visual representation of a 9-point scale comprising human-like figures in various emotional states. Valence is evaluated on a bipolar scale, with a value of 1 indicating negative affect and a value of 9 indicating positive affect. In contrast, arousal is measured on a unipolar scale, with a value of 1 indicating low arousal and a value of 9 indicating high arousal. The SAM scale is particularly effective for capturing affective dimensions due to its simple, non-verbal format, which allows participants to rate their emotional responses in an intuitive, visually guided manner. Since we are aiming for a conceptual replication of this study, we adapted our methodology to include alternative response formats for measuring valence. Specifically, we measured valence using two different response formats: the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and the Dual Range Slider (DRS). We want to find out whether the results of Anvari et al. (2023) can be replicated with the conceptually similar VAS and whether replication can also be achieved with the conceptually more distant DRS. The introduction of VAS and DRS allows us to investigate whether these formats can capture similar nuances in valence and ambivalence as the SAM scale used by Anvari et al. (2023). The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) involves rating the word on two scales, one ranging from neutral (0) to positive (100) and the other from neutral (0) to negative (-100), with the slider starting at the middle (50) which can be moved to the desired position on each scale. Depending on the position of the slider the resulting value can be between 0 and 100 or -100. This setup enables us to calculate the MIN stat similar to Anvari et al. (2023) from these ratings, which provides an objective measure of ambivalence based on the participants’ ratings on both the positive and negative dimensions. The Dual Range Slider (DRS) differs from the VAS in that it measures valence on a single bipolar scale with two sliders, allowing participants to indicate a range of emotional responses from negative to positive. This produces a range rather than a single value, potentially offering a broader depiction of the participant’s valence response and an alternative approach to assessing ambivalence, by looking at the width of the slider. The DRS allows both negative and positive values to be expressed simultaneously and could therefore overcome the problem of the bipolar scale used by Anvari et al. (2023), where this is not possible. In assessing arousal, we followed the approach of Anvari et al. (2023). We measured arousal using the 9-point Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale, with the verbal anchors “calm” (“ruhig”) and “exciting” (“aufgeregt”) provided only in the explanation of the example item. The use of the SAM scale for arousal in both studies ensures consistency in measuring this dimension, which allows for a more direct comparison between the studies. Anvari et al. (2023) selected 60 neutral words from the ANEW database, with valence scores ranging from 4.95 to 5.05 on a 9-point scale. Since our study is conducted in Germany, we used the BAWL-R database (Võ et al., 2009) for German words. We selected 40 neutral words ranging from -0.5 to 0.5 on a 7-point valence scale (-3 to 3), with 20 neutral words rated as high arousal and 20 rated as low arousal. Additionally, we selected 20 negative and 20 positive words as reference points, resulting in a total of 80 words. These selection criteria allowed us to approximate the valence range used by Anvari et al. (2023) within the BAWL-R’s framework, ensuring that our “neutral” stimuli meet comparable criteria for neutrality and arousal in a German-language context. In summary, our study builds upon Anvari et al. (2023) by examining if the valence and arousal ratings of words can be replicated using alternative response formats and a German language database. This approach serves not only to test the robustness of the results presented by Anvari et al., but also to extend their findings by introducing response formats that may capture finer emotional nuances. The use of a single bipolar interval response scale to assess ambivalence could contribute to the broader field of emotion measurement.

title_r: Social Value Orientation and Attachment: A Replication and Extension of Van Lange et al. (1997)
abstract_r: We report a replication and extension of a landmark finding from Van Lange et al.'s (1997) Study 1, which showed an association between Social Value Orientation and attachment security. We report a close, but not exact, replication, as we tested the premise with measures of attachment that are considered superior in comparison to the measures used by Van Lange et al. (1997), due to subsequent psychometric improvements. With a sample (N = 879) sufficiently large to detect d = .19 (and larger than the original study, N = 573), we failed to replicate the effect. Psychometric analysis showed that our attachment measures were reliable and valid, demonstrating theoretically predicted associations with other outcomes. We call for the use of solid psychometric measures to investigate the nomological network of Social Value Orientation. Based on the available evidence provided by Van Lange et al. (1997) and our study, we interpret as there being no evidence for the link between attachment security and Social Value Orientation, but further replication research that uses solid measures and large samples can provide more definite conclusions about the association between attachment and Social Value Orientation.

title_r: Direct Replication study of Fukushima (2003, study 1)
abstract_r: This study aims to directly replicate Fukushima (2003), Study 1. Fukushima (2003, Study 1) examined whether the desirability of trait judgments varied depending on interpersonal counterparts. This study intends to replicate Fukushima (2003)'s procedure as accurately as possible. However, it plans to incorporate several modifications. First, one additional interpersonal counterpart will be included. Fukushima (2003) used six conditions: “myself alone,” “with my father,” “with my mother,” “with my best friend,” “with someone of the opposite sex,” and “with a stranger.” Our study adds the condition “with someone I dislike.” Second, the trait words were reselected to better reflect current sensitivities. Third, we will conduct an online survey instead of a paper-based questionnaire, allowing for strict enforcement of the original study's time limit. These efforts contribute to the construction of reproducible scientific knowledge. Furthermore, Fukushima (2003) is one of the few studies in Japan that examined the complexity of self-knowledge. The structure of Japanese self-knowledge is a key aspect of self-research and cultural psychology. Gathering findings on these topics advances the theoretical development of social psychology, particularly in understanding the complexity of self-knowledge. title_r: Registered replication granted IPA 4 Feb 2025 at Cognition & Emotion
abstract_r: How do emotion and motivation affect the breadth of attention? Competing theoretical accounts propose that valence (pleasantness) or motivational intensity (strength of the urge to approach or avoid) drive changes in attentional breadth. Here we propose a registered conceptual replication of the seminal Gable and Harmon-Jones (2008) Study 2, where pictures of desserts narrowed attentional breadth relative to pictures of rocks. This was interpreted as higher motivational intensity narrowing attentional breadth, and this conclusion has been influential in informing thinking about the link between emotion/motivation and cognition. However, recent work questions whether emotion/motivation has any reliable effect on attentional breadth. Given this, it is important to assess the replicability of this result. Here, therefore, we will conduct a registered conceptual replication where we assess whether the narrowing of attentional breadth following dessert (vs rocks) pictures replicates with a new picture set. Further, in both Gable and Harmon-Jones (2008) and the literature more broadly, two other key dimensions have typically been confounded with differences in motivational intensity between conditions: valence and perceptual focality. Here, therefore, we will make a novel contribution by assessing the unique contribution of motivational intensity, valence, and perceptual focality, to assess which, if any, drives attentional breadth.

title_r: "Explaining How Long CO2 Stays in the Atmosphere: Does It Change Attitudes Toward Climate Change?" - a replication study (Joslyn & Demnitz, 2021)
abstract_r: Aus wissenschaftlicher Perspektive ist ein kritischer Punkt der globalen Erwärmung erreicht (Ripple et al., 2017). Trotzdem scheint die Wahrnehmung von Risiken bezüglich des Klimawandels erheblich zwischen Ländern (Eurobarometer, 2014) und Individuen (Botzen et al., 2016) zu variieren. Häufig wird der Klimawandel als ein zeitlich und räumlich entferntes Problem wahrgenommen (Lorenzoni & Hulme, 2009). Insbesondere Menschen mit einer konservativen politischen Ideologie scheinen dem Klimawandel dabei kritisch gegenüberzustehen (Funk & Rainie, 2015). Um zu überprüfen, wie sich diese Einstellungen zum Klimawandel verändern lassen, untersuchten Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) anhand einer repräsentativen nationalen Stichprobe aus den USA die Auswirkungen von zwei einfachen Strategien der Klimakommunikation auf das Verständnis und die Reaktion auf den Klimawandel bei verschiedenen politischen Ideologien. Dabei kamen sie zu dem Ergebnis, dass psychologisch gezielte Klimakommunikation die Einstellung zur globalen Erwärmung unabhängig von politischer Ideologie verändern kann. Mit dem Ziel, das derzeitige Wissen über den Einfluss psychologisch gezielter Klimakommunikation auf die Einstellungen zum Klimawandel in verschiedenen Ländern und Kulturen zu erweitern, wird die Studie von Joslyn und Demnitz (2021) in der vorliegenden Studie im Kontext der deutschen Bevölkerung repliziert. Dabei wollen wir unter anderem dem in der Psychologie weit verbreiteten Phänomen Rechnung tragen, dass Replikationen viel zu selten durchgeführt und veröffentlicht werden (Neuliep & Crandall, 1993) und zum Aufbau einer kumulativen Wissensbasis beitragen (Brandt et al., 2014; Dekkers et al., 2010).

title_r: Yang_JournMarketRes_2013_G1Lr - RRTeam_Jaeger_ML - Direct Replication - 387
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the main claim reported in Yang et al.’s (2013) experiment 1. The authors reported that the more prospect’s frame was associated with risk, the less buyers were willing to pay for that prospect: Framing a risky prospect as a “lottery ticket” (i.e., increased risk and uncertainty) compared with an uncertain “gift certificate” (i.e., reduced risk and uncertainty) reduced participants’ willingness to pay for the prospect. This claim was tested using an online between-subjects experiment (U.S. American participants recruited via Prolific). Participants indicated their willingness to pay for a risky prospect that was framed as either a “lottery ticket” or an “uncertain gift card”. In the lottery condition, the “lottery ticket” would for sure yield either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). In the gift card condition, the “gift card” would be either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). Participants were told that the authors would randomly select five respondents to get a $20 bonus and an opportunity to purchase a lottery ticket or a gift card. If their willingness to pay was above the reservation price (the reservation price of $15 was not revealed to participants), they would buy the lottery ticket or gift card at the authors’ reservation price. If their willingness to pay was below the reservation price, they would not buy the lottery ticket or gift card. The authors analyzed and compared willingness to pay with a t-test (Yang et al., 2013, p.726): “Participants in the lottery condition were willing to pay less (M = $5.68, SD = $6.69, Mdn = $5.00) than participants in the gift card condition (M = $9.52, SD = $4.48, Mdn = $ 7.50; t(99) = 3.43, p < .001, p 2 = .11; z = 2.93, p = .003).” The present study will replicate this claim, which has been selected for the SCORE program.

title_r: Direct Replication of a Research Claim from Yang et al. (2013), from the Journal of Marketing Research
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the main claim reported in Yang et al.’s (2013) experiment 1. The authors reported that the more a prospect’s frame was associated with risk, the less buyers were willing to pay for that prospect: Framing a risky prospect as a “lottery ticket” compared with a “gift card” reduced participants’ willingness to pay for the prospect. In a pretest, participants associated “risk and uncertainty” more with “lottery ticket” than with “gift card”, suggesting that even though the objective risk and uncertainty associated with the prospect in the two conditions were identical, simply framing a prospect as a “lottery ticket” increased the perceived risk associated with that prospect (relative to an “gift card”). This claim was tested using an online between-subjects experiment (Amazon Mechanical Turk participants). Participants indicated their willingness to pay for a risky prospect that was framed as either a “lottery ticket” or an “gift card”. In the lottery condition, the “lottery ticket” would for sure yield either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). In the gift card condition, the “gift card” would be either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). Participants in both conditions were also told that the researchers would randomly select five respondents from all survey respondents to get a $20 bonus. For each of the five selected respondent, if their willingness to pay for either the lottery ticket or the gift card was above the researchers’ reservation price (the reservation price of $15 was not revealed to participants), they would buy the lottery ticket or the gift card at the authors’ reservation price. If their willingness to pay was below the reservation price, they would not buy the lottery ticket or gift card. Furthermore, participants were not told how many other participants completed the survey, so they were unaware of the probability of being selected to receive the bonus. To detect participants who did not pay attention to the instructions, the authors administered an instructional manipulation check (Oppenheimer, Meyvis, and Davidenko 2009) at the beginning of the experiment. Participants could start the experiment only after they had correctly answered the instructional manipulation check. Finally, to check whether participants erroneously believed that $0 was a possible payoff, participants were asked, “What was the lowest possible outcome of the offer?” and chose an answer from the values $0, $5, $10, $15, and $20 (Simonsohn, 2009). The authors analyzed and compared willingness to pay with a t-test (Yang et al., 2013, p.726): “Participants in the lottery condition were willing to pay less (M = $5.68, SD = $6.69, Mdn = $5.00) than participants in the uncertain gift card condition (M = $9.52, SD = $4.48, Mdn = $ 7.50; t(99) = 3.43, p < .001, ηp2 = .11; z = 2.93, p = .003).” The present study will replicate this claim, which has been selected for the SCORE program.

title_r: Does Telling a Story in Reverse Elicit Cues to Deceit? A Replication and Extension of Vrij, Leal, Mann, and Fisher (2012)
abstract_r: Purpose The reverse order recall technique has been suggested as tool to improve deception detection accuracy (Vrij et al., 2008). Systematic reviews of cognitive approaches to deception have focused on detection judgements (Mac Giolla & Luke, 2020; Vrij et al., 2017) and not the cues judges are theoretically relying on to make such decisions. Yet, findings regarding the cues these techniques provoke are inconsistent. Thus, we will conduct a registered replication of Vrij et al., 2012, focusing on the cues the reverse order produces in senders. We will also investigate the link between cues and judgments, to provide a stronger theoretical basis for the technique. Methods Following Vrij et al., 2012, in Experiment 1, participants will complete one of two missions that they will be interviewed about twice, once lying and once telling the truth. Interviewers will ask participants to recount their experience in chronological and reverse order. We will then code these interviews for cues associated with deception according to a cognitive approach. In Experiment 2, participants will either view two videos of the senders or read two transcripts from Experiment 1 and will decide whether they are lying or telling the truth. Responses will submitted to a lens model mediation analysis to assess the link between production and utilization of cues.

abstract_r: We try to conceptually replicate the effect of Study 2 of Zuckerman and Gerbasi (1977), according to which the belief in a just world (BJW) measured with the scale of Rubin and Peplau (1973) is positively correlated with trust (which was operationalized as participants’ certainty about receiving a promised gift without any obligation). In addition, we have developed further hypotheses that relate to the differentiated consideration of the construct BJW in personal belief in a just world (PBJW) and general belief in a just world (GBJW) measured with the scales of Dalbert (1999). Concretely, we predict the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 1a: Participants high in BJW will be more likely to collect the gift. Hypothesis 1b: PBJW will show a stronger positive correlation with gift collection than GBJW. Hypothesis 2a: BJW will be positively correlated with general trust. title_r: Winning Hearts and Minds in Online Surveys: Replication and Extension of Searles and Mattes (2015)
abstract_r: How can we best induce emotions in online survey experiments? This project measures the effectiveness of eight anger inductions (three of which replicate treatments from Searles and Mattes 2015) and six gratitude inductions in the context of an online survey. Many emotion induction treatments have been used and/or validated in offline settings (see Searles and Mattes 2015 for validation of scenario vignettes, self-statements, and images; see also Young 2019 for examples of autobiographical emotional memory tasks). However, political scientists regularly study the effect of emotions using online survey experiments (e.g., Webster, Connors and Sinclair 2022), where participants are frequently inattentive and distracted (Ternovski and Orr 2022), potentially weakening treatment effects (Clifford and Jerit 2014). This project builds on the methodological literature on emotion induction by validating emotion induction techniques—including scenario vignettes, self-statements, images, and autobiographical emotional memory tasks (AEMTs)—for online contexts. We also introduce a deliberately bundled “two-step” AEMT treatment that asks people to recast the valence that they attach to emotional memories. This novel treatment is designed to reproduce the experience of specifically political emotions. In developing this treatment, we seek to test the microfoundations of emotional experiences prompted by propaganda and political persuasion. We will also, in the project, test reactions to research participation among participants, building on Weiss (2024). This analysis takes advantage of the set-up of the experiment, where we are priming both negative and positive emotions and doing so—in one treatment group—by using negative images. In this case, we are interested in confirming the expectations of a largely non-experimental literature on reactions to research participation, which would suggest that participants do not become significantly more distressed or resentful when participating in research that involves negative content versus neutral or positive content.

title_r: The Power-Sex Association and the Likelihood to Sexually Aggress: : A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Bargh, Raymond, Pryor, and Strack (1995)
abstract_r: The following study is a conceptual replication and extension of experiment two of Bargh, Raymond, Pryor, and Strack's (1995) paper. The experiment is translated into an online format, using Qualtrics. Updated measures have been used, in order to increase validity, and we are aiming to achieve a more representative sample. We are interested in seeing if the finding that men who are high in the likelihood to sexually aggress are more likely to find a woman more attractive if they have been primed with power, can be replicated. We also want to extend the research further to see if this relationship means that men would engage in sexually aggressive behaviour towards the female. In order to manipulate power, we will be using a word-fragment completion task using power-related words (as used in the original study). Participants will be exposed to a female confederate and asked to rate them on a series of attributes, including attractiveness. They will also be asked if they would like future contact with the confederate (through a skype call). We will be using a sexual aggression paradigm as a proxy for sexual aggression (described in the dependent variables section). To measure the likelihood to sexually aggress, we will be using the attraction to sexual aggression scale (Malamuth, 1989).
