title_r: Yang_JournMarketRes_2013_G1Lr - RRTeam_Sirota_ML - Direct Replication - 999g
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate the main claim reported in Yang et al.’s (2013) experiment 1. The authors reported that the more prospect’s frame was associated with risk, the less buyers were willing to pay for that prospect: Framing a risky prospect as a “lottery ticket” (i.e., increased risk and uncertainty) reduced participants’ willingness to pay for the prospect, compared with to an uncertain “gift certificate” (i.e. reduced risk and uncertainty). This claim was tested using an online between-subjects experiment (Amazon Mechanical Turk participants). Participants indicated their willingness to pay for a risky prospect that was framed as either a “lottery ticket” or an “uncertain gift card”. In the lottery condition, the “lottery ticket” would for sure yield either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). In the gift card condition, the “gift card” would be either a $10 or a $20 Best Buy gift card (both equally likely). To clarify, the two conditions had the same chance (50/50) and amounts to win, only the framing of the prospect was different. Participants were told that the authors would randomly select five respondents to get a $20 bonus and an opportunity to purchase a lottery ticket or a gift card with this bonus. If their willingness to pay was above the reservation price (the reservation price of $15 was not revealed to participants), they would buy the lottery ticket or gift card at the authors’ reservation price. If their willingness to pay was below the reservation price, they would not buy the lottery ticket or gift card. The authors analyzed and compared willingness to pay with a t-test (Yang et al., 2013, p.726): “Participants in the lottery condition were willing to pay less (M = $5.68, SD = $6.69, Mdn = $5.00) than participants in the gift card condition (M = $9.52, SD = $4.48, Mdn = $ 7.50; t(99) = 3.43, p < .001, p 2 = .11; z = 2.93, p = .003).” The present study will replicate this claim, which has been selected for the SCORE program.

title_r: Organic and Acquisitive Growth: Replicating and Extending Lockett, Wiklund, Davidsson, Girma (2011)
abstract_r: We replicate and extend the work from Lockett, Wiklund, Davidsson, and Girma (2011), investigating how organic and acquisitive growth strategies influence future organic growth rates. Analysing a panel of Dutch firms over the period 2011-2016, we confirm Lockett et al.’s finding that past organic growth exerts a restraining effect on current organic growth. Unlike the original paper, we also find that acquisitive growth hinders rather than sustains subsequent organic growth. We therefore extend Lockett et al.’s framework by explicitly accounting for how the relatedness and complementarity of acquisitions moderate this effect. We observe that this negative effect is less pronounced when acquisitive growth is less related and complementary. Finally, we refine the identification strategy further developing the empirical analysis.

title_r: Precarity and conspiracy: a replication attempt of Adam-Troian et al. 2022
abstract_r: The study aims at replicating findings of the Adam-Troian et al. (2022) study on the mediating effect of institutional trust in the relationship between precarity and conspiracy beliefs (CBs). The study corroborated the view that the subjective experience of financial insecurity enhances the endorsement of CBs because precarity is associated with a decrease in institutional trust and institutional trust is among best-recognised antecedents of CBs. Before pre-registering the study, we obtained results from the first two datasets (two waves of a longitudinal study; the results will be reported as Studies 1a and 1b). The studies included two operationalisations of precarity: financial threat scale adapted to reflect Covid-related (wave 1 and 2) and war-related (wave 2) financial threats and subjective socio-economic status - a visual ladder task (Cantril, 1965). Institutional trust was measured as an average score of trust in eight institutions. Conspiracy beliefs were operationalised as general conspiracy mentality (Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire, Bruder et al., 2013) and specific conspiracy beliefs concerning COVID-19 (C19-UB, Teličák & Halama, n.d.). The results of Study 1a and Study 1b show congruence with the original Adam-Troian et al. (2022) findings. After consultations with the authors of the replicated study, we also checked the results robustness by adding sex, age and religiosity as covariates (see https://osf.io/kbr9s/ for details and preliminary results). Second, based on the data from two other representative Slovak samples (based on quota characteristics for gender, age, region, and education), we attempt to replicate the findings by Adam-Troian et al. (2021) at individual level in Study 2 and Study 3. Both datasets include subjective socio-economic status (a visual ladder task, Cantril, 1965) as a proxy of precarity. In Study 2, CBs were measured using the Conspiracy Thinking Scale (Uscinski et al., 2020) and trust was operationalised as confidence in the pandemic management and 3 items measuring trust in scientists, government and WHO. In Study 3, CBs were measured by 4 items (e.g., “Much of our lives are being controlled by plots hatched in secret places”) and trust was measured by 7 items. After obtaining results from all four Slovak datasets, we plan to perform a mini meta-analysis of the effects (Studies 1a/b–3). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration. Finally, using the ESS10 (The European Social Survey Round 10) dataset, we attempt to replicate the original findings using high-quality international data on the subjective appraisal of economic situation (as an operationalisation of precarity), institutional trust measured as an average of trust in eight institutions and three questions capturing the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs (Study 4). The data have been collected but not analysed prior to the registration.

title_r: Reductive Allure Effects for Psychology Phenomena – Impact of Worker Recruitment Screening. A Pre-Registered Replication of Hopkins, Weisberg, & Taylor (2016).
abstract_r: Previous research (Hopkins et al., 2016) suggests that the presentation of reductive information influences people’s ability to judge the quality of a scientific explanation. For instance, people who are presented with neuroscience jargon in an explanation of a psychological phenomenon judge those explanations more favorably than explanations without the jargon, even if that information is logically irrelevant. In a previously pre-registered (osf.io/hvm8q) attempt to replicate and extend Hopkins et al. (2016), we were unable to replicate this basic reductive explanation effect across three scientific disciplines that were included in the original study (Psychology, Neuroscience, Biology). That is, participants in our study did not rate reductive explanations significantly higher than horizontal explanations in any of these three scientific disciplines, even though we used the same testing materials and procedure as Hopkins et al. (2016). One possible explanation for our inability to replicate the reductive allure effect observed by Hopkins et al. (2016) is that we employed a different participant pool. Specifically, we recruited our participants from Prolific.co, whereas Hopkins et al. recruited participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Thus, in order to rule out the different participant pools as the reason for the discrepant results, we conducted a second pre-registered experiment (osf.io/8af7k) to examine the effects of worker platform. In that second experiment, we conducted an abbreviated replication of Hopkins et al. (2016) using only their original descriptions of psychological phenomena (the scientific discipline that showed the largest reductive explanation effect) with a participant pool selected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. In this second experiment, we were again unable to replicate the basic reductive explanation effect for psychological phenomena found in Hopkins et al. (2016). Our failure to replicate the original reductive explanation effect in Experiment 2 was complicated by the fact that we encountered abnormally high rates of participant exclusion based on our pre-registered criteria (namely, failure on the instructions, failure on our attention check, or submission times ±3 SD away from the mean). Out of the 174 participants who completed the survey, 82 were removed, resulting in an exclusion rate greater than 40%. This excessively high exclusion rate raises serious concern about the quality of our data, even for the participants who were not excluded. As such, our inability to replicate Hopkins et al. (2016) may have resulted from a generally inattentive participant pool. To address this concern, we will attempt a third replication of Hopkins et al. (2016). In this third replication, we will use the same procedure as described in Experiment 2 (osf.io/8af7k), however, we will recruit MTURK participants using CloudResearch, a third-party website that pre-screens MTURK workers to improved data quality. In this way, we will limit our recruitment to “approved” workers that are more likely to produce high-quality data with an acceptable exclusion rate.

title_r: Meta-analysis and publication bias: How well does the FAT-PET-PEESE procedure work? A replication study of Alinaghi & Reed (Research Synthesis Methods, 2018)
abstract_r: A meta-analysis is a tool for aggregating estimates of a similar "effect" across many studies. Publication bias is the phenomenon where literature is sample selected in favor of studies having statistically significant results and/or having estimates that satisfy pre-conceived expectations. A popular procedure used for conducting meta-analyses in the presence of publication bias is the FAT-PET-PEESE (FPP) procedure. In a recent paper published in Research Synthesis Methods, Alinaghi and Reed (2018), utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, report that the FPP procedure does not work well when used in 'realistic' data environments where true effects differ both across and within studies. AR's findings are important because the FPP approach is dominant in the economics meta-analysis literature. I replicate their results and discover two mistakes, which I subsequently correct. The first mistake is found in a descriptive statistics table, misrepresenting the overview of simulated dataset. The second is associated with the fixed effect estimation, generating erroneous estimated effects and Type I error. Further, I extend their analysis by making their simulation environment even more realistic. Despite producing somewhat different results, my replications generally confirm AR's conclusions about the unreliability of the FPP procedure in realistic data environments.

title_r: A preregistered, direct replication of the CBCA Condition of Bogaard et al. (2014): Contextual bias in verbal credibility assessment
abstract_r: Child sexual abuse cases often lack physical evidence, leaving victim statements as the primary source for judgment. This requires credibility judgments through forensic psychologists. Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) is a 19-criterion method used to distinguish between truthful and fabricated statements purely based on the content of the statement, such as detail quantity. But, credibility judgments are embedded in the context of a case. Bogaard et al. (2014) showed that contextual information strongly impacts the CBCA scoring. Subsequent studies, however, found no contextual bias in the CBCA (Arui, 2024; Lindenkreuz, 2025; Schemmel et al., 2020). Resolving these contradictions is necessary to ensure the validity of the CBCA and inform on de-biasing measures. This study is a preregistered, direct replication of the CBCA condition of Bogaard et al. (2014). Participants will each rate four victim statements that are paired with either credibility-enhancing or reducing information, on the 19 CBCA criteria and give a final credibility judgment.

title_r: Strong evidence for expectation adaptation during language understanding, not a replication failure. A reply to Harrington Stack, James, and Watson (2018)
abstract_r: Recent input affects subsequent language processing. One explanation for this holds that comprehenders adapt their implicit linguistic expectations based on the input, so as to facilitate efficient processing. A number of studies have identified support for this hypothesis. Harrington Stack, James, and Watson (2018) report a failure to replicate one of these studies (Fine, Jaeger, Farmer, and Qian, 2013). We show that, to the contrary, the data from Harrington Stack and colleagues constitute strong support for the hypothesis of expectation adaptation. Several factors contribute to the difference in conclusions. For example, Harrington Stack and colleagues argue based on differences in p-values, which is known to be problematic. We instead employ well-formed Bayesian measures of evidentiary support to assess replication success. Most critically though, the new experiments by Harrington Stack and colleagues differ in design from the experiments they aim to replicate. We correct for these differences by means of the same single-parameter belief-updating model previously employed by Fine and colleagues. The model provides trial-level predictions for the surprisal that comprehenders experience, based on previous input within and outside of the experiment. Trial-level analyses find that surprisal based on adapted expectations strongly predicts reading times in both the original and the replication data. In fact, once the differences in design are corrected for, the two data are highly similar; replication tests estimate the posterior probability of a replication success to be ≫ .9999. We show how the same belief-updating model also predicts trial-to-trial priming, cumulative priming, and the inverse preference effect in priming.

title_r: Working memory capacity and the risky-choice framing effect: A preregistered replication and extension of Corbin et al. (2010)
abstract_r: Higher working memory capacity is associated with superior performance on a number of tasks but may it sometimes be paradoxically associated with suboptimal performance? Corbin et al. (2010) found that, in a between-subjects design, higher WMC is associated with a larger risky-choice framing effect, traditionally conceived of as a departure from rational principles. Such surprising findings are of potentially great theoretical importance, yet the original study was underpowered. In this registered report, we aim to replicate and extend the original findings, by conducting an online experiment among 400 participants. To extend the findings beyond the specific single tasks used in the original study, we use three WMC tasks with different processing components and six framing problems involving human lives.

title_r: A replication and extension of Scott and Landy (2023): moral character beliefs about medical treatment options
abstract_r: Treatment adherence is a known problem in healthcare. For example, low medication use and adherence are noticed in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder (COPD), even with a severe diagnosis (Ingebrigtsen et al., 2014). Likewise, psychiatric medication has stigma attached to it which increases the reluctance of patients to take medication. Research has shown that adolescents on psychiatric medication limited social interactions due to the shame which accompanies stigma (Kranke et al., 2010). One area to explain low treatment adherence are beliefs associated with specific treatments: for example, research has shown that the use of medication instead of behavioural or lifestyle changes is perceived to be a signal of lower willpower (Scott & Landy, 2023), while working hard and applying effort (i.e, willpower) is a socially acceptable positive moral characteristic (Amos et al., 2017). Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options therefore laid the groundwork for understanding the influence of moral virtues on medical decision-making. The study revealed a bias, with a preference for behavioural or lifestyle changes over pharmaceutical interventions as it is perceived to be reflective of a stronger moral character. The current study is a partial replication and an extension of Scott and Landy's (2023) work on moral judgements about medical treatment options. The present study aims to explore this theme in the contexts of physical health (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disorder; COPD), mental health (Depression) and neurodivergent conditions (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder). In their original study, Scott and Landy include COPD and depression, but did not compare these directly; that is, they did not examine if the effect of treatment type on moral judgements differed by type of conditions, which we expect to find given the known stigma around mental health and neurodivergence (Kranke et al., 2010). title_r: Pastotter_Cognition_2013_EQxa - Berry_6738 - Direct Replication
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Pastötter et al (2013) is that positive moods validate thoughts about pushing in the active decision frame (“yes, it is appropriate to push”) and validate thoughts about not pushing in the passive decision frame (“yes, it is not appropriate to push”), inducing utilitarian responding in the active frame and non utilitarian responding in the passive frame. In contrast, negative moods invalidate thoughts about pushing in the active decision frame (“no, it is not appropriate to push”) and invalidate thoughts about not pushing in the passive decision frame (“no, it is not appropriate to not push”), inducing non utilitarian responding in the active frame and utilitarian responding in the passive frame. This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “Compared to neutral moods, positive moods induced utilitarian responding (i.e., deciding to push) in the active decision frame, but induced non utilitarian responding (i.e., deciding to not push) in the passive decision frame; in negative moods, exactly the opposite picture arose.” Participants’ yes/no responses to the dilemma in Experiment 1 were analyzed using an F test with the between-subjects factors of mood (positive, negative) and frame (active, passive). The factor mood was manipulated by presenting different musical selections to induce positive (happy) and negative (sad) moods. The factor frame was manipulated by asking participants different closing questions after presentation of the footbridge scenario. This analysis yielded that affective influences on moral judgment varied with decision frame, F(1, 396) = 29.0, p < .001, partial eta squared = .07. The aim of this study is to replicate the claims made by Pastötter et al. (2013) about positive and negative moods on utilitarian responses. First, we will attempt to replicate that positive moods induce utilitarian responding in the active decision frame, but induce non-utilitarian responding in the passive decision frame. Second, we will attempt to replicate the claim that negative moods induce non-utilitarian responding in the active decision frame and utilitarian responding in the passive decision frame.

title_r: Productivity premia for many modes of internationalization. A replication study of Békés and Muraközy (Economics Letters, 2016) (replication study)
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate estimation results from Gábor Békés and Balázs Muraközy, Measuring productivity premia with many modes of internationalization, published in Economics Letters (2016). In this paper the authors use comparable firm-level data for seven European countries based on the EFIGE dataset to estimate the productivity premia of firms with various modes of internationalization by several empirical methods to demonstrate how results differ due to the method applied. While the EFIGE data are available free of charge from the web one core variable used by Békés and Muraközy is not, because total factor productivity (tfp) as computed by the authors is based on data from a commercial data base and, therefore, is available for users with a license to this database only. The freely available EFIGE data, however, come with another tfp-variable that can be used instead. In this replication study I use the EFIGE data with this publicly available tfp-variable to replicate (parts of) the estimations of Békés and Muraközy (2016) to see whether their results hold with the widely used public use version of the EFIGE data, too. It turns out that the big picture that emerges from using both productivity measures tends to be very similar. The use of the public use version of the EFIGE data for empirical investigations that deal with productivity, therefore, seems to be feasible.

title_r: The Parapsychological Association Convention 2004 1 THE INVISIBLE GAZE: THREE ATTEMPTS TO REPLICATE SHELDRAKE’S STARING EFFECTS
abstract_r: In three consecutive studies participants were asked to guess if someone was staring at them under conditions of sensory shielding. In total 188 sessions resulted in 4784 trials. The over-all hitrates were 50.6 % (N=53), 52.1 % (N=45), and 49.7 % (N=37) resp. In study 1 both skeptics and believers acted as starer. Hitrate was marginally significant only for skeptic starers. Extraversion of the participant was irrelevant. In study 2 the over-all hitrate of 52.1 % was not significant. In this study, skin conductance of the participant was also used as dependent variable. Initially, when participants were not informed of the staring, skin conductance showed no difference between stare and non-stare trials. After informing the participants, skin conductance was marginally higher for the stare trials. Study 3 compared hitrates for bonded pairs (friends) with non-bonded (strangers) pairs. In neither condition, not the slightest sign of a staring effect could be established. The conclusion of the three studies is that the staring paradigm is not the easily replicable paradigm that it is claimed to be. Apart from one internal effect all hitrates were very close to chance. Simulations with target sequences identical to those used in earlier studies involving feedback to the starees showed that results of these earlier studies can be explained by a combination of response bias and response strategies rather than psi. Other possible explanations of the failure to replicate concern difference in participants population, type of experimental setting, and rigor of the experimental procedures.

title_r: The Effect of Guilt and Shame on Construal Level : A Preregistered Replication Study of Han et al. (2014)
abstract_r: The purpose of this study is to replicate the effect of guilt and shame on construal level found by Han et al. (2014). Using autobiographical recall, we will induce either guilt or shame. That is, participants will have 10 minutes to recall an event that made them feel either guilt or shame and describe it as precisely as possible (conditions surrounding this event, feelings and thoughts associated). Participants in the control condition will have 10 minutes to describe a typical day in their life. Then, we will measure participants' construal level using the Behavior Identification Form (BIF, Wegner & Vallacher, 1989). We will use a translated and validated French version of this questionnaire (Belayachi & Van der Linden, unpublished), which contains 23 items. Specifically, we will ask participants to read action verbs (e.g., taking a test) and to choose which option, among two (e.g., answering questions [low-level construal] VS showing one’s knowledge [high-level construal]), describes better the way they represent the target action. After this measure, participants will rate the extent to which they feel guilt and shame (i.e., as a manipulation check). We will then measure psychological distance following Fiedler et al. (2012), by showing participants an action verb and ask them to imagine a situation in which they would engage themselves in a situation prompted by this action verb, to briefly describe the situation, and to judge the distance of the imagined situation concerning the social, temporal, spatial and probability distance dimensions. The psychological distance isn’t part of the original study, but we added it at the end in a more exploratory perspective in order to investigate the effect of these emotions on perceived psychological distance. Hence, we expect that (H1) participants in the guilt condition will have a lower construal level score than participants in the shame condition, with the control condition falling in between. This hypothesis is derived from Han et al. (2014) and is our replication and main hypothesis. We also expect that (H2) participants in the guilt condition will have a lower psychological distance score than participants in the shame condition, with the control condition falling in between. This constitutes our secondary hypothesis and we derive it from the Construal level theory (Trope et al, 2007; Trope et Liberman, 2010; Liberman, 2007).

title_r: Klusowski et al (2021) replication and extension
abstract_r: Cognitive distortions in gambling scenarios may explain risks to disordered gambling – a recognised psychopathology in DSM-V with a similar harm profile to severe alcohol abuse disorder (Browne & Rockloff, 2017). Specifically, an illusion of control in which increased perceptions of control induce overestimations in winning prospects and overconfidence (Langer, 1975) has been implicated as a cognitive distortion common in disordered gamblers (Goodie & Fortune, 2013; Orgaz et al., 2013). However, recently this contribution has been challenged, for instance by failing to associate the illusion of control with disordered gambling behaviours such as increased wagering (Dannewitz & Weatherley, 2007; Moritz et al., 2021). These challenges have been further advanced by Klusowski et al. (2021). For example, in their final experiment (Experiment 17), a simple lottery task, these authors asked participants to give winning probability estimations for each of 3 equivalent boxes. They firstly found no illusion of control i.e., probability estimations were not higher in a condition where participants could choose their own box (post-choice condition), as opposed to having a box selected randomly for them (post-no-choice) or giving estimations prior to box selection (pre-selection). Therefore the manipulation of choice (active control) was not associated with increased irrational perceptions of winning. However, 26% of participants gave irrational probability estimates for any of the boxes exceeding ⅓ chance displayed as ‘non-uniform probabilistic beliefs’ in all 3 conditions. Consequently, this suggests the possibility of ‘passive’ cognitive distortions outside of the active distortions implicated by the illusion of control. Therefore, there is a need to replicate these findings, and extend them to attempt to find predictors of non-uniform probabilistic beliefs beyond the illusion of control. Gambling behaviour is one relevant potential predictor. In Western countries around half of the adult population gambles in any one year, and around 0.5-1% of the adult population may meet the diagnostic criteria for disordered gambling, a mental health condition in the DSM-5 (Potenza et al., 2019; Public Health England, 2021). Gamblers have many other cognitive distortions beyond the illusion of control, such as the gambler’s fallacy e.g., believing red is more likely to come up in roulette if multiple previous spins have come up black (Barron & Leider, 2010). Therefore, gambling participation and disordered gambling symptomology among gamblers may predict non-uniform probabilistic beliefs in this task. Additionally, research has found overlaps between characteristics associated with beliefs in superstition - irrational beliefs in the supernatural and its influence in affecting events; often manifesting as luck (Faiza, 2018) - and irrational gambling beliefs (Leonard & Williams, 2018; Williams et al., 2021). For example, beliefs in personal luck have been associated with increased perceptions in winning (Wohl & Enzle, 2002). This suggests that characteristics associated with superstition such as false attribution of cause and effect between unrelated events and unobjective assessments of probability may underlie cognitive distortions across both domains; gambling and superstition. Therefore, this may explain the correlations between superstition and problem gambling (Joukhador et al., 2004; Mowen et al., 2009; Pongsakornrungsilp et al., 2011) and identify superstition not only as a predictor of false probabilistic beliefs but problem gambling measures also. Nevertheless, superstition is a versatile set of beliefs wherein certain beliefs may not necessarily predict other superstitions. However, one factor of superstitious beliefs has been proposed is ‘passive superstition’ - beliefs that factors beyond one’s control affect outcomes (Hernandez et al., 2008). Indeed, this is associated with gambling e.g., lottery players often believe numbers based on lucky numbers or special dates are more likely to win (Hraba & Lee, 1995; Wang et al., 2016). It has also been associated with problem gambling behaviours such as risk-taking wherein the presence of magical objects increased the willingness for participants to enter more riskier gambling scenarios (Chinchanachokchai et al., 2016). Consequently, passive superstition may predict not only false probabilistic beliefs but problem gambling also. Additionally, passive superstition may be particularly relevant to alternatively explaining probability estimations in illusion of control paradigms as it encompasses beliefs that do not require senses that one’s own control will affect the likelihood of winning. Therefore, if passive superstition can predict false probability estimation it cannot necessarily be attributed to underlying beliefs that lead to illusions of control but a separate cognitive distortion beyond any choice component. This would strengthen conclusions that other cognitive distortions are relevant to illusion of control tasks. We will also attempt to address various limitations in Klusowski et al.’s Experiment 17. We plan to increase their sample size by approximately a factor of 5 to 3,000 participants. We will also use Bayesian over frequentist analysis given the hypothesised null effect of the experimental control manipulation. The original study was performed on MTurk, and some data suggests that Prolific is a rival crowdsourcing platform which provides more reliable data (Douglas et al., 2023). We will take further steps to ensure reliable data by excluding participants based on an attention check (which were collected but not used to exclude participants by Klusowski et al.), and by including a further seriousness check (Brühlmann et al., 2020).

title_r: Direct Replication of Bago et al. (2023)
abstract_r: This study aims to conduct a direct replication of Bago et al. (2023), whose results challenge the Motivated System 2 Reasoning (MS2R) hypothesis (Kahan, 2013), which posits that analytical processing (Kahneman, 2011) strengthens motivated reasoning, particularly ideological. Using a two-response paradigm (an intuitive response followed by a deliberative one), Bago et al. (2023) showed that deliberation increases the consistency between individuals’ evaluations of climate change information and their prior factual beliefs, rather than with their political ideology. The goal of the present study is to replicate these findings while introducing several methodological improvements: (1) conducting power analyses based on the original study’s results to determine the most appropriate sample size; (2) controlling for participants’ prior beliefs at recruitment — by selecting only individuals who believe in climate change — in order to reduce inter-individual differences in our sample and minimize statistical noise that could affect the validity of the results; (3) implementing methodological improvements to the original study materials. Participants will be divided into two groups, each evaluating six vignettes adapted from Bago et al. (2023), presenting arguments either in favor of or against the existence of climate change or its human origin. In the experimental group, participants will follow a two-response paradigm: after completing a cognitive load task (Dot Memory Task; Miyake et al., 2001), they will first evaluate each vignette under time pressure (intuitive processing), then a second time without time constraints (analytical processing). The control group will evaluate the same vignettes only once, without time constraints or cognitive load. Replicating the approach of Bago et al. (2023), and consistent with their results, we expect that compared to intuitive processing, participants in the control condition (one response condition) are expected to be more influenced by their prior beliefs. We expect an interaction effect, such that participants in the control condition will show more agreement with arguments supporting (PRO) the existence of climate change than participants in the intuitive processing condition. Conversely, agreement with arguments opposing (CON) the existence of climate change is expected to be lower under the control condition than under intuitive processing. This interaction is expected regardless of participants' political ideology. On an exploratory basis, we will also perform a comparison between the intuitive and analytical processing conditions in the two-response paradigm group. We expect the same pattern as the previous hypothesis: Participants in the analytical processing condition will show more agreement with arguments supporting (PRO) the existence of climate change than participants in the intuitive processing condition. Conversely, agreement with arguments opposing (CON) the existence of climate change is expected to be lower under analytical processing than under intuitive processing. This interaction is expected regardless of participants' political ideology. These latter analyses will be conducted in an exploratory way, as it is possible that we observe an anchoring effect (as previously found by Bago et al. (2023)) of the initial response on the final response, thus reducing the magnitude of our interaction. This anchoring can be assessed by comparing final responses to those of a control group providing only a single response.

title_r: Direct replication of Staw (1976)
abstract_r: Escalation of commitment refers to the decision error in which people stick to their original decision despite negative feedback (Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara & Miles, 2012; Staw, 1976; Staw & Fox, 1977). In 1976, Staw initiated experimental research on escalating commitment. In his study Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy: A Study of Escalating Commitment to a Chosen Course of Action, he showed that escalation was particularly pronounced when people were personally responsible for negative decision consequences. The interaction between responsibility and consequence was significant (p = <.019). Since then, there have been numerous studies investigating the escalation of commitment and the underlying effects. The findings are ambivalent, as the results often do not match or even contradict those of Staw (1976). There are many studies that used Staw's (1976) stimulus material, the A&S Financial Decision Case, or were based on his approach (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Armstrong, Coviello & Safranek, 1993; Bialek, Węgrzyn, & Meyers, 2021; Conlon & Parks, 1987; McCain, 1986; Morgan & Hansen, 2006; Pfeiffer, Schönborn, Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt, 2007; Schoorman & Holahan, 1996; Schoorman, Mayer, Douglas & Hetrick, 1994; Singer, 1990; Singer & Singer, 1986). However, these studies did not test the interaction effect responsibility x consequence (Armstrong et al., 1993) and altered or excluded relevant aspects of the paradigm. For example, a different scenario and other variables were examined (Negrini, Riedl & Wibral, 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007) or the methodological approach was changed (Akinbobola & Ehigie, 2012; Bialek et al., 2021; Singer & Singer, 1986). For this reason, the planned study in the form of a direct replication should provide information on how robust and reliable Staw's (1976) results are if there are as few deviations as possible from the original study. Of particular interest is the replicability of the interaction effect personal responsibility x decision consequences. In addition, the reasons for the investment decisions are evaluated using content analysis. Armstrong et al. (1993) asked the participants to justify their decision, but did not analyze this. Other studies did not even include the justification in their design (Bialek et al., 2021; Negrini et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2007; Singer & Singer, 1986). The planned study therefore extends the existing literature with a replication of the study by Staw (1976), which not only records the participants' reasons for their decisions, but also evaluates them using content analysis.

title_r: Rediscovering the Uptake of Dashboard Feedback : A Conceptual Replication of Foung (2019)
abstract_r: Learning analytics has been widely used in the context of language education. Among the studies that have used this approach, many have developed a dashboard that aims to provide students with recommendations based on data so that they can act on these suggestions and improve their performance. To further our understanding of dashboard research, this study aims to replicate an earlier study using a new data mining strategy, association rule mining, to explore if the new strategy can (1) generate comparable results; and (2) provide new insights into feedback uptake in dashboard systems. The original study was conducted with 423 students at a Hong Kong university and implemented a dashboard for a suite of first-year composition courses. It used a classification tree to identify factors that could predict the uptake of tool-based and general recommendations made by the dashboard. After performing association rule mining with the original data set, this study found that this approach allowed for the identification of additional useful factors associated with the uptake of general and tool-based recommendations with a higher accuracy rate. The results of this study provide new insights for dashboard research and showcase the potential use of association rule mining in the context of language education.

title_r: Replication and Extension Sherf and Morrison (2020)
abstract_r: Sherf and Morrison (2020) describe that employees’ self-efficacy influences the perceived value of feedback and thus how much feedback they seek. Moreover, they argue that perspective taking plays a moderating role in the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking. Sherf and Morrison (2020) measured employees' valuation of feedback and observed that it mediated the relation between self-efficacy and feedback-seeking, however, that was the only benefits and costs of feedback that the authors included in their model. A common assumption in the feedback-seeking literature is that when employees consider whether to ask for feedback they conduct a mental calculation of perceived benefits and costs of such feedback (Anseel et al., 2015; Ashford, 1986; Ashford & Cummings, 1983). Extending Sherf and Morrison (2020), in this study we will examine how self-efficacy and perspective taking influence various benefits and costs of asking for feedback. Specifically, we will look at: feedback expectancy value, self-presentation and ego costs, and self-presentation and ego benefits.

title_r: 3 in 1000 August and October 2020 (A conceptual replication of a test of the effect of two messaging appeals for increasing organ donation registration intentions and attitudes and the reasons for that effect)
abstract_r: Rationale: The need for increasing organ donor registrations is pressing, as thousands of people die each year waiting for a transplant. Therefore, an understanding of the effectiveness of different persuasive appeals is needed. This study conceptually replicates a preregistered study of two appeals that have received relatively little research attention in the organ donor domain. This study will use new versions of each message to test their persuasive abilities. The “3 in a 1,000” appeal informs people that a very small number of people die in such a way that their organs are viable for transplantation. The “dynamic norms” appeal informs people that there is an increasing number of organ donors in our country. This conceptual replication will include an online survey very similar to a prior study and include an open-ended question about their reasons the message changed or didn’t change participants’ intention to register. Moreover, we will use different experimental stimuli to assess the effectiveness of the two approaches. Also, to rule out a possible rival hypothesis as to why the appeals worked, we did not include any specific reference to the lives that are saved as a result of organ donation. Manipulation: Messages about organ donation As in a prior study, we are considering that both of these appeals have potential benefits and risks. If people are sensitized to the rarity of being able to donate (3 in 1,000), they may experience a sense of urgency to address the scarcity of organs and be motivated to register. Conversely, they may be discouraged by the idea that there is so slim a chance that their organs would be used. If people are informed about the increasing numbers of people registering (dynamic norms), they may be reassured that organ donation is something they should do because other people are doing it. Conversely, they may get the sense that, if everyone else is doing it, they are not needed. Although we have no reason to expect one appeal will be better than the other, we will also assess if there are any differences between the two appeals.

title_r: The opportunity cost of time modulates cognitive effort – a replication study of Otto & Daw (2019) Neuropsychologia
abstract_r: It has been shown that there are different decision-making strategies: fast but error-prone heuristic decision-making, and slower but more accurate deliberative decision-making (Balleine & Dickinson, 1998; Daw, Gershman, Deymour, Dayan, & Dolan, 2011; Dolan & Dayan, 2013). While deliberative responding leads to more appropriate responses, it also requires more computational time, during which cognitive resources cannot be used for other computations that could lead to reward. It has been proposed that the brain approximates such opportunity costs of time by calculating the average reward rate of the environment (Niv, Daw, Joel, & Dayan, 2007). Using three experiments, Otto & Daw (2019) provide evidence that when the opportunity cost of time is higher, subjects make more mistakes and respond faster. These results therefore suggest that a higher average reward rate in the environment causes a shift towards more heuristic responding (Otto & Daw, 2019). I aim to reproduce these results using one of the experiments used by Otto and Daw (2019), namely a Simon task.

title_r: Does sequence learning engage the frontoparietal network in 8-month-old infants? A replication and extension of Baek et al. (2022)
abstract_r: Sequence learning is a critical ability which serves as the cornerstone for developing many other cognitive and motor skills (e.g., Säfström et al., 2014), and it appears early in life. For example, 3-month-olds were able to detect audiovisual sequences with 3 elements compared to 4 elements for 4-month-olds (Lewkowicz, 2008), and 11-month-olds were able to respond to spatially structured sequences (Kirkham et al., 2007). Considering the relatively immature brain structure and network connectivity in infants, exploring the underlying neural basis for this ability in early infancy can help with our understanding of the development and functional capability of responsible networks when compared with findings from adult studies. However, only few studies touched upon this and among which, Baek and colleagues (2022) found an attenuation of frontal, parietal, and occipital responses towards predictable and thus learnable sequences in 6-month-olds. This fNIRS finding corresponds to the reduced prediction error in the predictive coding model (Friston, 2005). Moreover, a significantly greater functional connectivity in the frontoparietal network during predictable sequences (PS) compared to unpredictable sequences (UPS) was revealed (Baek et al., 2022), suggesting the involvement of the frontoparietal network in sequence learning and its early functioning at 6 months. Despite the evidence in adult studies (e.g., Koban et al., 2019; Leong et al., 2017), it was the first study demonstrating the involvement of the frontoparietal network during sequence learning in infant brains. For the current study, we plan to carry out a replication of Baek et al (2022) on 8-month-olds to confirm the potential functional role the frontoparietal network plays during sequence learning on an additional group of infants at a slightly older age, providing more evidence for the neural underpinnings of this ability. Infants wear an fNIRS headgear (NIRx Sport, 48 channels) when presented with both PS and UPS conditions in a counterbalanced order across participants (i.e., PS first or UPS first). For the analysis, besides the univariate analysis comparing brain activations towards PS and UPS, the background functional connectivity approach, which regresses out synchronized task-evoked responses, will also be applied to examine interactions between regions during learning. We expect to replicate the attenuation effect in the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobe, as well as the effect of greater functional connectivity in the frontoparietal network during learning in 8-month-old infants.

title_r: Handedness and Brain Network Lateralization: A Conceptual Replication of Johnstone et al. (2021)
abstract_r: The two hemispheres of the human brain are functionally asymmetric, or lateralized. However, how that lateralization is related to hand dominance (handedness) has not been a straightforward line of inquiry. Previously, Mazoyer et al. (2014) documented the distribution of handedness related to language lateralization and noted that while right handers are mostly left-language dominant or bilateral, left handers are mostly left-language dominant and bilateral with a small subgroup being right-language dominant. This subgroup of right-language dominant left handers is intriguing given a recent finding that this pattern of atypical language dominance (right lateralization) is associated with global shifts in cortical organization (Labache et al., 2023). Similarly, Zago et al. (2016) identified a relationship between handedness and lateralization specific to left-handers. This was such that, in a group of left handers with a strong left-hand preference, there was a negative correlation between language lateralization and spatial attention lateralization (Zago et al., 2016). Beyond functional networks related to language and spatial attention, Johnstone et al. (2021) compared left and right handers for hemispheric dominance strength across verbal fluency, face perception, body perception, and scene perception. Left handers with typical patterns of lateralization (e.g., left-lateralized verbal fluency) were found to be less lateralized for language, face perception, and body perception than right handers with typical patterns of lateralization (Johnstone et al., 2021). Given this intriguing difference in lateralization strength between left and right handers across multiple functional networks, we propose the following set of conceptual replications. First, we propose to examine group differences in language task lateralization in a sample of adults. Next, we intend to explore group differences in lateralization using a resting-state fMRI-derived measure of lateralization across eight functional networks. Finally, we will perform several exploratory analyses surrounding left handers with reduced lateralization, and right and left handers with reversed network laterality, among others.

title_r: Resource scarcity priming and face perception: A replication and extension of Study 1 of Rodeheffer et al. (2012) in Taiwan
abstract_r: Rodeheffer et al. (2012) showed that when people perceive resource scarcity, they are more likely to judge racially ambiguous people as out-group members. This research is important because it suggests that in-group narrowing due to resource scarcity can occur “unconsciously” in the “perception” stage, before attitudes and behaviors. However, there are two challenges regarding this finding: generalizability and replicability. To address these issues, we conduct replication research of Rodeheffer et al.'s (2012) Study 1 in Taiwan. Additionally, we aim to explore the mediators and moderators of the resource scarcity priming effect on face perception.

title_r: Bartels_JournConsRes_2015_mrZ - Chandler_579 - Direct Replication
abstract_r: This study consists of two parts, a pilot study and a replication study. Pilot Study. To support the replication study, we will conduct a pilot test to identify a suitable product or product category to include in the study materials for this replication. A suitable product or product category is one that between 35% and 80% of people are willing to purchase. Replication Study. This study will replicate Study 1a of Bartels and Urminsky (2015), which found that cueing the opportunity cost potentiates the relationship between connectedness to the future self and choosing not to spend money. The relationship between caring about the future outcomes (as measured by the average of the two connectedness to the future self items) and choosing to save (as opposed to purchase) is only present when participants are reminded of the opportunity costs of purchasing. This reflects the following claim from the paper's abstract: “[C]ues that highlight opportunity costs reduce spending primarily when people …are more connected to their future selves.” The claim is tested by assessing the significance of the difference between two correlation coefficients using a z-test: correlation between an index of participants’ measured connection to future self and a dichotomous choice to spend or not spend money when opportunity cost is highlighted (point-biserial correlation r(43) = 0.41), versus the correlation between the connectedness measure and the dichotomous choice when opportunity cost is not highlighted (point-biserial correlation (r(45) = 0.04). This yielded a significant difference between correlation coefficients, z = 2.14, p < 0.05.

title_r: Calibration information reduces bias during estimation of factorials: A (partial) replication and extension of Tversky and Kahneman (1973)
abstract_r: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) found that, under time pressure, people massively underestimated the expansion of 8! (correct value 40,320), and this bias was mitigated for participants presented the descending (8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1; Median=2,250) vs. ascending order (1x2x3x4x5x6x7x8; Median=512). In a first-ever replication (N=140), we also found predominant underestimation, but no significant between-subjects descending vs. ascending order effect. However, when participants then estimated the opposite order, we reproduced this order effect within-subjects. Finally, participants received calibration information (the correct value of 6! or 10!) and again estimated both orders of 8!. Participants who received 10! made more accurate estimates for 8! (Median=38,000), which did not differ statistically from the correct value. Participants who received 6! still grossly underestimated (Median=2,678.5), despite 8! being closer to 6! than 10! in linear and log units. Thus, we surprisingly found the classic factorial estimation bias only within-subjects, and provide evidence for how calibration can reduce it.

title_r: Replicating and Extending Experiment 1 from Garcea and Mahon (2012) using only picture stimuli
abstract_r: In daily life, when we need to have a drink, we try to find a cup. Would we find it faster according to the object's function or based on the manipulation of the object? Garcea and Mahon (2012) used a modified neuropsychological test that used the response time (RT) and accuracy as the dependent measures. Three objects were presented in a triangular arrangement at the same time in one trial. The top object was the target. One of the two lower objects had a similar function to the target object, and the other had a similar manipulation to the target object. The participants had to judge which object of a triad had a similar function to the target object or which object had a similar manipulation to the target. Results showed that manipulation judgments were slower than function judgments, regardless of whether the objects were shown as words or as pictures. This finding suggests that it is unnecessary to first retrieve knowledge of object manipulation before one can retrieve knowledge of object function (Garcea & Mahon, 2012). The results of Garcea and Mahon contrast with the outcomes of another study (Ruotolo & Kalénine, 2020). Ruotolo and Kalénine (2020) used the Visual-World-Paradigm to present four objects to the participants at the same time. One of the four objects was the target. The rest of the objects were distractors that could have a similar function as the target, or a similar manipulation, or be completely unrelated to the target. They found that distractors with similar functions or manipulations attracted more attention from participants than unrelated distractors. Moreover, the results showed that eye fixations to objects with a similar manipulation occurred faster relative to the objects with a similar function. This is in contrast with Garcea and Mahon’s study, as it suggests that similarity in manipulation leads to quicker attentional orienting than similarity in function. In the current experiment, we will replicate Experiment 1 of Garcea and Mahon (2012), using only the condition with object pictures. Aside from testing the replicability of Garcea and Mahon’s finding of faster reaction times for function than for manipulation similarity, we will also examine whether differences in real-world size might have contributed to this difference in reaction time. Specifically, we reasoned that one explanation for the finding of slower manipulation judgments than function judgments in Garcea and Mahon (2012) could be that if the target object and two lower objects in the stimulus displayed differed in their real-world size in some trials, this might have caused participants to be slower on these trials as they would need to imagine the manipulation of two objects (the target and the non-target) of different sizes in the real world to decide which one matches the target. Arguably, this would slow participants down (because it takes more time to imagine two manipulations for objects that differ in real-world size than to imagine the manipulation for two objects with similar real-world size), and it, therefore, could explain why this study found slower RTs for manipulation judgments. In replicating the experiment, we are able to make use of the exact same stimuli as Garcea and Mahon (2012), as they kindly made these available to us. According to the classification from Fisher and Sperandio (2018), 10 of the 35 objects used by Garcea and Mahon can be classified as ”big objects” and the rest of the objects can be classified as “small objects”. title_r: Do infrahumanization or affective prejudice drive teacher discrimination against Romani students? A conceptual replication of Bruneau et al. (2020) in Germany.
abstract_r: Bruneau’s work repeatedly focused on the Roma minority, worldwide, one of the most dehumanized ethnic groups. In a preregistered design, we replicated one of his previous studies (Bruneau et al., 2020) in a different national context (i.e., Germany) in testing the hypotheses that pre-service teachers make biased educational-track recommendations discriminating against Romani students and that infrahumanization drives this behaviour. In line with Bruneau et al.’s work, pre-service teachers judged placing self-identified Romani students into lower educational tracks as more appropriate than self-identified Turkish-origin and German students, despite equal academic performance. Although participants infrahumanized Romani students at greater levels compared to non-Romani students, in contrast to the Bruneau et al.’s study, educational-track recommendations were positively associated with affective prejudice but not with infrahumanization. These findings extend Bruneau’s insights on dehumanization, prejudice, and discrimination against people of Romani background, highlighting the role of the social context in which these associations are studied.

title_r: Social Value Orientation and Attachment: A Replication and Extension of Van Lange et al. (1997)
abstract_r: We report a replication and extension of a landmark finding from Van Lange et al.'s (1997) Study 1, which showed an association between Social Value Orientation and attachment security. We report a close, but not exact, replication, as we tested the premise with measures of attachment that are considered superior in comparison to the measures used by Van Lange et al. (1997), due to subsequent psychometric improvements. With a sample (N = 879) sufficiently large to detect d = .19 (and larger than the original study, N = 573), we failed to replicate the effect. Psychometric analysis showed that our attachment measures were reliable and valid, demonstrating theoretically predicted associations with other outcomes. We call for the use of solid psychometric measures to investigate the nomological network of Social Value Orientation. Based on the available evidence provided by Van Lange et al. (1997) and our study, we interpret as there being no evidence for the link between attachment security and Social Value Orientation, but further replication research that uses solid measures and large samples can provide more definite conclusions about the association between attachment and Social Value Orientation.

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Ballard et al. (2016) is that in a multiple goal-pursuit task with a total of 24 conditions varying dual-goal difficulty, relative goal position, and goal frame (approach vs. avoid), participants would be less likely to prioritize the goal in the worse position than the optimal model when pursuing approach goals but more likely than the optimal model when pursuing avoidance goals. title_r: Effects of the Generic Masculine and Its Alternatives in Germanophone Countries: A Multi-Lab Replication and Extension of Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001).
abstract_r: In languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-inclusive form. Although meant as 'generic,' this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language. Specifically, listeners and readers are less likely to think of women when this form is used. Due to the societal relevance of gender-inclusive language, we directly replicated and extended a classic study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2) in a multi-lab setting and as a registered confirmatory report. We prompted participants from German-speaking countries to name up to three celebrities each in six categories (e.g., 'Name three politicians' or '(…) singers'). We then counted how often participants mentioned women. Participants were either prompted with the generic-masculine form, a neutralized control form or one out of three gender-inclusive forms. Our data from twelve labs and N = 2,697 participants replicated the original effect: when prompted with gender-inclusive forms participants mentioned more women than when the generic masculine and the control form were used. Moreover, the effect remained present in multilevel models and when controlling for participants' sex and their perceived base rate in these celebrity categories (i.e., the expected proportion of women). Other variables, such as political orientation or preference for gender-inclusive language, did not show large effects, either. We discuss the differences between specific gender-inclusive forms (e.g., the internal-I vs. feminine-masculine forms), implications for regulations and guidelines, as well as implications for non-binary and gender-diverse people.

title_r: A direct replication of Huth et al., 2012
abstract_r: We aim to directly replicate Huth et al., 2012 using the publicly available data provided by the original authors. In this experiment, subjects viewed multiple hours of naturalistic movies while lying in an MRI scanner while functional data (blood oxygenation dependent signal; BOLD) data was recorded. At each second of the movie, category labels were identified. These labels consisted of objects, agents, and actions that may have comprised that moment in time. Following this, a voxel-wise encoding model was constructed using the labels. It is this model we aim to reproduce. Essentially, this model can be used to predict brain data, based on measured responses to stimuli. It is done at the individual subject level and for every voxel of the brain. Following the encoding model procedure, a semantic map is created using dimensionality reduction techniques-again at the single subject granularity.

title_r: Not toeing the number line for simple arithmetic: Two large-n conceptual replications of Mathieu et al. (Cognition, 2016, Experiment 1)
abstract_r: We conducted two conceptual replications of Experiment 1 in Mathieu, Gourjon, Couderc, Thevenot, and Prado (2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2015.10.002). They tested a sample of 34 French adults on mixed-operation blocks of single-digit addition (4 + 3) and subtraction (4 – 3) with the three problem elements (O1, +/-, O2) presented sequentially. Addition was 34 ms faster if O2 appeared 300 ms after the operation sign and displaced 5° to the right of central fixation, whereas subtraction was 19 ms faster when O2 was displaced to the left. Replication Experiment 1 (n = 74 recruited at the University of Saskatchewan) used the same non-zero addition and subtraction problems and trial event sequence as Mathieu et al., but participants completed blocks of pure addition and pure subtraction followed by the mixed-operation condition used by Mathieu et al. Addition RT showed a 32 ms advantage with O2 shifted rightward relative to leftward but only in mixed-operation blocks. There was no effect of O2 position on subtraction RT. Experiment 2 (n = 74) was the same except mixed-operation blocks occurred before the pure-operation blocks. There was an overall 13 ms advantage with O2 shifted right relative to leftward but no interaction with operation or with mixture (i.e., pure vs mixed operations). Nonetheless, the rightward RT advantage was statistically significant for both addition and subtraction only in mixed-operation blocks. Taken together with the robust effects of mixture in Experiment 1, the results suggest that O2 position effects in this paradigm might reflect task specific demands associated with mixed operations.

title_r: The future failed: No evidence for precognition in a large scale replication attempt of Bem (2011).
abstract_r: Precognition describes the ability to anticipate information about a future event before this event occurs. The goal of our study was to test the occurrence of precognition by trying to replicate three experiments of the most central study in the field (Bem, 2011, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). In this study, Bem time-reversed wellestablished psychological effects so that a “causal” stimulus appeared after the participants gave their response. We conducted two priming experiments and a free recall experiment in the backward “precognition” version and, as a control manipulation, in the classic forward version. More than 2000 participants participated via the Internet; thus, our study had high statistical power. The results showed no precognition effects at all. We further conducted exploratory post hoc analyses on different variables and questionnaire items and found some significant effects. Further studies should validate these potentially interesting findings by using theory-driven hypotheses, preregistrations, and confirmatory data analyses.

title_r: Pragmatic and Syntactic Influences on Adjective Interpretation: A Conceptual Replication of Wittenberg, Barner, and Levy (2016)
abstract_r: This project investigates how sentence structure and adjective order influence the interpretation of gradable adjectives in referential contexts. The study tests whether definite noun phrases in commands trigger an existential presupposition that leads participants to adjust their interpretive threshold for scalar adjectives, for example, selecting a medium-height object as “tall” when no maximally tall object of the correct color is present. The study also manipulates adjective order (e.g., “tall red” vs. “red tall”), which systematically influences interpretation, showing that both sentence type and syntactic structure affect how scalar descriptions are resolved in context. Participants interact with the fictional character Fiba, a small alien who guides them through a series of object-identification tasks involving linguistic prompts and visual arrays. Each trial involves two visual displays. In the first, participants see an array of ten objects varying along one spatial dimension and in color and respond to a verbal prompt. In the second display, four new objects of the same type appear in a third color, accompanied by a follow-up prompt (e.g., “How many tall buildings would Fiba count here?”). This two-part structure allows the study to assess both immediate referential interpretation and whether interpretive thresholds persist beyond the initial prompt. This study is a conceptual replication of a project described in an abstract by Wittenberg, Barner, and Levy (2016).

title_r: Revisiting the impact of singularity on the Identified Victim Effect: Replication and extension of Kogut and Ritov (2005a) Study 2
abstract_r: The identified victim effect is the phenomenon in which people tend to contribute more to identified than to unidentified victims. Kogut and Ritov (2005a) found that the identified victim effect was limited to a single victim and driven by empathic emotions. In a pre-registered experiment with an online U.S. American MTurk sample on CloudResearch (N = 2003), we conducted a close replication and extension of Experiment 2 from Kogut and Ritov (2005a). The replication findings failed to provide empirical support for the identified single victim effect hypothesis since we found no evidence of differences in willingness to contribute when comparing a single identified victim to a single unidentified victim. (η2p = .00, 90% CI [0.00, 0.00]), and no indication for the target article’s interaction between singularity and identifiability (original: η2p = .062, 90% CI [0.01, 0.15]; replication: η2p = .00, 90% CI [0.00, 0.00]). Extending the replication to conduct a conceptual replication of Kogut and Ritov (2007), we investigated a boundary condition of the effect - group belonging. We found support for an ingroup bias in helping behaviors and indications for empathic emotions and perceived responsibility contributing to this effect. We discuss differences between our study and the target article and implications for the literature on the identified victim effect.

title_r: Reciprocal associations between executive function and academic achievement: A conceptual replication of Schmitt et al. (2017)
abstract_r: The goal of the current study was to conduct a conceptual replication of the reciprocal associations between executive function (EF) and academic achievement reported in Schmitt et al. (2017, https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000193). Using two independent samples (N (STAR) = 279, and N (Pathways) = 277), we examined whether the patterns of associations between EF and achievement across preschool and kindergarten reported in Schmitt et al. (2017) replicated using the same model specifications, similar EF and achievement measures, and across a similar developmental age period. Specifically, in the STAR sample, EF predicted math achievement from preschool to kindergarten, and kindergarten to first grade. In the Pathways sample, EF at kindergarten predicted both math and literacy achievement in first grade. However, contrary to the original findings, we were unable to replicate the bidirectional associations between math achievement and EF in either of the replication samples. Overall, the current conceptual replication has revealed that bidirectional associations between EF and academic skills might not be robust to slight differences in EF measures and number of measurement occasions, which has implications for our understanding of the development EF and academic skills across early childhood. title_r: The Psychological Typhoon Eye Effect: A Conceptual Replication and Examination of Working Mechanisms in the 2020 Petrinja Earthquake
abstract_r: The psychological typhoon eye effect is a relatively newly described effect and entails that those living in the epicenter of natural disasters or public emergencies exhibit lower levels of psychological distress and health concerns than those living further away from the epicenter (Li et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020). The effect has been described for several natural disasters and emergencies such as the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake and the COVID-19 pandemic. Previous studies suggest that the psychological typhoon eye effect may be related to subjective risk perceptions and perceived coping efficacy. In December 2020, an earthquake of a magnitude of 6.4 on the Richter scale occurred near Petrinja, Croatia. Seven people died, 26 were injured and materialistic damages amounted to 5.5 billion euros. The earthquake was the strongest one experienced in Croatia in over 180 years. This natural disaster provides an appropriate context for further examining the psychological typhoon eye effect. The aim of this study is to conceptually replicate the psychological typhoon eye effect using the original measures utilized by Li et al., (2008), and to try to replicate the same effect using the validated DASS scale. Furthermore, in case of a successful replication, a secondary aim is to examine the possible working mechanisms of the effect. Previous research has found that the psychological typhoon eye effect might be mediated by the coping self-efficacy. Our study would like to examine if coping self-efficacy really mediates the relationship between the level of devastation and the level of psychological distress that individuals experience.

title_r: Fear generalization: a direct replication of Lissek et al. (2010)
abstract_r: Panic disorder is a prevalent and chronic anxiety disorder characterized by reoccurring panic attacks (Kessler et al., 2006). Panic attacks are sudden, often unexpected periods of intense fear, that can be accompanied by physical symptoms like sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, or others (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Fear is often caused by anxiety or the anticipation of danger. However, prior research has shown that such fear may not always be associated with only the stimuli that had been previously associated with a panic attack (e.g. getting a panic attack while being in the gym, so now the gym is predictive of a panic attack), but generalized to similar stimuli (e.g. all types of gyms). Lissek et al. (2010) have researched this fear generalisation and found that individuals diagnosed with panic disorder generalise fear more readily than healthy controls. Their findings led to numerous experimental and clinical studies, but no direct replication of this study has been done yet. However, replication of Lissek et al. (2010) is urgently needed for at least three reasons. First, an unpublished direct replication of the initial study design was unsuccessful. Second, Lissek et al.’s (2010) results are already being used in research that attempts to block or reduce fear generalization. Because of this, it is important to determine whether generalization has a role in panic disorder indeed and consequently whether relevant intervention studies may be useful for reducing panic symptomatology. Third, since a single lab replication is often not sufficient to assess the replicability of a study, the current research will replicate the study across multiple labs. In accordance with Lissek et al. (2010), we predict that participants with panic disorder will show more generalized avoidance compared to control subjects. Objective: The main goal of this research is to test whether individuals with a panic disorder diagnosis differ in the level of fear generalization compared to matched controls. This would be a direct replication of the seminal study by Lissek et al. (2010). Study design: This study will be a blinded between-subject study employing individuals with a panic diagnosis and healthy matched controls. Study population: Per clinic 25 individuals aged 18-65 with a prior diagnosis of a panic disorder and matched controls with no history of a mental disorder will be recruited, making a total of 50 individuals per clinic. Intervention: This study uses a fear generalization procedure consisting of three phases: pre-acquisition, fear acquisition, and a generalization test. In the pre-acquisition phase participants will see a small and a large circle, which will serve as the conditioned stimuli (CS). During the acquisition phase, the smallest and largest circles will serve as CS+ (the danger cue) and CS- (the safety cue), counterbalanced. One of these circles will be followed by shock administration (CS+), and the other circle is not followed by a shock (CS-). In the generalization test phase, participants see both CSs, as well as eight intermediate circles (generalization stimuli; GSs). Fear responses will be measured primarily by measuring startle responses, via electromyography (EMG), to a loud noise during the CS and GS presentations. Additionally, risk ratings as well as the accompanying reaction times (RT) will be collected by asking participants to estimate the level of risk during the experiment, with the available answers being 1 = no risk, 2 = moderate risk, and 3 = high risk. Main study parameters/endpoints: Electromyography (EMG) responses and reported risk ratings for each CS and GS. Online risk ratings and reaction time for the risk ratings. Both electromyograph responses and risk ratings will be used to test between-group differences in the course of learning. A self-report of anxiety levels after the main experiment will be used for testing between group differences. The Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al. 1997), State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (Spielberger et al. 1983) and Beck Depression Inventory (Beck et al. 1996) will be used to test for between group differences before the beginning of the study.

title_r: Materiality in the CSR-investor reaction relationship: A replication and extension of Flammer (2013)
abstract_r: We replicate and extend Flammer’s (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility (CSR). Flammer found that investors reacted positively to eco-friendly events and negatively to eco-harmful events from 1980-2009 and that reaction to positive events decreased while reaction to negative events increased over time. We find similar results for Flamer’s original sample and an expanded sample including the same type of firms (U.S.-listed public firms) from 1980-2019. We then extend Flammer’s results by examining how materiality affects investor reaction over time. We find that investors only react to material events and that positive reaction to material eco-friendly events diminishes over time, while negative reaction to material eco-harmful events increases over time, suggesting that materiality is a key factor driving Flammer’s results.

title_r: Conceptual Replication of Mussweiler and Strack (2000, Study 2) Using Temperature Anchoring and a Season-Related LDT
abstract_r: This study conceptually replicates Study 2 by Mussweiler and Strack (2000), which tested the Selective Accessibility Model (SAM) of the anchoring effect. According to SAM, anchoring occurs through the selective activation of anchor-consistent knowledge, driven by hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming. In the original study, participants first completed a standard comparative anchoring task (judging whether the average price of a new car was higher or lower than U.S. $11,000 or $22,000), followed by a Lexical Decision Task (LDT). After the LDT, they estimated the average price of a new car in an absolute judgment task. The results supported SAM, demonstrating a significant interaction between anchor condition and word type in the LDT. In the present study, we conducted a conceptual replication of this design, using an anchoring task involving temperature estimates and an LDT employing season-related words (summer- and winter-related words).

title_r: Exact replication of Kozłowska et al. (2023) The Napoleon complex, revisited: Those high on the Dark Triad traits are dissatisfied with their height and are short
abstract_r: The dark triad is a personality taxonomy that, unlike the Big Five, focuses primarily on negative social personality traits: Psychopathy, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism. It has attracted much attention over the past 20 years after Paulhurst et al. coined the term in 2002, and research on the correlation between Dark Triad traits and other factors has increased drastically. One such example is the correlation of the Dark Triad traits with height dissatisfaction and with physical height itself. Kozłowska et al. recently published these results (2023) and concluded that the theory of the so-called "Napoleon complex" seems to be correct. Briefly summarized, the "Napoleon complex" is the idea that smaller men are at a disadvantage and compensate for this through negative behavior. In their results, Kozłowska et al. found that there was a significant negative correlation between Dark Triad traits and height in men. They also found that those scoring high on Dark Triad traits are more dissatisfied with their own height. This is interesting because it is one of the first studies to examine the relationship between Dark Triad traits and attitudes towards height, as well as physical height. Other studies of height in psychology often show no, or a positive, correlation. Therefore, it is of interest to conduct an exact replication study to verify or reject these findings in order to strengthen the current evidence base and thus lay the groundwork for further research on this topic.
