title_r: Petersen_Cognition_2017_yJwG - Snyder - Direct Replication - 9ky
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Petersen et al. (2017) is from Experiment 1, in which participants were to report the identity of a post-masked letter that was presented for varying exposure durations immediately after an auditory cue or no cue. Equations based on a theory of visual attention were fit to the data for each participant (see equations p. 74), separately for cue and no-cue trials, with the result that the parameter for processing speed (v) was faster following an auditory cue, compared to no-cue trials. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “[P]hasic auditory alertness affects visual perception by increasing the visual processing speed and lowering the threshold of conscious perception (Experiment 1).” Using the equations shown on page 74, for each condition (no cue, 85 dB cue), v and t0 parameters were estimated separately for each subject by a maximum-likelihood estimation using the Nelder-Mead simplex optimization algorithm. To improve the estimation of parameters, a high-threshold guessing model was introduced, which assumes that with a certain probability, subjects guess randomly among the 20 letters if they fail to encode the presented letter into visual short term memory. Paired t tests were used to compare these parameter values between conditions. This analysis yielded that there was faster processing speed v, t(27) = 4.71, p < 0.001, dz = 0.89, and a lower perceptual threshold t0, t(27) = 3.52, p = 0.002, dz = 0.67, when an 85 dB SPL cue is presented prior to the letter, compared to when no cue was present.

title_r: Disgust and the rubber hand illusion: A registered replication report of Jalal, Krishnakumar, and Ramachandran (2015)
abstract_r: Heightened experience of disgust is a feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), particularly in contamination-related OCD (C-OCD). Previous studies of the rubber hand illusion (RHI) reported that the sense of body ownership is related to the interaction between vision, touch, and proprioception. A recent study demonstrated a link between the RHI and disgust, reporting an interaction between these three perceptual modalities and disgust (Jalal, Krishnakumar, Ramachandran, 2015). However, there have been no direct replications of this initial study. We proposed a direct replication of Jalal et al.’s (2015) study. Based on a power analysis, we examined a minimum of 119 participants to determine whether placing contamination-related stimuli on a rubber hand causes OCD-like disgust among healthy participants while experiencing the RHI. In addition, we tested the cross-cultural validity of the previous findings, testing whether Japanese participants experience more intense disgust when a rubber hand and a participant’s hidden hand were stroked synchronously, compared with asynchronous stroking. This replication provides insight into potential applications of this study protocol in the treatment of OCD.

title_r: FT56.6 - Does Expressive Writing Blunt the Effects of Math Anxiety on Math Performance? A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Park et al. (2014)
abstract_r: Abstract: Math anxiety (MA) is negatively related to math performance. One proposed intervention with potential to disrupt the MA-math performance link is expressive writing. The current study aimed to conceptually replicate Park and colleagues (2014). In that study, the authors concluded that expressive writing effectively boosted math anxious students’ performance. In our current sample of 168 college students, participants randomly assigned to the expressive writing condition were no more accurate at posttest than were other participants assigned to a math self-concept intervention, active control, or passive control. Additionally, participants in the math self-concept and active control conditions reported lower state MA immediately following the intervention; participants in the expressive writing and passive control conditions reported no differences between pretest and posttest state MA. The current study provides boundary conditions for the effectiveness of expressive writing interventions in ameliorating MA during difficult math tasks and illuminates potential mechanisms underlying MA. title_r: Do Institutional Characteristics Predict Markers of Adulthood? A Close Replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016)
abstract_r: Recent research reveals that some variability in personality differences can be explained by contextual factors such as location. Though little research has systematically evaluated how such variables predict individual differences in Emerging Adulthood, Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) revealed that characteristics of one's university such as selectivity and liberal arts classification did predict respondents' perceived importance and attainment of milestones associated with adulthood. As a close replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016), the present findings supported our pre-registered hypotheses that liberal arts status predicted decreased perceived importance and lower attainment of some constructs of Markers of Adulthood, but did not support predictions that selectivity would also predict such differences. Our findings provide further evidence of the institutional effects that emerge in multi-sample individual difference studies and extends those findings with a broader and more diverse sample than was considered previously.

abstract_r: This study is part of a research project aiming to explore pain perception biases in different contexts (including physical, psychological and social pain), in turn seeking to better understand and address the factors that contribute to the health disparities faced by neurodivergent populations. Therefore, the project investigates potential biases in the perception of pain when experienced by neurodivergent individuals, and explores how these biases contribute to health disparities. Previous research has identified health disparities between neurodivergent and non-neurodivergent populations, such as higher premature mortality in individuals with ADHD and autism. These differences may stem in part from differences in access to health care services, which may be influenced by implicit biases in others' pain perception. Therefore this first experiment aims to determine whether a bias exists in judgements about physical pain when the person experiencing the pain is neurodivergent. title_r: Reproduction Package for FSE 2024 Submission `A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification'
abstract_r:
Reproduction Package A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification Abstract This artifact is a reproduction package for the manuscript “A Replication Study of Interpolation-Based Hardware Model Checking for Software Verification”, submitted to FSE 2024. In the replication study, the transferability of the results reported by two prior publications on interpolation-based hardware model checking to software verification is investigated. The two publications are (1) Interpolation-Sequence-Based Model Checking (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009) and (2) Intertwined Forward-Backward Reachability Analysis Using Interpolants (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). The purpose of this artifact is to reproduce the experiments conducted to validate the claims made in the above two publications. The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the evaluation of the replication study, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code and binaries of CPAchecker (at revision 44757 of branch “cfa-single-loop-transformation”), which implements the verification algorithms compared in the submitted manuscript, the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark suite, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments. This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The VM has all the required dependencies installed. If you test this artifact with it, all installation steps below can be skipped. Contents This artifact contains the following items: README.*: this documentation fse2024-paper483.pdf: the manuscript submitted to FSE 2024 License.txt: license information of the artifact cpachecker/: a directory containing the source code and precompiled binaries of CPAchecker sv-benchmarks/: a directory containing the SV-COMP ’23 benchmark tasks used in our evaluation data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data produced from our full evaluation (used in the manuscript, under paper-results/) and from a demo experiment (prepared for this reproduction package, under demo-results/) bench-defs/: a directory containing the benchmark and table definitions of the experiments (used by BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking) This readme file will guide you through the following steps: Execute CPAchecker Perform experiments View the experimental results Execute CPAchecker System requirements for CPAchecker To execute CPAchecker, Java Runtime Environment (JRE) version ≥ 17 is required. For more information, please refer to cpachecker/INSTALL.md. Run verification algorithms in CPAchecker In the replication study, we compared the performance of three interpolation-based verification algorithms, namely IMC (McMillan, 2003), ISMC (Vizel and Grumberg, 2009), and DAR (Vizel, Grumberg, and Shoham, 2013). ISMC and DAR are the algorithms proposed by the two prior publications, respectively, and IMC is the first interpolation-based model-checking approach, which was used as the baseline in the two publications. All the algorithms have been implemented in CPAchecker. Below we list the commands to run the evaluated verification algorithms. These example commands use sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c as the input program. You can replace it with another program. IMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolation \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ -setprop imc.loopBoundIncrementStrategyForBMC=CONST \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
ISMC: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop imc.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
DAR: 
# expected verification result: TRUE cpachecker/scripts/cpa.sh -32 -spec sv-comp-reachability \ -bmc-interpolationDualSequence \ -setprop cpa.predicate.memoryAllocationsAlwaysSucceed=true \ -setprop cpa.predicate.refinement.verifyInterpolants=true \ -setprop cfa.transformIntoSingleLoop=true \ -setprop dar.fallBack=false \ sv-benchmarks/c/loop-invariants/even.c
For more information on how to run CPAchecker, see cpachcker/README.md. Understand the output of CPAchecker The following is an example output shown on the console after an analysis is finished. 
[...redacted...] Verification result: TRUE. No property violation found by chosen configuration. More details about the verification run can be found in the directory "./output". Graphical representation included in the file "./output/Report.html".
There are 3 possible outcomes of the verification result: TRUE: the program is “safe”, i.e., it satisfies the given safety property FALSE: the program is “unsafe”, i.e., it contains a violation to the given safety property UNKNOWN: the analysis was inconclusive CPAchecker also generates an HTML report for conveniently browsing the results. Please refer to cpachecker/doc/Report.md for more information. Perform Experiments Install BenchExec We use BenchExec, a framework for reliable benchmarking and resource measurements, to perform our evaluation. Please follow the installation guide to set up the benchmarking environment. Experimental settings The settings are described in the XML file bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. This XML file is used by BenchExec for limiting computing resources and scheduling runs. For the execution of a task, a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 1800 seconds of CPU time, and 15 GB of memory is imposed. Run the Full Evaluation To run the full experiment over the 8813 benchmark tasks reported in the manuscript, execute the following command. 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/
Run Partial Evaluation The full evaluation requires roughly 6 months of CPA time on a 3.40 GHz core. To run the experiment on a subset of benchmark tasks, you could add -t <tasks_name> to the above command, where <task_name> refer to the task names defined in bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml. For example: 
benchexec bench-defs/cpachecker-slt.xml \ --tool-directory cpachecker/ -o results/ \ --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir . --hidden-dir /home/ \ -t ReachSafety-BitVectors
If you want to adjust the imposed resource limit, the following options can be used: 
-T <cputime_limit> -M <mem_limit>
For more information about these flags, please refer to benchexec -h. View the Experimental Results Generate Tables After the execution of an experiment, you can generate an interactive HTML by table-generator. Simply run: 
table-generator -x bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml \ -f html --no-diff -o results
Note that if the experiment is only performed on a single task set (via -t <tasks_name>), you have to replace bench-defs/overall-slt-stats.xml by bench-defs/subset-slt-stats.xml. Results from Our Experiments The results (both raw and processed data) of the partial run (on ReachSafety-BitVectors) and the full run obtained by our machines are in folders data-submission/demo-results/ and data-submission/paper-results/, respectively. The generated HTML tables are named overall-slt-stats.table.html under each respective folder. In the replication study, there are eight hypotheses extracted from the two prior publications. We list them below to make this document more standalone. For details, please refer to the bundled manuscript. Claims in the ISMC Publication H1.A: ISMC is faster than IMC on tasks with property violation. H1.B: ISMC is faster than IMC when IMC finds a proof only at high unrolling bounds. H1.C: Overall, ISMC is faster than IMC (by 30 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H1.A also for software verification, but H1.B and H1.C did not hold. Claims in the DAR Publication H2.A: For DAR, the ratio between iterations using global strengthening to the total number of iterations is less than 0.5 in most tasks. H2.B: IMC finds a proof slower than DAR in many tasks even though it has a smaller convergence length. H2.C: DAR computes more interpolants than IMC. H2.D: DAR’s run-time is more sensitive to the sizes of interpolants than IMC. H2.E: Overall, DAR is faster than IMC (by 36 % in this experiment). In our experiments, we confirmed H2.A and H2.C also for software verification, but H2.B, H2.D, and H2.E did not hold. title_r: Direct replication of a research claim from Goerg et al. (2010), in Journal of Labor Economics
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Goerg et al. (2010) is that the discriminating reward scheme under the production function of complementarity achieves almost maximum efficiency, whereas it leads to significantly lower efficiency rates under the production function of substitutability. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Our experimental results demonstrate that unequal rewards can potentially increase productivity by facilitating coordination and that the effect strongly interacts with the exact shape of the production function." The study implements an experiment where three players work on a joint project and exert costly efforts. Their total sum of effort determines the number of some goods produced by the joint project for a given production function. The payoff of a player is given by productivity (i.e., the number of produced goods) multiplied by an individual reward, minus the cost of effort. The authors create four different treatments by manipulating the characteristics of the production function (either a function of complementarity or of substitutability) as well as of the reward scheme (either a symmetrical or a discriminating mechanism). The evidence for the finding used by the SCORE program comes from a comparison, with a rank-sum test, of the mean effort level in rounds 1-5 between the 345COM and 345SUB conditions, which are both subject to the discriminating treatment. Focusing on the discriminating reward scheme, overall effort levels are significantly higher (p = .0004, two-tailed) under a production function of complementarity than under a production function of substitutability: 91.7% of all effort decisions in 345COM are to work hard, compared to only 65.3% in treatment 345SUB.

title_r: DRIVER DISTRACTION: A REPLICATION AND EXTENSION OF BROWN, TICKNER & SIMMONS (1969)
abstract_r: The study reported here replicates and extends a study by Brown et al (1969) in which concurrent performance of a verbal reasoning task was shown to disrupt drivers' ability to judge whether or not the car they were driving would fit through gaps of different widths. In the present study, the test-track-based gap judgement task was again combined with the original verbal reasoning task, but also with a task requiring largely executive (PASAT) or visuo-spatial (imagery-based clock face comparison) processing. Results showed that ability to perform the verbal reasoning and PASAT task was reliably reduced when combined with gap judgement, but effects were largely absent when the secondary task imposed a high degree of visuo-spatial load. Although no effect of concurrent tasks was observed on gap judgement, the results observed are consistent with the original findings, since substantial evidence of performance trade-off was observed. title_r: Replication Study: Google Effects on Memory, Exp. 2 (Sparrow et al., 2011)
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to replicate the findings of experiment 2 conducted by Sparrow et al. (2011) regarding the transactive memory theory and, specifically, the Google effect on memory. The experiment was designed to be an exact replication of the original study with minor changes to setting and materials. In the original experiment, participants first had to type a number of trivia statements and later completed a free recall memory task as well as a recognition task. The study followed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. Half of the participants were instructed to try to remember the statements, whilst the other half did not receive explicit memory instructions. In addition, in each memory condition, half of the participants believed the computer would save the typed statements for later access and the other half were told the statements were deleted after typing. Those participants who thought the typed statements would be erased remembered more statements in the free recall condition than participants thinking the statements were saved for later access. In addition, an interaction effect was found in the recognition task. Participants who were instructed to remember the statements in the erased-condition had the best recognition, whereas those who were told to remember the statements in the saved-condition had the worst recognition performance. The memory for those who were not explicitly told to remember the statements fell in between those other two conditions.

title_r: Do Reading Goals Make a Difference for Refutation Text Effectiveness? A conceptual replication of Asberger et al. (2024 )
abstract_r: There are many misconceptions about educational topics. For instance, it is a widespread assumption that differences in hemispheric dominance (left brain, right brain), originally and scientifically referring to task-related specialization in the brain, can explain individual differences between learners. To overcome such misconceptions, refutation texts appear to be a promising approach. However, it is yet an open question, which factors influence the effectiveness of refutation texts. One factor that possibly influences the effectiveness of refutation interventions may be individuals’ reading goals. A recent study (Asberger et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2024.2358480) showed mixed results regarding the influence of reading goals on conceptual change. We will follow up on their study to further investigate whether different reading goals (reading for an explanation vs. for entertainment) moderate potential effects of a refutation text to elicit conceptual change within preservice teachers about an educational neuromyth (i.e. hemispheric dominance). Specifically, we study in which way text type (refutation vs. traditional text), reading goal (for an explanation vs. for entertainment) and time (before vs. after reading the respective text type) interact and affect beliefs in the hemispheric dominance neuromyth and their confidence-accuracy. The primary change compared to Asberger et al. (2024) concerns the operationalization of the reading goal instructions.

title_r: Does approximate numeracy predict superior decision making beyond objective and subjective numeracy? Registered replication report on Schley and Peters (2014)
abstract_r: Everyday decision making requires dealing with numbers related to potential outcomes and their probabilities. A bulk of research from Judgement and Decision Making field (for a review see: Cokely et al., 2018; Garcia-Retamero, Sobkow, Petrova, Garrido, & Traczyk, 2019) showed that superior decision making is largely driven by individual differences in objective statistical numeracy—an ability to understand statistical and probability information and to use it in everyday contexts. Nevertheless, a few recent studies suggested that an ability to estimate quantities and to map symbolic numbers into mental number line may be an equally important predictor of decision making as objective numeracy. The aim of the present research is to replicate one of the first and most important studies showing this effect (study 2 from Schley & Peters, 2014; Psychological Science; more than 100 citations). In this study, 99 participants completed an adaptive decision task (a series of monetary gambles), enabling estimation of parameters from the Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Moreover, participants solved a number-line task to measure symbolic-number mapping (Siegler & Opfer, 2003), a set of mathematical tasks measuring objective numeracy (Weller et al., 2013) and answered few questions regarding demography (age, sex, income, education). The results of this study showed that participants with more exact symbolic-number mappings exhibited more linear value functions in a decision task. Moreover, more exact symbolic-number mapping mediated the relationship between objective numeracy and value-function parameters suggesting that this ability may (at least partially) explain the relationship between numeracy and decision making. In our research, we plan to extend this experimental procedure by including the Subjective Numeracy Scale (Fagerlin et al., 2007) as a measure of numeric confidence. This approach would allow us to test the replicability of the relationship between symbolic-number mapping and value function parameters as well as to compare the relative contribution of three types of numeric competencies: objective numeracy, approximate numeracy, and subjective numeracy proposed recently by Peters and Bjalkebring (2015).

title_r: Prevalence-induced Concept Change in the Judgement of Male Bodies: A Replication and Extension of Devine et al. (2023)
abstract_r: The following study aims to replicate H1b from Devine et al. (2023). Here, the authors found that men were sensitive to prevalence-induced concept changes (PICC) when judging whether male bodies varying in muscularity were muscular or not, but not when judging whether male bodies varying in body fat were overweight or not. Furthermore, they found that men were overall faster in judging whether a body is muscular compared to judging whether a body is overweight. Taken together, these results lead the authors to suspect that men might have an attentional bias towards idealized male bodies, which manifests in faster and more selective extraction of muscle-related body information. Thus, Devine et al. show that PICC may not represent a general perceptual effect, but rather could be moderated by the specific stimulus category. Our main goal of the current study is to replicate the effect found that the strength of PICC in the judgment of male bodies depends on the specific stimulus category (weight-related, muscle-related). Furthermore, we intend to replicate the difference in response times between the judgments of these stimulus categories. The study design will be adjusted to control for possible confounding factors such as the order of the presented stimulus category. In addition, the stimulus material (computer-generated male bodies) will be adapted in order to achieve better comparability between the stimulus categories. title_r: Direct replication of a research claim (Study 3) from Usta & Häubl (2011), in Journal of Marketing Research
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Usta & Häubl (2011) is that remembering a decision that a person delegated in the past depletes self-regulatory resources more than remembering an independently made decision (H3). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Moreover, when people remember a past decision that they delegated, their self-control is impaired more than when they remember a decision made independently (studies 3 and 4)." Participants were randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions: They were asked to remember a past decision that they delegated or one that they made independently. In both conditions they were asked to briefly describe the decision and then describe the thoughts and feelings that experiencing the decision caused them to have. Participants were also shown pictures of two desserts (a chocolate cake and a fruit salad) and asked to indicate which one they would eat if they had the two desserts in front of them right then. All participants were administered a self-monitoring scale (Snyder, 1974) at the beginning of the study, and at the end, a past decision and consequences questionnaire and a PANAS scale (Watson, Clark and Tellegen, 1988). The measure of self-regulatory resource depletion in Study 3 was participants’ choice of dessert, which was analyzed with a logistic regression. A logistic regression analysis showed that the choice share of the chocolate cake among those who had been instructed to recall a delegated decision (70.6%) was significantly greater than among participants who had been asked to recall an independent decision (31.6%; χ2(1, 36) = 5.46, p < .03).

title_r: Registered replication of Traczyk et al. (2018). Numerate decision makers don’t use more effortful strategies unless it pays.
abstract_r: The original study investigated skilled and adaptive strategy selection in risky decision making. We wish to replicate the effect shown by Traczyk et al. (2018), where people with higher objective statistical numeracy (measured by Berlin Numeracy Test, BNT, Cokely et al., 2012), in comparison to people with lower numeracy, adaptively select choice strategy depending on the task structure or the characteristics of the environment. Put differently, highly numerate people do not use more effortful strategies unless it is strictly required; in trivial choice problems, they employ fast and frugal heuristic processing, but in meaningful problems, they engage more elaborate and effortful information processing. We propose that people with high objective statistical numeracy are able to learn the importance of the decision problems. If it is meaningful, they are likely to deliberate longer to make a superior decision, making choices consistent with predictions of more effortful and reward maximizing choice strategies predicted by Cumulative Prospect Theory/Expected Value (CPT/EV) theory, but if the decision problems are trivial and lead to comparable payoffs, they make faster but normatively suboptimal choices consistent with predictions of fast and frugal priority heuristic (PH). Reference- Cokely, E. T., Galesic, M., Schulz, E., Garcia-Retamero, R., & Ghazal, S. (2012). Measuring Risk Literacy: The Berlin Numeracy Test. Judgment and Decision Making, 7(1), 23. title_r: Combining manipulations of working memory and individual-difference approaches to explore the dependence of distractor devaluation on working memory resources: A conceptual replication and extension of Goolsby et al. (2009)
abstract_r: Stimuli appearing as distractors in visual-search tasks subsequently receive more negative affective ratings than novel stimuli or the targets of attention. By demonstrating that this ‘distractor-devaluation effect’ is eliminated with a concurrent visual working-memory load, Goolsby et al. (2009) provided evidence that visual working memory resources may be important for encoding associative links between the perceptual details of a distractor and the cognitive-affective processes that lead it to receive negative evaluations. The current project provides a conceptual replication and extension of Goolsby et al. by using a similar within-participant experimental manipulation of level of concurrent working-memory load during the measurement of distractor devaluation, while also using an individual-difference approach to provide a converging test of the hypothesis that distractor devaluation requires working-memory resources. Furthermore, by using a battery of different working-memory capacity measurement tasks to assess individual differences in various aspects of visual storage capacity and attention-related working-memory abilities, the present work seeks to test whether the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation primarily concerns the mere maintenance of visual information, or the active manipulation of information during working-memory maintenance. Our project also builds on Goolsby et al.by changing the type of stimuli and increasing their number in the task used to measure distractor devaluation. Support for the hypothesis that distractor devaluation requires visual working memory resources would be evident in 1) a replication of the finding that distractor devaluation is eliminated with a concurrent visual working memory load but occurs without a load, and 2) the finding that the magnitude of distractor devaluation is reduced in participants with relatively low visual-working memory capacities when compared to that obtained in individuals with relatively high visual-working memory capacities. If the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation concerns the maintenance of visual information, then individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation should be predicted by differences in the performance of those individuals in any working-memory task that is sensitive to the number of visual representations that can be simultaneously maintained in working memory. If the role of visual working memory in mediating distractor devaluation concerns the active manipulation of information during working-memory maintenance, then individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation should be predicted by performance differences only in the working-memory tasks that require attentional selection during memory maintenance. Given our lab’s interest in boredom as a manifestation of negative affect linked to difficulties with attentional engagement, the present project also includes an exploratory assessment of the link between individual differences in the tendency to experience boredom (i.e., trait boredom proneness) and individual differences in the magnitude of distractor devaluation.

title_r: Federal minimum wage hikes do reduce teenage employment. A replication study of Bazen & Marimoutou (Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 2002)
abstract_r: In 2002 we published a paper in which we used state space time series methods to analyse the teenage employment-federal minimum wage relationship in the US (Bazen and Marimoutou, 2002). The study used quarterly data for the 46 year period running from 1954 to 1999. We detected a small, negative but statistically significant effect of the federal minimum wage on teenage employment, at a time when some studies were casting doubt on the existence of such an effect. In this note we re-estimate the original model with a further 16 years of data (up to 2015). We find that the model satisfactorily tracks the path of the teenage employment-population ratio over this 60 year period, and yields a consistently negative and statistically significant effect of minimum wages on teenage employment. The conclusion reached is the same as in the original paper, and the elasticity estimates very similar: federal minimum wage hikes lead to a reduction in teenage employment with a short run elasticity of around – 0.13. The estimated long run elasticity of between – 0.37 and – 0.47 is less stable, but is nevertheless negative and statistically significant.

title_r: Temporal Framing for Pro-Environmental Attitudes: Replications and Extensions of Baldwin & Lammers (2016)
abstract_r: More conservative people are more likely to reject climate protection policies than more liberal people (Bateman & O'Connor, 2016). As Climate protection gets more and more important, it is crucial to find a way to communicate climate change issues and solutions to appeal for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). In their study, Baldwin & Lammers (2016) theorized that the groups might prefer different temporal comparisons for many different reasons, for example because conservatives tend to compare the present with the past and liberals tend to compare the present with the future. Since appeals for climate protection measures are often formulated in terms of the future, they are probably not convincing for conservatives (Baldwin & Lammers, 2016). The idea is to provide the appeals with a past-related comparison (ibid.). In the studies by Baldwin & Lammers (2016), past-related comparisons led to stronger pro-environmental attitudes and more pro-environmental behavior among more conservative individuals. However, the current study situation is mixed: in some cases the effect could not be replicated (Kim et al., 2021; Stanley et al., 2021), in others it could (Herberz et al., 2023). The aim of the planned study is to investigate this effect again by also extending their work and adding a present frame to the past and the future frame. It will investigate whether conservatives show stronger pro-environmental approval of a text and stronger support for an environmental protection measure when it is formulated in terms of the past or present compared to a future-oriented formulation. This is also the outcome we expect. In addition, it will be investigated whether this effect is mediated by the psychological perception of distance and whether a past- or present-oriented frame reduces the perceived temporal and hypothetical distance of climate change among conservatives compared to a future-oriented frame. Here we assume that psychological distance only has an effect on conservatives, since liberals' pro-evironmental attitudes tend to be less influenced by framing.

title_r: Bodily Self-Perception under Vestibular Galvanic Stimulation in Virtual Reality: A Replication and Extension of Karnath et al. (2019)
abstract_r: Virtual reality (VR) provides a tool for studying bodily self-perception by allowing the controlled manipulation of sensory inputs and body representations. Past studies produced inconclusive results regarding the impact of vestibular signals on body schema. For example, one study reported increased perceived hand sizes due to vestibular stimulation, while another study failed to show such an effect on perceived arm or leg length. We aimed to replicate the later study and added conditions to overcome potential shortcomings, particularly regarding the stimulation type and the stimulation intensity. Twenty participants engaged with an avatar seen from first person perspective in a VR setup, adjusting its arm to match their perceived arm length. Galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) was applied using both direct current (DC) GVS and alternating current (AC) GVS at intensities of 0.375 mA and 1 mA. VR allowed precise control over task conditions and immersive engagement with the virtual body, fostering a heightened sense of embodiment. Despite the immersive VR environment and novel stimulation methods, effects of DC-GVS and AC-GVS on avatars’ arm size were, as in the original study, absent. By highlighting the interaction between vestibular input and bodily representation within a VR framework, this study underscores the potential of immersive technologies to advance research on bodily self- perception. Future research should explore alternative VR paradigms and stimulation protocols to better capture subtle shifts in body schema. VR remains a promising avenue for disentangling the complex sensory processes underlying bodily self-awareness.

title_r: The Effects of Exposure, Explicit Stereotypes, and Social Networks on Veracity Judgments of Polish-accented English Speech: A Replication and Extension of Boduch-Grabka & Lev-Ari (2021)
abstract_r: This study will be conducted by the Fall 2022 Linguistics Senior Capstone Class at the University of Utah under the supervision of Professor Rachel Hayes-Harb.. Lev-Ari and Keysar (2010) demonstrated that so-called “native” English speaking listeners judged statements produced by “foreign-accented” talkers as less likely to be true than statements produced by so-called “native” speakers. They further found that raising listeners’ awareness to the (presumed) source of difficulty by asking them to rate the speech for ease of understanding partially moderated the negative effect, leading the authors to conclude that these judgments of reduced veracity are (largely) attributable to processing difficulty. Additional studies have similarly investigated listeners’ judgments of the veracity of statements produced by “native” and “non-native” speakers, with mixed results. Some have observed no reduction in veracity judgments for “non-native” speech (e.g., Souza & Markman 2013), even when their listeners show evidence of holding stereotypes about the credibility of “non-native” speakers in a separate task (e.g., Stocker 2017). Importantly, there is debate in this literature concerning whether observed reductions in veracity judgments for “non-native” speech are attributable to processing difficulty, accent-based prejudice, or both (e.g., Castillo et al. 2014). These studies have varied along several dimensions, including national and linguistic context, “native” and “non-native” language combinations, speech content, and type of rating task, leading to crucial questions about the “nature, repeatability, and generalizability” of the effect. Building on this growing line of research, Boduch-Grabka and Lev-Ari (2021; henceforth BG&LA 2021) sought to further isolate the impact of processing difficulty on veracity judgments by easing this difficulty through exposure to the accents prior to the truth judgment task. Studies have shown that comprehension of “accented” speech improves following even a few seconds of exposure (e.g., Clarke & Garrett 2004), and BG&LA (2021) hypothesized that if the “[veracity judgment] effect is at least partly due to difficulty of processing the speech, then improving listeners’ ability to understand the speech should reduce their tendency to find the speech less credible” (p. 5). In the study, 220 “native” speakers of British English (henceforth BE) were randomly assigned to BE- or Polish-accented exposure conditions. During the exposure phase, they listened to eight brief stories (M = 179 words), each read aloud by a different “native” BE or “native” Polish speaker, depending on exposure condition. Next, participants listened to one of two counterbalanced lists of 50 trivia statements, half produced by eight Polish speakers and the other half by six BE speakers; half were true and half were false. Participants judged each statement on a 1-100 continuous false-true scale. Finally, all participants heard eight sentences extracted from the exposure phase stories produced by the Polish speakers and transcribed the sentences. Results indicated that (1) participants in the BE exposure condition judged BE-accented trivia statements as more true than those produced by Polish speakers, (2) there was an interaction of exposure and trivia statement accent such that the effect of trivia statement accent was smaller in the Polish exposure condition, (3) Polish exposure participants judged Polish-accented trivia statements as more true than did BE exposure participants, (4) Polish exposure participants were more accurate than BE exposure participants at transcribing the Polish-accented sentences in the comprehension task, and (5) a mediation test indicated that once comprehension score was taken into account, the effect of exposure condition was no longer significant. BG&LA (2021) concluded that exposure to Polish-accented speech led to more accurate comprehension, which in turn moderated the negative effect of “non-native” speech on veracity judgments. We will conduct a "close replication" of BG&LA (2021) following the characterization provided by Porte & McManus (2019, starting p. 72). The most significant modification is the addition of a new continuous participant background variable: an index of accent-based prejudice (adapting the explicit bias task in Babel & Russell 2015). Given the mixed results and relatively small effect sizes associated with earlier studies, along with the debate over the source of the veracity effect, the addition of this variable may help to clarify the factors that control the effect size, source, and generalizability of the findings. Another, more minor, change is that we will collect and report detailed information from study participants about their language backgrounds using instruments recommended by Cheng et al. (2021). Cheng et al. (2021) note that “[s]imply reporting that ‘native speakers’ participated or recorded stimuli clearly does not provide information adequate for replication”, and that unacknowledged differences in the definition of the term “native” may be partially responsible for the replication crisis in psychology and related fields. title_r: Process Models of Causal Learning - Conceptual Replication of Danks & Schwartz (2005)
abstract_r: There exists a rich literature on computational models trying to solve the question of how people learn the causal relationships between stimuli. However, these have mainly been evaluated on the average behaviour of individual learners, who, as demonstrated in the animal domain by Daw and Courville (2008), might not be well represented by the mean. For example, while models of the average population learning behaviour suggest smooth (and late) adaptation to newly observed data, individual learning trajectories show distinctly more pronounced jumps in beliefs and high variability. Here, we use the different available models to describe human learning behaviour at the individual level, casting individual differences in behaviour as differences in the best fitting model or its parameters. In this first study we carry out a conceptual replication of Danks & Schwarz (2005). We change the cover stories participants receive and slightly modify the sequences they presented.

title_r: Original Article Evidence of Systematic Bias in Sexual Over- and Underperception of Naturally Occurring Events: A direct Replication of Haselton (2003) in a
abstract_r: 2006) maintains that natural selection has engineered adaptations for judgment under uncertainty to minimize the overall cost of making errors, leading to universal biases in judgments of sexual interest in men and women. This study, using a sample of heterosexual Norwegian students (n = 308), was carried out as a direct replication of Haselton’s (2003) original study of naturally occurring events of sexual misperception. The results strongly supported the main hypotheses in the original study, showing that women reported being subject to opposite-sex sexual overperception far more often relative to underperception, and that this difference was small for men. In support of Error Management Theory, and in contrast to Social Role / Structure Theory expectations, the pattern of misperception for women and men was largely invariant across studies and across demographic groups within a culture. The findings suggest that cross-national differences in the level of gender inequality do not influence reports of sexual over- and underperception in women and men. Beyond sex, factors associated with more sexual overperception relative to underperception were being single, young, and having attitudes condoning casual sex.

title_r: Does Scarcity Frame Value? Direct Replication of Shah et al. (2015)
abstract_r: In an influential article, Shah et al. (2015) hypothesized that resource scarcity weakens the effect of irrelevant contextual factors on economic valuations. The hypothesis that “scarcity frames value” is significant for the applicability of standard economic theories of rationality as well as the psychology of economic decisions. We will provide a large-scale direct replication of the key studies in the original article.

title_r: Investor Assessment of Reputational Penalties for Environmental Violations: A Replication and Extension Study of U.S. Firms from 1980-2016
abstract_r: Do firms face reputational penalties for committing environmental violations? This paper replicates the work of a previous empirical study to confirm the relationship between abnormal returns and legal penalties following the announcement of a violation. It then goes on to extend the study using more recent data to assess how reputational costs change over time. Across both sets of data, firms suffer abnormal stock price decreases following the announcement of an environmental crime. The size of prospective legal penalties is on average larger than the decrease in market value, indicating that investors base their reaction to violations off the present value of legal costs faced by the firm. Average abnormal returns decreased in size between the two studies, indicating that over time as investors started paying more attention to environmental responsibility, they became less surprised by new violations. The results of the studies taken together have public policy implications, indicating that at present investors face immediate penalties following a violation in the form of regulatory costs, but in the long term may also face reputational penalties due to increased investor attention to environmental performance.

title_r: “Your Brain On Video Games”: A re-analysis, replication and extension of Martinez et al. (2023)
abstract_r: This research is being carried out in the context of a second year Master’s dissertation. The field of research on the psychology of video games is about as divided as it is recent (Chaput, 2023). Studies and meta-analyses alike cannot seem to reach a consensus about the effects of this relatively new media on affects, socialisation, or cognitive performance. Among several concerns, the field suffers from a lack of unity in terminology, research methods, and analytical models (Elson & Ferguson, 2014). The issue is further illustrated in psychological research at large, as evidenced by the current replicability crisis (Balafoutas et al., 2025; Rouphael, 2022). To overcome the matter, several good practices are recommended by experts in the field, such as replication and accountability. The present study therefore aims to replicate a recent study on the psychology of video game play, investigating the links between playing practice and cognitive performance (Martinez et al., 2023). The proposed replication follows a first phase of thorough re-analysis of the original clean dataset, which was made available in open access by the authors. In this second phase, new data will be collected to re-assess the original findings, using updated analytical models. Furthermore, we will extend the original protocol by investigating two additional relevant variables, which were not previously taken into account: participants’ starting age of video game practice (Hambrick et al., 2014) and overall level of cognitive performance (Matton et al., 2022; Wolfram, 2023). Throughout the entire project, we are involving the authors of the original study (Dr Léa Martinez, Dr Manuel Gimenes and Dr Eric Lamber), who kindly volunteered their materials for the purposes of this replication. In addition to this pre-registration, we will be sharing the full anonymised dataset in open access after data collection is completed. With this project, we aim to further our understanding of the links between video game practice and cognition, as well as to contribute to better practices in video game research. title_r: Socio-Affective Processes of Narcissism in Daily Life: A Pre-registered Replication and Extension of Wright et al. 2017
abstract_r: Narcissism is associated with significant interpersonal problems (e.g., Campbell et al., 2005; Ogrodniczuk et al., 2009; Pincus et al., 2009). To understand specific triggers for narcissistic expression and potential mechanisms that generate interpersonal dysfunction, examining how individual differences in narcissism manifest in momentary interpersonal processes is necessary. However, despite much evidence that narcissism is associated with negative interpersonal outcomes (e.g., Miller et al., 2007), to date there are a limited number of studies that explicitly explore how narcissism contributes to momentary interpersonal processes. Recently, Wright and colleagues (2017) examined how narcissism amplifies links between interpersonal perceptions and one’s own behavior during social interactions in naturalistic settings. In particular, the authors explored how narcissism amplified the link between perceptions of others' dominance, negative affect, and one’s own quarrelsomeness (or low affiliation). Results revealed that others’ dominance did not predict one’s own dominant behavior in the interaction, but was associated with quarrelsome behavior. Negative affect was additionally found to account for the association of perceptions of others’ dominance and one’s own quarrelsome behavior. Further, it was identified that narcissism amplified the link between perceptions of others’ dominance and one’s own quarrelsomeness, as well as the link between others’ dominance and negative affect. These findings suggest that narcissism has important associations with momentary interpersonal and affective processes. Specifically, that perceptions of others’ dominance lead to negative affect and quarrelsomeness, especially for those high in narcissism. The present study serves as a replication of Wright and colleagues (2017). In particular, we aim to re-examine associations between momentary affective and interpersonal processes and whether narcissism amplifies these linkages. The current study extends Wright and colleagues (2017) by testing whether these effects are robust to sampling and assessment. We will explore these associations in a large community sample, oversampled for low modesty, a trait that is associated with narcissism. The original sample was a clinical sample with high levels of psychopathology. Whereas Wright and colleagues (2017) used diagnostic interviews to measure narcissism (and personality pathology more broadly), here we use contemporary narcissism measures that can be scored for grandiose and vulnerable features, as well as the three-factor structure of narcissism (e.g., Krizan & Herlache, 2018; Miller et al., 2017; Wright & Edershile, 2018). This is an important extension as there are likely differential effects of grandiosity and vulnerability, as well as exhibitionistic grandiosity, entitlement, and vulnerability. Teasing apart which components of narcissism are primarily responsible for moderation effects is an important extension of Wright and colleagues (2017). Given established connections between grandiosity and dominance (e.g., Johnson et al., 2012), it is possible that grandiosity moderates the association between perceived dominance and one’s own warmth. However, vulnerability is associated with dysregulation (e.g., Edershile et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2018). Therefore, it is also possible that the narcissistic response is driven primarily by vulnerability. The inclusion of a three-factor structure will also help to further elucidate these findings, as it may be entitlement that primarily drives associations.

title_r: Inhibition-of-return-like effects in working memory? A preregistered replication study of Johnson et al. (2013)
abstract_r: The present study concerns a preregistered replication of the study conducted by Johnson et al. (2013), in which they showed an inhibition-of-return-like effect in working memory. Inhibition of return is a well-known phenomenon observed in the field of perception and refers to the observation that it takes longer to look back at a location that has recently been explored than to look at an unexplored location. Working memory is a central concept in the field of cognitive psychology and refers to the capacity to process and maintain information simultaneously over short periods of time. Johnson’s study applied the inhibition of return paradigm to the concept of working memory. Their results showed that it is harder to access a working memory representation that had just been thought of, i.e., refreshed, in comparison to an unrefreshed working memory representation. Contrary to this study of Johnson et al., who observed refreshing to result in inhibitory processes, most studies on refreshing have described its effect as increasing/prolonging the level of activation of the memory representations. In an attempt to integrate these opposite patterns produced by “refreshing”, we started by replicating one of the studies on inhibition of return in working memory reported by Johnson et al. (2013).

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Cutright et al (2011) is the Experiment 5 claim that individuals measured to be low (vs. high) in system confidence respond differently to the opportunity to directly vs. indirectly support the system through a choice of national vs. international T-shirt: when provided with a chance for indirect support, low- (but not high) confidence individuals will respond to a threat by selecting national brands; when provided with a chance to directly support the system, the pattern will reverse such that high-confidence individuals only will respond to a threat by choosing the national brand T-shirt. This claim is based on the following sentence from the paper’s abstract: ““[W]hen an important system is (verbally) attacked, individuals who are the least confident in the legitimacy of the system seek and appreciate consumption choices that allow them to indirectly and subtly defend the system, [while] individuals who are highly confident in the system … seek consumption choices that allow them to defend the system in direct and explicit ways.”” The claim is tested with a repeated-measures logistic regression (three choices per participant) on T-shirt choice (national vs. international) with threat condition (high/none), the system confidence measure, and type of national brand (direct/indirect support) as predictors. This analysis found a three-way interaction of threat condition (high threat vs. no threat), system confidence, and type of brand (direct vs. indirect support), B = -1.29, Z = -3.15, p < 0.01.

title_r: Effects of the Generic Masculine and its Alternatives in Germanophone countries. A Multi-lab Replication and Extension of Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun, 2001
abstract_r: In languages such as German, French, or Hindi, plural forms of job occupations and societal roles are often in a generic-masculine form instead of a gender-neutral form. Although meant as “generic”, this generic-masculine form excludes women from everyday language and might even entail the cognitive effect that listeners and readers will less likely think of women. Several studies have demonstrated this and related cognitive effects in the past. Due to the societal relevance of gender-neutral language, we propose a direct replication and extension of a classic study by Stahlberg, Sczesny, and Braun (2001, Experiment 2) in a multi-lab setting. We already present preliminary evidence showing that people indeed come up with more female exemplars when they are asked to name celebrities from several domains, such as politics and sports in gender-neutral forms compared to the generic-masculine form. The proposed multi-lab study will be conducted among 12 labs, collecting data from more than N = 2,000 participants.

title_r: Does Proactive Policing Really Increase Major Crime? A Replication Study of Sullivan and O’Keeffe (Nature Human Behaviour, 2017)
abstract_r: In December 2014 and January 2015, police officers in New York City engaged in an organized slowdown of police work to protest the murder of two police officers who were targeted by a gunman while sitting in their patrol car. An influential 2017 article in Nature Human Behaviour studies the effect of the NYPD’s work slowdown on major crimes and concludes that the slowdown led to a significant improvement in public safety. Contrary to the remainder of the literature, the authors conclude that proactive policing can cause an increase in crime. We re-evaluate this claim and point out several fatal weaknesses in the authors’ analysis— which purports to be a difference-in-differences analysis but isn’t— that call this finding into question. In particular, we note that there was considerable variation in the intensity of the slowdown across NYC communities and that the communities which experienced a more pronounced reduction in police proactivity did not experience the largest reductions in major crime. The authors’ analysis constitutes a quintessential fallacy in statistical reasoning, a logical miscalculation in which inferences from aggregated data are mistakenly applied to a more granular phenomenon. We raise several additional and equally compelling concerns regarding the tests presented in the paper and conclude that there is little evidence that the slowdown led to short-term changes in major crimes in either direction.

title_r: Perceptual Learning and Individual Differences in Auditory Processing [Replication and extension of Kraljic, Samuel, &amp; Brennan (2008)]
abstract_r: Understanding spoken language is a complex process that comes to most people easily, yet past research demonstrates that some people face difficulties with auditory processing. Listeners integrate auditory, visual, and other cues to understand speech. However, people with auditory processing difficulties rely less on visual cues, such as lip-reading. We investigated how listeners' reported difficulties in perceiving auditory information interact with their use of visual cues. This was a replication and extension of a study by Kraljic, Samuel, and Brennan (2008). Participants viewed a speaker pronouncing some words in one of four conditions, depending on which phoneme was changed (?S or ?SH) and whether the speaker held a pen-in-hand (characteristic) or had a pen-in-mouth (incidental) while producing these words. We assessed each participant’s phonemic boundaries in a category-identification task, in which participants categorized ambiguous sounds as being more S-like or SH-like. We measured participants' perceptual learning—the restructuring of their phonemic boundaries—based on their categorization of these ambiguous sounds. Afterward, participants were surveyed on their language background and their auditory processing difficulties. We did not replicate the findings on the effect of visual context on perceptual learning from the original study by Kraljic et al. (2008). Contrary to our predictions, we also did not find an effect of individual differences in auditory processing on perceptual learning and no interaction with visual context. Given that the effect of visual context has been replicated before, our results are inconclusive. The effect of individual differences on perceptual learning should be explored further to gain insight into the underpinnings of perceptual learning and how to improve speech perception for those with auditory difficulties.\n\nWe used videos created for a replication by Babel (2016), modelled after the original videos of Kraljic et al. (2008). We link to Babel's OSF repository under project components.

title_r: LeBoeuf_JournMarketRes_2010_EKBZ - Yoon - Direct Replication - 618k
abstract_r: LeBoeuf & Simmons (2010) has shown that products predominantly associated with utilitarian attitudes at the category level support less utilitarian and more symbolic attitudes at the brand level and products predominantly associated with symbolic attitudes at the category level support less symbolic and more utilitarian attitudes at the brand level. The current research aims to test the robustness and replicability of this finding with a larger new sample. The claim selected from LeBoeuf et al. (2010) is that products predominantly associated with utilitarian attitudes at the category level support less utilitarian and more symbolic attitudes at the brand level. Products predominantly associated with symbolic attitudes at the category level support less symbolic and more utilitarian attitudes at the brand level (H1). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: “Specifically, product categories that are generally associated with utilitarian attitudes are associated with less utilitarian, more symbolic attitudes when branded, whereas product categories that are generally associated with symbolic attitudes are associated with more utilitarian, less symbolic attitudes when branded.” To test the claim, participants evaluated eight products (four utilitarian products and four symbolic products), with product order counterbalanced and symbolic and utilitarian products intermixed. The authors randomly assigned participants to evaluate branded or unbranded products, and they further randomly assigned those evaluating branded products to one of two sets of brand names. Participants rated each product’s associations with symbols and benefits, and the authors obtain difference scores by subtracting each product’s symbolism rating from its benefits rating, revealing the degree to which each product supports, on balance, more utilitarian (higher numbers) or more symbolic (lower numbers) attitudes. The authors perform a 2 (level: category or brand) × 2 (unbranded product type: utilitarian or symbolic) mixed ANOVA on the difference scores (averaged for each product type). A 2 (level: category or brand) × 2 (unbranded product type: utilitarian or symbolic) mixed ANOVA on the difference scores (averaged for each product type) revealed the predicted level × product type interaction (F(1, 204) = 7.70, p = 0.006).

abstract_r: Recent findings indicate that letting people with chronic anger management problems make avoidance movements towards angry faces with a joystick lowers anger and aggression among this group (Veenstra, Schneider, &amp; Koole, 2017). Instead of joystick movements, however, we will manipulate whole body movements in a Virtual Reality (VR) environment among 78 undergraduate students. Participants with varying levels of trait anger will be randomly allocated to an experimental or control condition. In the experimental condition, participants will be instructed to lean backwards in response to avatars with angry facial expressions and to lean forward towards avatars with happy facial expressions. In the control condition, participants will receive the same instruction for happy-looking avatars, but not for angry-looking avatars, who will not appear in the VR environment. We predict that the experimental training will reduce anger and aggressive impulses among participants high (rather than low) in trait anger. The proposed study will provide a further test of embodied motivational models of anger management and fosters the development of VR-techniques that complements traditional cognitively based interventions.

title_r: Individual differences in receptivity to scientific bullshit: a pre-registered replication study of Evans et al. (2020).
abstract_r: Research on the processes underlying bullshit receptivity is underway to understand why people are influenced by misinformation and how it operates. Evans et al. (2020) extended existing research by introducing a new measure of scientific bullshit receptivity, building on previous research on pseudo-profound bullshit receptivity (Pennycook et al., 2015). They also examined how the two types of bullshit receptivity, pseudo-profound and scientific, are related to factors such as belief in science, political conservatism, and individual differences in need for cognition. As a result, strong positive correlations emerged between the two types of bullshit receptivity, and both were positively correlated with belief in science, political conservatism, and faith in intuition. These results remained robust when controlling for acquiescence bias. Furthermore, scientific bullshit sensitivity was positively correlated with belief in science and negatively correlated with political conservatism and faith in intuition. To test the cultural generalizability of these results, the present study conducts a pre-registered replication of Study 2 by Evans et al. (2020) with Japanese participants.

abstract_r: The replication package reproduces the results presented in the paper "The Long-Term Effects of Measles Vaccination on Earnings and Employment. A Replication Study of Atwood (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2022)" by Mara Barschkett, Mathias Huebener, Andreas Leibing, Jan Marcus and Shushanik Margaryan, published in: Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics, Volume 2, 2023-4. Abstract: Atwood analyzes the effects of the 1963 U.S. measles vaccination on long-run labor market outcomes, using a generalized difference-in-differences approach. We reproduce the results of this paper and perform a battery of robustness checks. Overall, we confirm that the measles vaccination had positive labor market effects. While the negative effect on the likelihood of living in poverty and the positive effect on the probability of being employed are very robust across the different specifications, the headline estimate—the effect on earnings—is more sensitive to the exclusion of certain regions and survey years.

title_r: Virtual tool embodiment: A replication and extension of Cardinali et al. (2009) in a virtual environment
abstract_r: Recently, it has been suggested that movements in virtual environments may leverage different mechanisms than those in real environments, making it essential to validate virtual reality for the study of motor control and related processes, such as tool-use (Harris et al., 2019). A predominant theory of tool-use, termed tool embodiment, posits that tool-use is facilitated by changes to a highly plastic, action-oriented body representation termed the body schema (Martel, Cardinali, Roy, & Farnè, 2016). Following seminal work by Cardinali et al. (2009), changes in reaching kinematics and participants' localization of body landmarks have been taken as an indicators of tool embodiment. To determine whether the use of a virtual environment influences these tool-use effects, the present study seeks to replicate Cardinali et al. (2009)'s original work with several extensions, including the projection of a virtual environment via head-mounted display. Additionally, this work aims to clarify questions which remain unanswered by the literature substantiating the tool embodiment perspective. For example, it is unclear whether measures of the body representation are valid for their purpose: Kinematics have no clear relationship with the properties of the arm said to be altered by tool-use. Further, there are no instances wherein two tool embodiment measures have been successfully correlated within the same sample of participants.

title_r: Does the Corollary Discharge Provide the Sensory Content of Inner Speech? A Preregistered Direct Replication and Extension of Scott (2013)
abstract_r: The mental production of speech or "inner speech" is a remarkable and foundational ability in humans, involved in many daily activities such as reading, writing, remembering, or planning. Inner speech is generally accompanied by a subjective multisensory (mainly auditory) experience. However, the cognitive processes leading to these sensory percepts remain poorly known. One prominent perspective is that the sensory content of inner speech would correspond to the predicted sensory consequences of inhibited speech acts. Scott (2013) provided experimental evidence suggesting that inner speech indeed involves the mental simulation of speech acts, as evidenced by the attenuation of the effect of an external sound. However, Scott (2013) assessed silent speech, but not inner speech, which in contrast to silent speech, does not involve visible articulatory movements. The present work aims to replicate and extend the study of Scott (2013) to assess whether inner speech attenuates the perception of concomitant external speech sounds.

title_r: Meta-analysis and publication bias: How well does the FAT-PET-PEESE procedure work? A replication study of Alinaghi & Reed (Research Synthesis Methods, 2018)
abstract_r: This R-code produces the results of the replication study. Abstract of the paper: A meta-analysis is a tool for aggregating estimates of a similar “effect” across many studies. Publication bias is the phenomenon where literature is sample selected in favor of studies having statistically significant results and/or having estimates that satisfy pre-conceived expectations. A popular procedure used for conducting meta-analyses in the presence of publication bias is the FAT-PET-PEESE (FPP) procedure. In a recent paper published in \emph{Research Synthesis Methods}, Alinaghi and Reed (2018), utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, report that the FPP procedure does not work well when used in “realistic” data environments where true effects differ both across and within studies. AR’s findings are important because the FPP approach is dominant in the economics meta-analysis literature. I replicate their results and discover two mistakes, which I subsequently correct. The first mistake is found in a descriptive statistics table, misrepresenting the overview of simulated dataset. The second is associated with the fixed effect estimation, generating erroneous estimated effects and Type I error. Further, I extend their analysis by making their simulation environment even more realistic. Despite producing somewhat different results, my replications generally confirm AR’s conclusions about the unreliability of the FPP procedure in realistic data environments.

title_r: Generating resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories through inoculation messages: A conceptual replication study from Banas et al. (2023)
abstract_r: Inoculation is one of the communication strategies that can effectively generate resistance to conspiracy theories (O'Mahony et al., 2023; Banas & Miller, 2013; Banas et al., 2023). Many studies have been conducted to test the effectiveness of inoculation messages to confer resistance to various conspiracy theories, including 9/11 conspiracy theories (Banas & Miller, 2013) and anti-vaccine conspiracy theories (Banas et al., 2023). Inoculation messages involve two core components, (1) threat, messages that oppose arguments that the audience may encounter and (2) refutational preemption, the element within messages that will refute the weakened counterarguments by providing evidence and reasons to the person. Inoculation messages provide a weakened counterargument to influence persons with pre-bunking rather than debunking (contrasting counterarguments) to persuade others and change minds. The concept of inoculation messages is derived from inoculation theory that explains attitude and belief can be made resistant to persuasion (Compton & Pfau, 2005). This theory uses the medical analogy of vaccines to describe how weakened counter arguments within inoculation messages persuade people and change their attitudes. Aside from these, cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1975) is another foundation for inoculation messages. This theory describes that people are likely to change their attitudes when they are experiencing discomfort. Thus, inoculation messages through weakened counterarguments are the stimulus that may stimulate discomfort. This study will follow up the findings from Banas et al. (2023) where inoculation messages effectively generate resistance to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories. The study applied fact-based and logic-based inoculation messages describing the valid information about MMR vaccines and countering information from the movies, Vaxxed. Even though the message was specifically addressing MMR vaccines and anti-vaccine conspiracy theories, the logic-based inoculation was assumed to stimulate critical thinking that may be active to counter different conspiracy theories (e.g., Chemtrails, FEMA and Illuminati). However, designed inoculation messages failed to create cross protection towards other conspiracy theories. Thus, we assume that the inoculation message in this study is effective to confer resistance to conspiracy theories that are generated from misinformation, but not for conspiracy theories that are produced from conspiracy mentality. Conspiracy mentality or conspiracist ideation reflects a general worldview that some events occurred due to agreement between malicious and powerful parties (Bruder et al., 2013). Based on the study conducted by Imhoff et al. (2022), in terms of stability, conspiracy mentality is seen as a more stable trait compared to content-specific conspiracy theories, while content-specific conspiracy theories are seen as the symptom of conspiracy mentality. Therefore, we predict, participants with a high conspiracy mentality would still endorse anti-vaccine conspiracy theories, even after they are being exposed with the stimulus.

title_r: Buyer confusion and market prices – a replication study of Kalayci and Potters (2011)
abstract_r: In this master’s thesis I report my close replication attempt of Kalayci and Potters (2011). They examine experimentally whether some of the complexity in consumer markets could be explained by firms’ attempts to take advantage of consumers bounded rationality. In their experimental markets sellers can try complicate buyers’ evaluation of the qualities of their goods. Their results show that price offers and transaction prices are significantly higher when sellers can use complexity to confuse buyers. This leads Kalayci and Potters (2011) to conclude that buyer confusion can, indeed, constitute a source of market power. The objective of my research is to study whether these results are replicated with a different sample from a similar pool of participants and a different experimenter. To that end, I reproduce the procedures of data gathering and analysis of the original research as exactly as possible. The replication experimental sessions were conducted in Turku University’s PCRC lab in May 2016 using the z-Tree program code employed in the original research, with only minor modifications, including translations into Finnish. The analysis is conducted following the original research and replicability is assessed by set criteria. The results on replicability are mixed: In the replication experimental data, as in the original research, price offers and transaction prices are higher when sellers sell to human buyers, and prices increase with average complexity. These effects are, however, smaller in size, and furthermore, I find that the high and low quality sellers’ prices respond differently to average complexity, which contradicts the original findings. I therefore deem my replication of Kalayci and Potters (2011) a partial success.

abstract_r: Experimental research has explored the effects of wage delegation on employee performance, with the pioneering attempt by (Charness et al., Am Econ Rev 102:2358–2379, 2012) in “The Hidden Advantage of Delegation: Pareto Improvements in a Gift Exchange Game”, published in the American Economic Review. We conducted a replication of their experiment for two main reasons: first, to validate the original findings that have influenced subsequent research, and second, to examine whether these results hold in contexts with reduced social proximity between workers and employers, a relevant issue due to the rise of remote work. Our online experiment, involving 410 participants, followed the original study’s design but used a different sample. We successfully replicated the main finding that wage delegation increases employee effort, though the effect was smaller and largely due to employees granting themselves higher wages. These results support the notion that with decreasing social proximity, formal controls increase in importance.

title_r: High Quality Direct Replications Matter: Response to Williams (2014)
abstract_r: We respond to Williams’ (2014) comments on our three failures to replicate of Study 2 fromWilliams and Bargh (2008). We clarify our conclusions on this topic, making clear that although the results of our studies cast doubt on the specific effect reported in Williams and Bargh (i.e., that instant hot and cold packs influence choice of reward for self or friend), a more complete understanding of the embodiment hypothesis in question requires consideration of relevant conceptual replications. Accordingly, we consider the strength of the evidence in the conceptual replications that Williams identifies and find that small samples appear to be the norm. We conclude that in order for researchers to move forward, future studies must take seriously issues of power, researcher degrees of freedom, and file drawer problems. Doing so will ensure that future studies are more informative tests of this hypothesis.
