title_r: Conceptual replication of Dignath et al., 2022, experiment 3 - particular focus on emotional Stroop task (E.g., Soutscheck and Schubert, 2013) 'Do self-related primes influence the processing of conflicts in the emotional domain?'
abstract_r: Previous research has shown (e.g., Dignath et al., 2022) that Congruency Effects (CE) in a gender Stroop task are significantly reduced when self-related primes are used compared neutral primes in a control condition. The significant interaction of the factors ‘congruency’ and ‘prime’, indicated reduced CEs in experimental blocks with self-referential information compared to control blocks. Here, we ask whether this phenomenon can be replicated also in the emotional domain. We will closely replicate experiment 3 of Dignath et al. (2022), but instead of a gender task, emotional Stroop task will be employed (modelled after Soutscheck & Schubert, 2013), in which participants must classify facial expressions as positive or negative, while ignoring clearly positive or negative valenced words. In line with the study of Dignath et al. (2022), the main question of this experiment is how self-referential primes modulate CEs. Going beyond previous research, we ask whether similar effects can be generalized to the emotional domain. We consider two possible accounts. The attentional bias account assumes that CEs should be increased in the self-referential condition, because self-referential primes draw attention towards the task-irrelevant dimension and hence should enhance CEs. Specifically, for emotional stimuli, it has been suggested that attention is not only quicker engaged by emotional stimuli, but also impairs attentional disengagement. In contrast, the priming of control account holds that CEs in the self-referential condition should be reduced, because self-relevance boosts cognitive control over task-irrelevant response tendencies. Indeed, it has been suggested that the inextricable link between control and self-referential information is particularly strong for emotional material.

title_r: Replication and Extension of Kool et al. (2010) at the University of Chicago
abstract_r: Sara Hockett, a fourth-year student at the University of Chicago, is replicating and extending the finding of Kool et al.'s (2010) experiment. This study found evidence supporting the law of least mental effort: that people will choose a less cognitively demanding course of action when given the opportunity. The current study will focus on the presence of this bias, which is hypothesized to exist even without direct awareness of a difference in cognitive demand. I hope to answer the question of whether anticipated cognitive demand is a significant element in decision making. The key test in the original study found that the option associated with higher cognitive was chosen more often than the option that was less cognitively demanding. We will also test if the high demand condition is higher than the low demand condition using the same analyses as in the original study. As an extension, I am also curious about whether the insufficient justification effect as it relates to cognitive dissonance could be induced regarding participants' appraisal of the tedious task. The insufficient justification effect argues that people will demonstrate positive attitude change towards an action they received insufficient justification for enacting. Such an attitude change reduces the cognitive dissonance arising between the effort of performing a tedious task and the lack of sufficient justification for doing so. We will test this effect with an experimental condition manipulating awareness of a gift-card prize for completion of the study. With this, we hope to answer the extent to which having extrinsic motivation for a dull task will reduce the cognitive dissonance of participants. Sara and her collaborators will be performing this study in efforts to attain her honors thesis in Psychology at the University of Chicago. A total of 130 participants will be collected so as to have 65 participants in each of the two conditions in the extension. The stopping point for data collection is the end of the University of Chicago's 2021 Spring Quarter.

title_r: Interindustry merger patterns and resource dependence: a replication and extension of Pfeffer (1972)
abstract_r: This paper reexamines Pfeffer’s (1972) classic study on interindustry merger patterns by replicating and then extending his findings. Pfeffer argued and found that resource dependencies, as measured by interindustry economic transactions, explained merger patterns. The replication investigates how robust the resource dependence explanation for interindustry mergers is when more precise methods are applied to a data set that essentially recreates Pfeffer’s. The extension examines the strength of the resouce dependence effect over time, and offers hypotheses that seek to explain both longitudinal and cross-sectional variation in the strength of this effect. Results indicate that while the significance of the resource dependence effect is once again observed, after applying more refined analytical methods to the data the explanatory power of resource dependence is greatly diminished. In addition, variation in the strength of the resource dependence effect suggests some boundary conditions for the theory, at least with respect to its ability to predict interindustry mergers. © 1997 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

title_r: Conceptual replication of Experiment 1 in Erdfelder, Berres, Quevedo Pütter, and Küpper-Tetzel (2023)
abstract_r: Erdfelder, Berres, Quevedo Pütter, and Küpper-Tetzel (2023, Experiment 1) assessed effects of sleep on episodic memory in a completely randomized 2 (Study Time) x 2 (Retention Interval) design. Half of the participants learned 40 weakly associated word pairs at 9 am, the other half at 9 pm (Study Time factor). Half of the participants of each group received a free-then-cued-recall memory test after a short retention interval (6 min), the other half after a long retention interval (12 h; Retention Interval factor). Memory performance differences between groups studying at 9 am vs. 9 pm were negligible in the short retention interval condition. In contrast, after a 12 h retention interval, the 9 pm group (i.e., the group that slept during the retention interval) showed better memory than the 9 am group (i.e., that group that stayed awake during the retention interval), in line with the sleep benefit hypothesis. However, the latter effect failed to reach statistical significance in free recall and also in a model-based retrieval measure. Since these results were based on N = 60 participants only, we plan a more powerful conceptual replication employing the same basic study design and statistical analyses plus a few methodological refinements compared to the original study.

This indicates that having a moderate level of narcissism characterized by using only strategies from the admiration pathway is related to the highest self-esteem level (see Table 5). All regression coefficients were significant at p < 0.05.

title_r: How strong is the rhythm of perception? A registered replication of Hickok, Farahbod, and Saberi (2015)
abstract_r: Our ability to predict upcoming events is a fundamental component of human cognition. One way in which we do so is to exploit temporal regularities in sensory signals: the ticking of a clock, falling of footsteps, and the motion of waves each provide a structure that may facilitate anticipation. But how strong is the effect of rhythmic anticipation on perception? And to what degree do people vary in their ability to capitalize on these regularities? Hickok, Farahbod, and Saberi (2015) introduced a behavioral paradigm to assess how a rhythmic auditory stimulus affects perception of subsequent targets. They tested five listeners, and found that perception – that is, target detection accuracy – fluctuated rhythmically just like the sound rhythm. Here we aim to replicate the original finding, to assess how likely the finding is to be observed for any individual, and to quantify effect size in a relatively large sample of listeners. We introduce a model-based approach for analyzing the data that allows separate estimates of amplitude and phase information in target detection responses, and quantifies effect size for individual listeners.

title_r: The effects of reading fiction on openmindedness: A replication and extension of Djikic et al. (2013)
abstract_r: This experiment aims to determine the way in which different kinds of reading open our minds and facilitate a more flexible thinking style. title_r: Replication study of DK effect(1999) Study 3
abstract_r: In order to explore the mechanism behind the fact that people tend to hold overly favorable views of their abilities, Kruger and Dunning suggest that low metacognitive ability may result in cognitive bias by conducting a series of experiments. This study replicate and expand the key experiment of the original study and further put forward the potential influence that social comparison might has on the accuracy of self-evaluation from the collectivistic perspective. In the first study, incompetence subjects overestimated themselves and thus proved the cross-cultural robustness of Dunning-Kruger effect. In the second study, the subjects were asked to reassess themselves after observing the responses of the others. Neither high score group nor low score group showed significant difference between two assessments, which might be the result of the combined effects of metacognitive ability and social comparison.

title_r: Perceivers’ Categorizations of Multiracial Faces as a Function of Geographic Context: A Pre-Registered Replication of Pauker et al. (2018)
abstract_r: This study attempts to replicate the key finding reported in Pauker et al. (2018) that perceivers' ability to categorize multiracial faces as multiracial depends on geographic contexts. In line with the original Pauker et al. (2018) study, participants will be sampled from Hawaii and outside of Hawaii (specifically Southern California) and multiracial categorization data for these two samples will be compared. In addition to this primary test, we will also test three additional hypotheses that were explored by Pauker et al. (2018), though to be clear, we view these tests as secondary to the primary goal of the current replication attempt. First, we will explore whether the composition of the multiracial faces corresponds with differences in categorizations as multiracial, and second, we will test whether racial composition interacts with sample location. Finally, we will test whether contact with multiracial people mediates the relationship between region and multiracial categorizations. In attempting to replicate these focal effects, we will also test for potential differences in hypodescent.

abstract_r: The present study aims to conduct a conceptual replication of Amit, Wakslak and Trope’s (2013, Experiment 2) study, which explored the effect of social (psychological) distance on peoples’ medium preferences for interpersonal communication. The results showed that participants preferred mediums dominated by pictures for socially ‘close’ targets and mediums dominated by words for socially ‘distant’ targets. These findings support construal level theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010) which propose that people use more abstract representations when mentalizing targets that are more psychologically distant. title_r: The Language of War: A Replication and Extension of Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013)
abstract_r: Legislative bodies have very important roles and understanding the psychology of their decision-making processes is a useful area of study. We add to this area by replicating two previous studies Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) in the context of a legislative body. The present study hypothesized that legislators who support war measures be externally focused and less cognitively complex in their speeches while opponents of war measures would be internally focused. Speeches were obtained pertaining to the decisions for the U.S. to take military action in Kosovo, Iraq, and Libya. While we found mixed results depending on the circumstances of a specific conflict, we demonstrate how automated language analysis can be combined with voting records to better understand behavioral action, such as legislative decision.

title_r: The Incremental Validity of Average States: A Replication and Extension of Finnigan & Vazire (2018)
abstract_r: States refer to our momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Average states (aggregates across multiple time points) are discussed as a more accurate and objective measure of personality compared to global self-reports since they do not only rely on people’s general beliefs about themselves. Specifically, Finnigan and Vazire (2018) argued that, if average states better capture what a person is actually like, this should be reflected in their unique association with informant-reports of personality, and tested this idea based on two experience-sampling studies. Their results showed, however, that average self-reported states did not predict global informant-reported personality above and beyond global self-reports. In this research, we aimed at replicating and extending these results. We used data of five studies (total N = 806) that involved global self- and informant reports and employed a variety of different experience-sampling methods (time-based with different sampling schedules, event-based). Across all studies, the original results (i.e., no incremental effects of average self-reported states) were replicated. Furthermore, as an extension to the original study, we found that average other-reported states (provided by peers, results based on one study) did indeed predict global informant-reports above and beyond global self-reports. These findings highlight the importance of differentiating between method effects (global reports vs average states) from source of information effects (self vs. other). We discuss these results, focusing on the suitability of using informant-reports as a criterion variable and conceptual differences between assessment methods.

title_r: Does Speed of Recognition predict Two-Alternatives Forced-Choice Performance? Replicating and Extending Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018)
abstract_r: Does the speed of single-word recognition errors predict performance in subsequent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) trials that include the error item? Starns, Dubé, and Frelinger (2018) found effects of this kind in two experiments and account for them in terms of a continuous memory-strength signal guiding recognition decisions. In the 2AFC task, Starns et al. (2018) always paired an item that had been responded to falsely in a preceding single-word recognition task with an item that had been responded to correctly. Participants were instructed to identify and correct the error made in the single-word recognition test via their response in the 2AFC trial. As suggested by Malejka and Bröder (2016) for a source memory task, feedback regarding error items can indeed influence memory decisions. The present study is an adversarial collaboration that aims (a) to replicate Starns et al.’s (2018) results in a replication condition and (b) to test whether the effects of error speed reflect an artefact due to an error-correction strategy that uses response latency as a heuristic cue. For this purpose, we will implement a replication as well as an extension condition in which error feedback is removed. This study will contribute to the broader research question of whether a continuous memory-strength signal or discrete states underlie recognition decisions.

title_r: Selecting the special or choosing the common? A high-powered conceptual replication of Kim and Markus’ (1999) pen study
abstract_r: Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3) found that 74% of European Americans selected a pen with an uncommon (vs. common) color, whereas only 24% of East Asians made such a choice, highlighting a pronounced cross-cultural difference in the extent to which people opt for originality or make majority-based choices. The present high-powered study (N = 729) conceptually replicates the results from Kim and Markus (1999; Study 3), although our effect size (r = .12) is significantly weaker than that of the original study (r = .52). Interestingly, a larger proportion of Chinese, but not the US, participants selected a pen with an uncommon color now than during the original study. Thus, our findings indicate a potential transmission of certain western values to cultures traditionally characterized by collectivism and conformity, likely exacerbated by the globalization of mass media and the rapid economic growth in many East Asian countries.

title_r: Is There a Positive Association between Working Memory Capacity and Mind Wandering in a Low-Demand Breathing Task? A Preregistered Replication of Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012)
abstract_r: Levinson, Smallwood, and Davidson (2012, Experiment 2) found that working memory capacity (WMC) correlated positively with mind-wandering propensity measured by thought probes in a breath-monitoring task, but was unassociated with the tendency to self-catch mind-wandering. Here, I sought to replicate the associations between mind-wandering and WMC in the Levinson et al. breath task. With data from a large sample of subjects and two measures of WMC, the data from the current study suggests that, if WMC correlates with probe-caught mind wandering, it is most likely negative. In addition, the evidence regarding self-caught mind wandering is consistent with Levinson et al. for the sum of self-caught responses, but when self-caught responses are considered in proportion to probe-caught mind wandering, modest evidence was found for a positive association with WMC.

title_r: Replication and extension of: Large language models associate Muslims with violence by Abid et al., 2021
abstract_r: The main purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the results in Abid et al. (2021; Nature Machine Intelligence). Building on preliminary evidence provided by the creators of GPT-2 and GPT-3 (state-of-the-art text generation algorithms; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), the authors showed biased automated text generation when religious identities are cued in text completion prompts. GPT-3 completions for prompts formatted as “Two X walk into a” contained violent content much more often if X was replaced with “Muslims” rather than adjectives signifying other major religions. Since the smallest difference was found between “Muslim” and “Christian”, our replication attempt focuses on this more conservative measure of the model’s religion bias. However, we include the “Hindu” category as well to control for the impact of majority/minority difference between “Muslim” and “Christian”. We extend these results by exploring whether naming specific individuals reduces the propensity of the model to rely on biased group-level representations. For instance, using “Y walks into a” where Y is replaced with a common Muslim name compared with names common among adherents of Christianity and Hinduism. We also examine whether the model is sensitive to differing degrees of genericity in the main referent of prompts, which can vary along a continuum. Generic kinds like “Muslim” lie near one end of the spectrum. Individual celebrities whose personal information presumably features strongly in GPT-3’s training data (from CommonCrawl.org), lie near the other end. Common names associated with social kinds like “Muslim” (e.g., Ali Islam) are somewhere in-between, albeit closer to the specific end of the genericity spectrum. We expect reduced bias as the specificity of the prompts are increased.

title_r: Task material for "The Impact of Co-Opetition on Cognitive Flexibility: A Replication Study of Landkammer and Sassenberg (2016)"
abstract_r: Social interactions often involve conflicting demands, where pursuing one goal hinders another. Landkammer and Sassenberg (2016) studied the impact of co-opetition – the conflicting simultaneous demand to cooperate and compete with the same target – on cognitive flexibility. They found that compared to pure competition and cooperation, experiencing coopetition increases cognitive flexibility (i.e., reduced rigidity in decision-making and generating more diverse ideas in a brainstorming task). Two conceptual and one direct replication (total N = 1,340) found no difference in cognitive flexibility contingent to interdependence, and Bayesian analysis showed strong evidence against an effect (BF10 < 0.05). Our results failed to replicate the impact of co-opetition on flexibility, suggesting that conflicting demands might facilitate cognitive flexibility only in case of other types of intraindividual conflict.

title_r: Are STEM Faculty Biased Against Female Applicants? A Robust Replication and Extension of Moss-Racusin and Colleagues (2012)
abstract_r: Abstract (as of 6/1/20): In a seminal study investigating gender bias in academic science, Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) found bias against female lab manager applicants with respect to competence, hireability, mentoring, and salary conferral. This topic will be revisited through four studies--two direct replications, one extension, and a meta analysis. The present set of studies, all using the same methods and materials as the original, will sample from a larger and broader pool of faculty, collectively representing the breadth of STEM disciplines at R1 universities across the United States. The proposed studies will have high power to detect smaller effect sizes than in the original. Furthermore, a priori criteria have been explicitly articulated for what will be accepted as hypothesis confirmation and replication, and for evidence of gender bias. The pre-registered data analysis plans will provide a strong test assessing the replicability of Moss-Racusin et al. (2012)’s finding that STEM faculty were biased against women who applied for a lab manager position.

title_r: Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication and Extension
abstract_r: The goal of this study is to replicate memory updating findings by Hupbach et al., 2007 (Experiment 1) and explore the impact of ad hoc category belongingness and stress on memory updating effects. Hupbach et al., 2007 had participants learn a list of objects at Session 1. Two days later, they learned a second list of objects at Session 2. Prior to learning the second list, some of the participants were reminded of the Session 1 learning experience (memory reactivation group) and some were not (no-reactivation group). When asked to recall the Session 1 list a couple days later at Session 3, participants in the memory reactivation group misattributed objects from Session 2 to Session 1 more often than participants in the no-reactivation group. We first aim to replicate this effect in an online version of the study (see “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication” pre-registration). Next, we aim to explore the impact of using an ad hoc category of covid-related objects, instead of neutral unrelated objects as done in the original study, on memory updating effects. We will also include an additional control using an ad hoc category of beach-related objects, to account for ad hoc category belongingness in general. This pre-registration should be considered alongside the “Hupbach et al. 2007 Replication” pre-registration as the Neutral groups in this study comprise that replication. We have further described those groups and procedures in a separate pre-registration in order to make use of the Replication Recipe (Brandt et al., 2013) template.

title_r: When less confident forecasts signal more expertise: A close replication of Study 1 (Palmeira & Heath, 2025)
abstract_r: This project is a close replication of Study 1 from the paper 'When less confident forecasts signal more expertise' by Palmeira and Heath (2025). The primary objective is to verify the finding that cognitive reflection moderates the relationship between an advisor's expressed confidence and their perceived expertise. Specifically, we aim to replicate the reversal of the confidence heuristic, where individuals with higher cognitive reflection scores (CRT) prefer moderately confident advisors over highly confident ones, whereas individuals with lower CRT scores show the opposite preference. We will use the original materials (economist scenario) and the modified CRT scale described in the original study. All study materials will be translated into Czech for data collection which will be done on a sample from the Czech population.

title_r: Pragmatic and Syntactic Influences on Adjective Interpretation 2.0: A Conceptual Replication of Wittenberg, Barner, and Levy (2016)
abstract_r: This study employs a 2×2 between-subjects design crossing Sentence Type (command vs. question) with Adjective Order (canonical “tall red” vs. non-canonical “red tall”). Each participant is assigned to one condition and encounters only sentences of that type. On Display 1, participants see a 5×2 grid of 10 objects that vary along a color continuum (the relevant graded dimension) and an additional scalar property (e.g., height). On each trial, they are presented with a sentence from their assigned condition, such as: Canonical command: “Click on the tall red building!” Non-canonical command: “Click on the red tall building!” Canonical question: “Is there a tall red building?” Non-canonical question: “Is there a red tall building?” On Display 2, four new objects of the same type appear: two clear members of a target color, one ambiguous-color object, and one clear non-member. Participants then answer a follow-up question, such as: “How many red buildings would Fiba count here?” They respond by selecting any number of the four objects. This second display assesses whether any threshold adjustment from Display 1 (e.g., treating the ambiguous object as “red”) generalizes to a new array.

title_r: The Effect of Uncontrollable vs. Controllable Acute Stress on Inhibition as a boundary condition: A Replication and Extension of Starcke et al. (2016)
abstract_r: Executive functions (EF) are as set of higher-order, goal directed mental processes that enable individuals to focus, inhibitate, regulate their behaviour and manage complex tasks, particularly in situations where automatic responses are not enough (Diamond, 2012, p.136). Miyake et al. (2000) propose that there are three core EFs, working memory, inhibitory control and the flexible shifting of attention and that these abilities are essential for performing goal-oriented behavior by integrating various streams of information. Also, these cognitive processes are dependent on prefrontal cortex, making them particularly vulnerable to disruption by phsiological and psychological states such as acute stress. However, as emphasized in a recent review by Plieger and Reuter (2020), emprical finding on stress and executive functioning remain complex, some studies report impairments, while others suggest improvements, largely depending on moderating variables such as task complexity and the type of the stressor. The authors argue that stress may not simply reduce cognitive capacity but may instead make the brain rely more on automatic responses to preserve energy under stress A meta analysis by Shields et al. (2016) supports the sensivity of EFs, though the effect are not uniform across all domains. They demonstrated that acute stress significantly impairs core executive fuctions, espacially working memory and cognitive flexibilty. The impact on inhibition is less straightforward and showed more nuanced pattern. While stress tends to impair cognitive inhibition, it may sometimes enhance response inhibition. Consistent with the impairment view, Starcke et al. (2016) used the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test (PASAT-C) to induce acute stress and found that stressed participants performed significantly worse than the non-stressed participants on the Color-Word Interference Test (stroop), meaning that uncontrollable stress distort the ability to filter interference. However, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) might not be due to stress intensity alone, but rather the uncontrollable nature of the stressor (unavoidable aversive noise). Henderson et al. (2012) investigated this distinction and found that controllability is a key moderater. In their study, participants exposed to uncontrollable stress showed no relationship between stress and performance whereas those who learned to control the stressor showed reduced Stroop interference, meaning that realizing that they had control over the stressor improved their performance. This suggests that the perception of control buffers individuals against the effects of stress on executive funtions. In other words, when individuals percieve that they have some degree of control over a stressful stimulus, their cognitive functions are less disrupted. Furthermore, in line with the Hendorson et al. (2012), Gathmann et al. (2014) showed that in certain high-demand conditions, brain uses adaptive mechanisms to preserve performance. This adaptive mechanisms allow individuals to maintain acurracy in stressful situations. In this context, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) may be caused by the lack of perceived control in their stress manipulation. The primary motivation for this study is to resolve inconsistencies regarding the impact of acute stress on executive functions. While starcke et al. (2016) provided evidence that acute stress impairs inhibition, they used PASAT-C stress induction paradigm which is strictly uncontrollable stressor, leaving it unclear whether the observed impairment was driven by phsiological intensity of stress or the psychological state of helplesness. As highlightened by Plieger and Reuter (2020), identifying moderating factors such as controlability is essential when we try to understand the relationship between stress and executive functions. A clearer understanding of this relationship would lead to a better understanding of cognitive resilience. Therefore, this study aims to replicate the inhibitory impairment reported by Starcke et al (2016) while introducing “perceived controllability” as a manipulated boundary condition. To directly address the original study’s concern that the length of test battery may reduce the stress response over time, the current study will focus only on the Attention and Inhibition component (Stroop Test), administered immediately after the stress induction. By comparing an Uncontrollable Stress group, a Controllable Stress group and a Control group, present study aims to show distorting impact of acute stress on inhibitory performance is reduced when individuals believe they have some degree of control over the stressor.

title_r: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Newland et al. (2013): Improving the Measurement and Prediction of Mental Toughness in Basketball Athletes
abstract_r: Mental toughness plays a major role in sports, and many athletes and coaches treat it as essential for successful performance. Researchers define mental toughness in different ways, which creates challenges for accurate measurement. Some definitions focus on confidence and emotional control, while others describe resilience and persistence. A recent review found that mental toughness tends to support better performance, but the strength of this effect depends on how researchers define and measure it (Cowden, 2017). Because basketball emphasizes psychological resilience and high-pressure decision making, I want to study mental toughness using stronger methods than earlier research. Newland et al. (2013) examined how mental toughness predicted basketball performance. They used the Psychological Performance Inventory Alternative (PPIA) and calculated performance with the PERF score. They also tested gender and starting status as moderators. They found that mental toughness predicted performance only for male starters. They also found that men scored higher on mental toughness than women. These findings raised questions about measurement quality and fairness. The PPIA has unclear structure and limited theoretical grounding, and the PERF score does not consider playing time, which affects how athletes accumulate statistics. I want to replicate this study because these limitations reduce confidence in the original findings. Researchers have noted that older mental toughness scales such as the PPIA do not match modern theories and often fail to measure mental toughness consistently (Crum, 2022). Hughes (2019) describes this as part of psychology’s measurement crisis, where weak tools lead to weak conclusions. A conceptual replication that uses stronger measurement can address this problem. I also want to improve the performance metric because the original PERF score did not adjust for minutes played. Adjusting each statistic by minutes creates a more accurate indicator of true performance. Generalizability is another concern. The original sample included only college athletes from a narrow set of schools. Ghai et al. (2025) explain that psychology often makes broad claims based on limited samples, which they call MASKing. To address this problem, I plan to recruit high school and college athletes and intentionally include Native American and Polynesian athletes. This helps create a more inclusive understanding of mental toughness that reflects different competitive and cultural backgrounds. To improve measurement quality, I plan to replace the PPIA with the Sports Mental Toughness Questionnaire (SMTQ). The SMTQ measures confidence, constancy, and control and shows stronger reliability and clearer structure (Sheard et al., 2009). Research shows that newer mental toughness tools predict performance and emotional stability more consistently than older measures (Cowden, 2017). New findings challenge assumptions about gender differences as well. Kumari and Chauhan (2025) found that female student athletes sometimes score higher on mental toughness than males when researchers use valid tools. This suggests that gender patterns may change when researchers use stronger measures. I also plan to extend the study by including sleep quality as a predictor. Sleep influences recovery, reaction time, focus, and mood. Coel et al. (2022) found that adolescent athletes often experience poor sleep, which affects performance. Silva et al. (2021) found that improving sleep often enhances accuracy and speed. To include sleep in my study, I will use a short version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. My sample will include 200 high school athletes and 200 college athletes. I will also include Native American and Polynesian athletes to improve diversity. Banks et al. (2019) emphasize the importance of preregistration and transparency. I will preregister my hypotheses, measures, and analyses to follow these guidelines. Based on this research, I expect the conceptual replication to show a stronger relationship between mental toughness and performance than the original study. I expect this because the SMTQ is a better measure and because adjusting performance by minutes played will reduce error. I also expect sleep quality to strengthen the effect of mental toughness and predict performance on its own. Finally, I expect the SMTQ to work well for both men and women. If it does not, this study will help identify whether sport psychology needs more inclusive tools. Hypothesis 1: I expect my conceptual replication to show a stronger mental toughness and performance relationship than the original study because of the improved measurement tools and adjusted performance metric. Hypothesis 2: I expect mental toughness and sleep quality to predict basketball performance together, and I expect this combined effect to be stronger than the effect of mental toughness alone.

title_r: Conceptual Replication and Extension of Cohen et al. (1991) Stress, Sleep, and Illness Susceptibility in a Naturalistic Setting
abstract_r: The results of Cohen et al. (1991), who discovered that higher psychological stress levels increased susceptibility to the common cold, are conceptually replicated in this work. Participants in the current research will not be exposed to a virus, in contrast to the initial study. Rather, over the course of three weeks, the study will examine the relationship between everyday sickness symptoms and naturally occurring stress in a sample of college students. An expansion of this study looks at sleep quality as a moderator. The objective is to find out if people who have more stress and less sleep exhibit more signs of illness than people who simply have one of these risk factors.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 3 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r: People often find bullet points easier to understand than prose and generally prefer simpler explanations over complex ones. This preference reflects Occam’s razor—the idea that unnecessary assumptions should be avoided—and is considered an “explanatory virtue.” Some argue that simple explanations are more likely to be true, though probability alone may not fully explain the phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022). Sehl et al. (2024) propose that the preference for simplicity reflects a broader tendency to favor efficiency in goal-directed activities. Explanation is one such activity: understanding an outcome is more efficient when fewer causes or assumptions are invoked. From this “efficiency” perspective, the preference for simplicity should appear not only in explanatory judgments (why an outcome occurred) but also in process judgments (how an outcome could be achieved). The theory further predicts that statistical information about reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates, likelihoods) can reduce or even reverse the simplicity preference. Seven preregistered experiments supported these predictions. Because prior participants were mostly from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), questions remain about the universality of these findings. The present study replicates Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), testing the claim that preferences for simpler explanations reflect pursuit of efficiency. By using Japanese participants, we examine cross-cultural generality, extend the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on cultural variation in cognition. This study (Study 3 of the project) focuses on replicating Sehl et al.’s Study 7. Their findings indicated that when a complex cause was more probable, the preference for the simple explanation diminished, particularly in process judgments. In Study 7 of the previous work, participants more often chose the simple cause in explanatory than in process judgments. They also showed stronger preference for the simple cause when likelihoods were 80% vs. 65% than when they were 90% vs. 65%. Although the interaction was not statistically significant, a single-sample test revealed that only in the process-judgment condition with 90% vs. 65% likelihoods was the complex cause chosen significantly more often. Judgments overall were shaped more by perceived probability of success (that an explanation was true or a process would succeed) than by ease of comprehension or number of factors. Probability information had greater weight in process judgments, whereas number of factors mattered more in explanatory choices.

title_r: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 1 and 2 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al. (2024).
abstract_r: People often find information presented in bullet points easier to understand than lengthy prose, and in general prefer simpler explanations over more complex ones. This preference aligns with the principle of Occam’s razor, which holds that unnecessary assumptions should not be introduced, and has been regarded as one of the “explanatory virtues” used to evaluate the quality of explanations. Some have argued that simple explanations are more likely to be true than complex ones. However, it has also been suggested that probability alone cannot fully account for this phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022). Sehl et al. (2024) propose a novel theory that the preference for simplicity is not unique to explanation itself, but rather stems from a broader tendency to favor efficient means of achieving goals. Providing an explanation is a goal-directed activity aimed at understanding the causes of an outcome, and from this perspective, explanations with fewer causes and assumptions can be seen as more efficient. According to this “doing things efficiently” account, the preference for simpler causes should manifest not only when judging why an outcome occurred (explanatory judgments), but also when evaluating how an outcome could be achieved (process judgments). Moreover, the theory predicts that when statistical information about the reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates or likelihood of effect occurrence) is provided, the preference for simplicity may weaken or even reverse. Sehl et al. support these predictions with evidence from seven preregistered experiments. However, participants in prior studies were recruited primarily from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), leaving open questions about the universality of these findings. The present study attempts to replicate Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), focusing on the claim that preferences for simpler explanations result from the pursuit of efficiency. By conducting this replication with Japanese participants, we aim to test the cross-cultural generality of the findings, broaden the scope of the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on potential cultural differences in cognitive processes. In this study, we will try to replicate Sehl et al. (2024)’s Study 1 and 2.

title_r: Does empathy promote helping by activating altruistic motivation or concern about social evaluation? A direct replication of Fultz et al. (1986).
abstract_r: prosocial behavior? And if so, does it activate genuine concern or more self-interested motivations? To rule out the alternative hypothesis that empathy motivates prosocial behavior by generating fear of social disapproval for acting selfishly, Fultz et al. (1986) manipulated empathy for a lonely stranger using perspective-taking instructions; they also manipulated whether subjects believed their decision to help would remain anonymous. However, Fultz et al. conducted their experiment decades ago, with few subjects, and before some potentially important cultural changes in college students' values and social lives. Here, in a preregistered replication with 280 undergraduates, we tested Fultz et al.'s key assertions. The perspective-taking and social evaluation manipulations influenced scores on the manipulation check measures mostly in theory-consistent ways but did not significantly influence helping. Consistent with theory, empathy was positively associated with prosocial behavior. We also found evidence that endorsement of the principle of care reflects genuine concern for needy strangers and that moral identity symbolization reflects a desire to help in order to avoid social disapproval. We consider these results a partially successful replication of key tenets of the empathy-altruism hypothesis, though questions remain about the conditions under which perspective-taking promotes prosocial behavior and about the generalizability of our findings to populations beyond undergraduate women circa 1986. Our results also help illuminate the motivational underpinnings of two individual differences that predicted prosocial behavior in previous research. title_r: Suicides among military conscripts between 1991–2007 in Finland—A descriptive replication study
abstract_r: BACKGROUND: Suicide mortality in Finland particularly among young people remains high, compared with other European countries. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among military conscripts in Finland. AIMS: In this record-based study, we investigated characteristics of all 48 suicides among Finnish conscripts during the period 1991-2007. METHODS: We collected and analyzed healthcare records during military service and medicolegal investigations (medicolegal autopsy) of suicide victims. RESULTS: Of the 48 suicides, 36 (75%) were completed during leave days. Shooting, hanging and jumping were the most common methods used; a service gun was used in four (14%) of the 29 shooting cases. One-third of the victims had been in contact with military healthcare during the week preceding their suicide, and two-thirds during the preceding month. CONCLUSIONS: When conscripts use healthcare services, suicidal thoughts should be actively asked of those conscripts with history of any risk factors for suicidal behavior.

Contrary to expectations, we found no shift in implicit racial evaluations in two close replication attempts (Experiments 1-2). Experiments 3-4 ruled out the possibility of insufficiently strong exemplar valence and subtyping as explanations for the failures to replicate. In Experiment 5, implicit racial evaluations did exhibit malleability in response to two different procedures relying on repeated evaluative pairings and evaluative statements, suggesting that they are capable of change. title_r: A replication and extension of “Task difficulty modulates the disrupting effects of oral respiration on visual search performance” (Yoshimura et al. 2019)
abstract_r: The relationship between breathing and cognition is gaining increasing interest, with nasal breathing linked to greater neurophysiological synchrony compared to oral breathing. This synchrony could impact cognitive functions like attention and memory. Yoshimura et al. (2019) examined whether respiratory pathway (oral vs. nasal) affects visual search performance. In their second experiment, oral breathing combined with reduced target discriminability led to increased reaction time (RT) intercepts compared to nasal breathing, but only in the most difficult search condition. In this pre-registered report, we aim to replicate their RT effects and provide a more sensitive test of respiration effects by examining search efficiency across a wider range of difficulties. Using a within-subjects design, participants will complete a visual search task under oral and nasal breathing conditions, with target-distractor orientation differences ranging from 2° to 6°. This will show whether oral breathing speeds RT under difficult conditions (replicating Yoshimura et al.) and reduces search slopes (extending their findings). By examining both intercept and slope effects, we seek to determine whether oral breathing disrupts pre-search or post-search processing and/or impairs search efficiency. This research contributes to understanding how breathing pathway influences attentional processing during visual search tasks.

title_r: Modeling gender differences in the job promotion process: Replication and extension of Martell et al. (1996).
abstract_r: Differences in employee evaluations due to gender bias may be small in any given rating cycle, but they may accumulate to produce large disparities in the number of women and men promoted to the top of an organization. A highly cited simulation by Martell et al. (1996) demonstrates this cumulative advantage process in a multilevel organization. We replicated this simulation to uncover important details about its operating assumptions, and we extended the simulation to examine a range of variables that may impact the cumulative effects of gender bias. The replication revealed that the male cumulative advantage in the Martell et al. simulation requires (a) decades of typical promotion cycles to produce, (b) constant mean differences in the performance ratings of women and men but equal within-group variances, and (c) attrition that occurs randomly at a low and constant rate. Our extended simulation demonstrates that (a) cumulative effects of gender bias are higher when the attrition rate is lower, (b) gender biases are mitigated when attrition is more strongly associated with good or poor performance, and (c) the cumulative effects of mean gender differences in performance ratings can often be smaller than the cumulative effects of variance differences between gender subgroups. Results suggest that talent development and recognition of high performers might have a greater positive impact on female representation at top levels of a firm than programs aimed at reducing bias in employee evaluations. We encourage additional simulation work that further explores the dynamics of cumulative advantage in employment settings. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2024 APA, all rights reserved).

title_r: The Individual and Situational Factors Predicting Unethical Behaviour in the Workplace: A Direct and Conceptual Replication of Jones & Kavanagh (1996)
abstract_r: Intentions to act unethically in the workplace are purported to be driven by a number of situational and individual factors. Across two seminal vignette experiments, Jones and Kavanagh reported inconsistent effect sizes for manager and peer influence and locus of control, consistent significant effects for work quality and Machiavellianism, and consistent non-significant effects for gender. Using an innovative multi-site collaboration, the current Registered Report represents a direct replication of these experiments (N = 2218), and adds a longitudinal conceptual replication capturing self-reported unethical work behaviour (N = 1747). Both replications found a consistent small effect of having a more external locus of control and male identity, and a consistent moderate effect of machiavellianism, for increasing unethical intentions and behaviour. The situational factors, whilst consistent in direction with that of the original study, varied more substantively in effect size. Our results highlight the value of multi-site collaborations and different replication types in developing conceptual, methodological, measurement and theoretical clarity to ensure future works can progress more rapidly to minimize the negative impacts of unethical workplace behaviour and improve individual’s working lives. All materials, code and data for this project can be found here: osf.io/d3arx.

title_r: Does background color affect moral judgment? Three pre-registered replications of Zarkadi and Schnall’s (2012) Study 1
abstract_r: Do colored backgrounds lead to polarized judgments? Zarkadi and Schnall (2012) found in their Study 1 that, indeed, exposing participants to a black-and-white (versus other colored) background polarized participants’ judgments in a moral dilemma task. This study supported a moral intuitionist model of moral judgment and lent further support to so-called Conceptual Metaphor Theories (Lakoff & Johnson, 1999). We replicated the effect in three high-powered preregistered studies (total N = 846). We successfully replicated the same result of ZS1 in one study (Study 2), but were unable to replicate the effect in two other studies (Studies 1 and 3). A meso-analysis including both our 3 replications and the original study showed no significant effect of background color on moral judgment. We infer that, based on the wide confidence interval of the original study and the lack of evidence in the replication studies, there is no relationship between color of background and polarized judgments. We call for highly-powered within-designs to study the relationship between color and moral judgment. Materials, data, and code available at https://osf.io/8ksqj/.

title_r: Genetic association of missense (rs2919643), intergenic (rs2057178) and a 3’UTR (rs1009170) variant with tuberculosis: A replication study from India
abstract_r: To investigate host genetic susceptibility to tuberculosis (TB), we conducted a replication study focussed on candidate SNPs, previously reported to be associated with TB. We examined nine candidate SNPs and genotyped them in an independent cohort of TB cases and household contacts from West Bengal, India. The association with TB was replicated for rs2919643 (Chr 18), rs2057178 (Chr 11) and rs1009170 (Chr 14). rs2919643-C ( p =8.81E-5) was a risk allele and rs2057178-A ( p =0.04188) was protective against TB in our population. Association of rs1009170; previously reported by us with TB was also replicated in the new set of samples ( p =0.0359). rs2919643 is a missense variant present in linkage disequilibrium with a TB associated synonymous SNP rs61104666. The risk genotype rs2919643-CC was associated with higher levels of plasma RANTES and IL5 in household contacts. rs2919643 is an eQTL for an immunosuppressive gene SIGLEC15 and autophagy related gene EPG5. rs2057178 is an eQTL for a pseudogene and present within weak enhancer marks in the lungs. The genomic locus around this SNP rs1009170 encompasses an active transcription factor peak in CD14 + monocytes and also serves as an eQTL for NDUFB1, ATXN3 and SLC24A4. TB cases with rs1009170-TT genotype showed lower expression of plasma RANTES compared to the heterozygote . All three associated SNPs have putative regulatory role in lungs and immune associated cells and organs which may be relevant to TB pathogenesis. • rs2057178, rs1009170, and rs2919643 were found associated with TB in Indian population. • Intergenic rs2057178-A is protective, while missense rs2919643-C is a risk allele for TB susceptibility. • Genotypes of 3’UTR SNP rs1009170 are linked with differential levels of MCP1 and RANTES in TB patients. • rs2919643 genotype impact levels of IL5 and RANTES in controls, indicating its role in immune regulation. • Association of SNPs with cytokines and chemokines levels, indicate regulation of immune responses.

title_r: The language of lies: A preregistered direct replication of Suchotzki and Gamer (2018; Experiment 2)
abstract_r: Is lying in a different language easier or more difficult? The Emotional Distance and the Cognitive Load hypothesis give competing answers. Suchotzki and Gamer (2018; hereafter SG18) measured the time native German speakers needed to initiate honest and deceptive answers to German and English questions. Lie-truth difference in RTs were smaller in the non-native compared to the native language, d = .97, 95%CI [.58; 1.35]. In our preregistered replication, we tested native Dutch speakers in Dutch and English. While the observed effect was smaller, d = .54 [95% CI: .27, .80], we also found that foreign language use diminishes lie-truth differences in RTs, because primarily truth telling is impeded by foreign language use The findings indicate that non-native speakers struggle with quickly retrieving the truth, hampering lie-truth discrimination for statements in non-native language. Caution should be exerted when judging the credibility of statements given in non-native language.

title_r: Does the Implicit Association Test Predict Suicidal Behavior? Direct Replication of Nock, Park, Finn, Deliberto, Dour, &amp; Banaji (2010)
abstract_r: Recent research suggests that a simple behavioral test, the Suicide-Implicit Association Test (Suicide-IAT; Nock et al., 2010), can reliably predict recent and future suicide attempts. We tested whether we could obtain similar findings in a direct and independent replication. Patients (N = 165) presenting themselves at the psychiatric emergency service of a hospital in France were recruited over a two-year period. We assessed implicit association between self and death/suicide using the Suicide-IAT. Patients also completed the Self Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors Interview and the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation. Six months later, we contacted patients by phone and examined their hospital medical records to determine if new suicide attempts had occurred. The results showed that the Suicide-IAT did not discriminate between patients with and without recent suicide attempt. However, as in the original study, the Suicide-IAT predicted suicide attempts at 6-month follow-up. The test correctly classified 83.5% of patients.

title_r: Does Willpower Mindset Really Moderate the Ego-Depletion Effect? A Preregistered Direct Replication of Job, Dweck, and Walton's (2010) Study 1
abstract_r: This article reports a preregistered study in which we attempted to directly replicate an influential study on the ego-depletion effect conducted by Job, Dweck, and Walton (2010, Study 1, N=60). As in the original study, participants (N=187) performed a self-control task (Stroop color-word interference task) after performing the control or depletion version of a letter-cancelation task. Despite extensive analyses, we failed to reproduce Job et al.’s (2010) key findings: (a) a significant main effect of ego depletion (i.e., worse Stroop performance in the depletion condition than in the control condition) and (b) a significant moderation of this ego-depletion effect by individual differences in willpower mindset (i.e., primarily individuals holding the belief that willpower is limited demonstrate the ego-depletion effect). These results suggest that the willpower-mindset moderation effect proposed by Job et al. (2010) may not be as robust as initially suggested or may be applicable under more circumscribed situations.

title_r: Strong evidence for expectation adaptation during language understanding, not a replication failure. A reply to Harrington Stack, James, and Watson (2018)
abstract_r: Recent input affects subsequent language processing. One explanation for this holds that comprehenders adapt their implicit linguistic expectations based on the input, so as to facilitate efficient processing. A number of studies have identified support for this hypothesis. Harrington Stack, James, and Watson (2018) report a failure to replicate one of these studies (Fine, Jaeger, Farmer, and Qian, 2013). We show that, to the contrary, the data from Harrington Stack and colleagues constitute strong support for the hypothesis of expectation adaptation. Several factors contribute to the difference in conclusions. For example, Harrington Stack and colleagues argue based on differences in p-values, which is known to be problematic. We instead employ well-formed Bayesian measures of evidentiary support to assess replication success. Most critically though, the new experiments by Harrington Stack and colleagues differ in design from the experiments they aim to replicate. We correct for these differences by means of the same single-parameter belief-updating model previously employed by Fine and colleagues. The model provides trial-level predictions for the surprisal that comprehenders experience, based on previous input within and outside of the experiment. Trial-level analyses find that surprisal based on adapted expectations strongly predicts reading times in both the original and the replication data. In fact, once the differences in design are corrected for, the two data are highly similar; replication tests estimate the posterior probability of a replication success to be ≫ .9999. We show how the same belief-updating model also predicts trial-to-trial priming, cumulative priming, and the inverse preference effect in priming.

title_r: Perceptual Learning and Individual Differences in Auditory Processing [Replication and extension of Kraljic, Samuel, & Brennan (2008)]
abstract_r: Understanding spoken language is a complex process that comes to most people easily, yet past research demonstrates that some people face difficulties with auditory processing. Listeners integrate auditory, visual, and other cues to understand speech. However, people with auditory processing difficulties rely less on visual cues, such as lip-reading. We investigated how listeners' reported difficulties in perceiving auditory information interact with their use of visual cues. This was a replication and extension of a study by Kraljic, Samuel, and Brennan (2008). Participants viewed a speaker pronouncing some words in one of four conditions, depending on which phoneme was changed (?S or ?SH) and whether the speaker held a pen-in-hand (characteristic) or had a pen-in-mouth (incidental) while producing these words. We assessed each participant’s phonemic boundaries in a category-identification task, in which participants categorized ambiguous sounds as being more S-like or SH-like. We measured participants' perceptual learning—the restructuring of their phonemic boundaries—based on their categorization of these ambiguous sounds. Afterward, participants were surveyed on their language background and their auditory processing difficulties. We did not replicate the findings on the effect of visual context on perceptual learning from the original study by Kraljic et al. (2008). Contrary to our predictions, we also did not find an effect of individual differences in auditory processing on perceptual learning and no interaction with visual context. Given that the effect of visual context has been replicated before, our results are inconclusive. The effect of individual differences on perceptual learning should be explored further to gain insight into the underpinnings of perceptual learning and how to improve speech perception for those with auditory difficulties. We used videos created for a replication by Babel (2016), modelled after the original videos of Kraljic et al. (2008). We link to Babel's OSF repository under project components.

title_r: Reply to Nicholas et al. Using a ResNet-18 network to detect features of Alzheimer’s disease on functional magnetic resonance imaging: a failed replication. Comment on “Odusami et al. Analysis of features of Alzheimer’s disease: detection of early stage from functional brain changes in magnetic resonance images using a finetuned ResNet18 Network. Diagnostics 2021, 11, 1071” /
abstract_r: We have studied the manuscript of Nicholas et al. [1] very attentively; here are our comments: The authors have used a different dataset (ADNI-3, rather than ADNI-2 used in [2]). The protocols of ADNI-2 and ADNI-3 datasets are not fully consistent [3]. The ADNI MR data set includes a wide range of scanner platforms; however, there has been a broad gap between older MRI systems and the state-of-the-art systems within each vendor’s product line. In ADNI-3, the “ADNI 3 Basic” and “ADNI 3 Advanced” protocols were used. The authors failed to mention if the images they used were made using a protocol compatible with ADNI-2. The dMRI spatial resolution was improved between ADNI-2 and ADNI-3 by reducing the voxel size from 2.7 x 2.7 x 2.7 mm to 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm [4]. This may have influenced the results. Moreover, the classification results among these studies are not directly comparable, because they differ in terms of the sets of participants. We fully agree that the replication of important findings by multiple independent investigators is fundamental to the accumulation of scientific evidence [5]. Deep learning network models are notoriously known for being difficult to replicate, even if the same sets of parameters are used. The training of neural network models is not deterministic, so the models are likely to produce differing results [6]. The strive of the authors to precisely replicate the results may not be achievable. [...].

title_r: ERIC ED341931: Organization-Based Self-Esteem among Mental Health Workers: A Replication and Extension.
abstract_r: In the field of human resources management, self-esteem has been one of the most researched personality variables. Recently, the construct of organization-based self-esteem also has come under investigation. Organization-based self-esteem is defined as "the degree to which organizational members believe that they can satisfy their needs by participating in roles within the context of an organization." This study was conducted to further validate and explore the construct validity of a scale developed to measure organization-based self-esteem. Mental health workers (N=155) from the Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation in the State of Tennessee completed the organization-based self-esteem scale and provided information on demographic, personality, and organizational variables. The results of a step-wise multiple regression analysis showed that organization-based self-esteem was related to subjects' global self-esteem, need for achievement, organizational citizenship, organizational commitment, motivating potential score, and education. Subject status in the organization (direct care employee, administrative staff, managerial personnel) was not related to organization-based self-esteem. The findings suggest that organization-based self-esteem is related to many variables that are intrinsic to the employees' subjective feelings in an organization. (Author/NB)

We are interested in seeing if the finding that men who are high in the likelihood to sexually aggress are more likely to find a woman more attractive if they have been primed with power, can be replicated. We also want to extend the research further to see if this relationship means that men would engage in sexually aggressive behaviour towards the female. In order to manipulate power, we will be using a word-fragment completion task using power-related words (as used in the original study). Participants will be exposed to a female confederate and asked to rate them on a series of attributes, including attractiveness. They will also be asked if they would like future contact with the confederate (through a skype call). We will be using a sexual aggression paradigm as a proxy for sexual aggression (described in the dependent variables section). To measure the likelihood to sexually aggress, we will be using the attraction to sexual aggression scale (Malamuth, 1989).

title_r: Do Institutional Characteristics Predict Markers of Adulthood? A Close Replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016)
abstract_r: Recent research reveals that some variability in personality differences can be explained by contextual factors such as location. Though little research has systematically evaluated how such variables predict individual differences in Emerging Adulthood, Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) revealed that characteristics of one's university such as selectivity and liberal arts classification did predict respondents' perceived importance and attainment of milestones associated with adulthood. As a close replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016), the present findings supported our pre-registered hypotheses that liberal arts status predicted decreased perceived importance and lower attainment of some constructs of Markers of Adulthood, but did not support predictions that selectivity would also predict such differences. Our findings provide further evidence of the institutional effects that emerge in multi-sample individual difference studies and extends those findings with a broader and more diverse sample than was considered previously.

title_r: Dataset used in the publication : "The power of social influence: A replication and extension of the Asch experiment" by Axel Franzen and Sebastian Mader (PLOS ONE 2023)
abstract_r: In this paper, we pursue four goals: First, we replicate the original Asch experiment with five confederates and one naïve subject in each group (N = 210). Second, in a randomized trial we incentivize the decisions in the line experiment and demonstrate that monetary incentives lower the error rate, but that social influence is still at work. Third, we confront subjects with different political statements and show that the power of social influence can be generalized to matters of political opinion. Finally, we investigate whether intelligence, self-esteem, the need for social approval, and the Big Five are related to the susceptibility to provide conforming answers. We find an error rate of 33% for the standard length-of-line experiment which replicates the original findings by Asch (1951, 1955, 1956). Furthermore, in the incentivized condition the error rate decreases to 25%. For political opinions we find a conformity rate of 38%. However, besides openness, none of the investigated personality traits are convincingly related to the susceptibility of group pressure.

title_r: Multiple Aspects and Correlates of Body Figure Ratings: A Replication and Extension of Fallon and Rozin (1985)
abstract_r: College females, using a set of nine figure drawings reflecting very thin to very heavy figures, rated their current figure (based on how they thought they looked versus how they felt), ideal figure, how they appeared to others, and the figure they deemed most attractive to men. A subsample of the 123 subjects also completed measures of body satisfaction, depression, eating disturbance, teasing, and noted the age of menarche. The results replicated and extended the findings of Fallon and Rozin (1985), who found that ideal figures were smaller than ratings of current size. Additionally, there was a significant difference between the two protocols for current size, indicating that subjects rated their size as larger when asked to rate based on affective instructions. Figure ratings based on cognitive/rational instructions did not differ from those based on how they conceptualized others' views of their bodies. Significant correlations were observed among figure ratings, body satisfaction, eating disturbance, depression, and teasing. The need to focus on etiological mechanisms of disturbed body image and eating behavior is addressed, and the role of teasing as a possible precipitant is examined.

title_r: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper, 1988
abstract_r: According to the facial feedback hypothesis, people’s affective responses can be influenced by their own facial expression (e.g., smiling, pouting), even when their expression did not result from their emotional experiences. For example, Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) instructed participants to rate the funniness of cartoons using a pen that they held in their mouth. In line with the facial feedback hypothesis, when participants held the pen with their teeth (inducing a “smile”), they rated the cartoons as funnier than when they held the pen with their lips (inducing a “pout”). This seminal study of the facial feedback hypothesis has not been replicated directly. This Registered Replication Report describes the results of 17 independent direct replications of Study 1 from Strack et al. (1988), all of which followed the same vetted protocol. A meta-analysis of these studies examined the difference in funniness ratings between the “smile” and “pout” conditions. The original Strack et al. (1988) study reported a rating difference of 0.82 units on a 10-point Likert scale. Our meta-analysis revealed a rating difference of 0.03 units with a 95% confidence interval ranging from −0.11 to 0.16. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title_r: No Evidence that Experiencing Physical Warmth Promotes Interpersonal Warmth: Two Failures to Replicate Williams and Bargh (2008)
abstract_r: Williams and Bargh (2008) reported that holding a hot cup of coffee caused participants to judge a person’s personality as warmer, and that holding a therapeutic heat pad caused participants to choose rewards for other people rather than for themselves. These experiments featured large effects (r = .28 and .31), small sample sizes (41 and 53 participants), and barely statistically significant results. We attempted to replicate both experiments in field settings with more than triple the sample sizes (128 and 177) and double-blind procedures, but found near-zero effects (r = –.03 and .02). In both cases, Bayesian analyses suggest there is substantially more evidence for the null hypothesis of no effect than for the original physical warmth priming hypothesis.

title_r: Defaults versus framing: Revisiting Default Effect and Framing Effect with a replication and extension of Johnson and Goldstein (2003) and Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse (2002)
abstract_r: People tend to stick with a default option instead of switching to another option. For instance, Johnson and Goldstein (2003) found a default effect in an organ donation scenario: if organ donation is the default option, people are more inclined to consent to it. Johnson et al. (2002) found a similar default effect in health-survey scenarios: if receiving more information about your health is the default, people are more inclined to consent to it. Much of the highly cited, impactful work on these default effects, however, has not been replicated in well-powered samples. In two well-powered samples (N = 1920), we conducted a close replication of the default effect in Johnson and Goldstein (2003) and in Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse (2002). We successfully replicated Johnson and Goldstein (2003). In an extension of the original findings, we also show that default effects are unaffected by the permanence of these selections. We, however, failed to replicate the findings of Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse’s (2002) study; we did not find evidence for a default effect. We did, however, find a framing effect: participants who read a positively-framed scenario consented to receive health-related information at a higher rate than participants who read a negatively framed scenario. We also conducted a conceptual replication of Johnson et al. (2002) that was based on an organ-donation scenario, but this attempt failed to find a default effect. Our results suggest that default effects depend on framing and context. Materials, data, and code are available on: https://osf.io/8wd2b/.

title_r: Does Willpower Mindset Really Moderate the Ego-Depletion Effect? A Preregistered Direct Replication of Job, Dweck, and Walton's (2010) Study 1
abstract_r: This article reports a preregistered study in which we attempted to directly replicate an influential study on the ego-depletion effect conducted by Job, Dweck, and Walton (2010, Study 1, N=60). As in the original study, participants (N=187) performed a self-control task (Stroop color-word interference task) after performing the control or depletion version of a letter-cancelation task. Despite extensive analyses, we failed to reproduce Job et al.’s (2010) key findings: (a) a significant main effect of ego depletion (i.e., worse Stroop performance in the depletion condition than in the control condition) and (b) a significant moderation of this ego-depletion effect by individual differences in willpower mindset (i.e., primarily individuals holding the belief that willpower is limited demonstrate the ego-depletion effect). These results suggest that the willpower-mindset moderation effect proposed by Job et al. (2010) may not be as robust as initially suggested or may be applicable under more circumscribed situations.

title_r: More or Less Violence in Schools? A Replication Study from 1996-2014 in Saxon Schools
abstract_r: Der verbreiteten Annahme einer ständigen Gewaltzunahme an Schulen stehen bisher nur wenige Studien im Zeitvergleich gegenüber. Der vorliegende Beitrag will diese Lücke schließen, indem er Ergebnisse einer aktuellen Replikationsstudie vorstellt und damit die Frage beantwortet, ob die Gewalt an Schulen im Vergleich zur Mitte der 1990er Jahre zu- oder abgenommen hat. Anhand einer repräsentativen sächsischen Stichprobe zeigt sich, dass im Jahr 2014 im Vergleich zu 1996 über weniger Gewalt an Schulen berichtet wird. Dies betrifft die Gewalt unter Schü ler(inne)n und die Gewalt gegen Lehrkräfte. Parallel hat die Interventionsbereitschaft unter der Lehrer- und Schülerschaft zugenommen. Zugleich macht die Studie auf differente Entwicklungstrends zwischen den Schülergruppen aufmerksam. Trotz eines insgesamt niedrigen Gewaltniveaus im Vergleich zur Mitte der 1990er Jahre legen die Befunde den Schluss nahe, bei den Präventionsbemühungen nicht nachzulassen. Veryfew studies have investigated the widely held assumption that violence in schools has constantly increased in recent years. The current study aims to fill this gap by presenting results of a recent replication study in Germany, as well as answering the question as to whether violence in schools increased or decreased in comparison with the mid-1990s. Based on a representative sample of Saxon students, this study shows that less violence was reported in schools in 2014 compared to 1996. This relates to both violence among students and their violent actions against teachers. Moreover, the willingness of teachers and students to intervene has increased. At the same time, this study draws attention to developmental trends between groups of students. Despite a general low level of violence in schools compared to the mid-1990s, the findings suggest that prevention efforts must be continued.
